tip: Ask the butcher to mince a lean leg of lamb. It keeps the moussaka light and not greasy.
ingredients: for the two portions, 1 jumbo egg

name: Roast trout with tomatoes, olives and lemony greens
inspiredBy: Greek plaki, fish baked with tomato, garlic and olive oil
about: Trout fillets roasted on a bed of cherry tomatoes, olives, capers and garlic, served with kale braised until silky in lemon and olive oil, the way Greek horta are served. It is a Greek-island plaki dinner, and the trout brings **omega-3 and vitamin D** while the kale adds calcium and vitamin C.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Rinse the olives and capers under cold water and pat them dry. Toss the tomatoes, onion, sliced garlic, olives and capers on a tray with about half the olive oil, the oregano and a pinch of salt.
Roast for 10 minutes, until the tomatoes start to burst.
Pat the trout dry, rub it with a little olive oil, salt and pepper, and lay the fillets skin side up on the tomatoes.
Roast another 8 to 10 minutes, until the skin is blistered and the flesh flakes easily.

While it cooks, strip the kale from its stems and chop it. Warm a little olive oil in a pan with a splash of water and cook the kale with a pinch of salt until silky, about 6 minutes. Take it off the heat and dress with half the lemon juice and the rest of the olive oil.
Plate the kale, then the trout and tomatoes, and spoon the tomato juices over the fish. Finish with parsley and the remaining lemon.
ingredients: leaves only, most of a small bunch

name: Warm olives with rosemary and hazelnuts
inspiredBy: Spanish tapas bar olives and nuts
about: Black olives and whole hazelnuts warmed in olive oil with rosemary and a squeeze of lemon, which makes them taste like a bar snack in Catalonia. The hazelnuts give you **vitamin E and magnesium** with very few carbs.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a small pan over medium heat. Add the hazelnuts and rosemary and toast for 2 minutes, stirring, until the hazelnuts smell nutty.
Add the rinsed olives and warm through for 1 minute.
Tip into a bowl and squeeze a little lemon over the top.

name: Garlic mushrooms with parsley and lemon
inspiredBy: Spanish champiñones al ajillo
about: Mushrooms sautéed hard in olive oil until golden, then tossed with sizzling garlic, parsley and a squeeze of lemon. It is a classic Spanish tapa, and mushrooms are a surprisingly good source of **B vitamins and potassium**.
steps: Heat the olive oil in a wide frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms in one layer with a pinch of salt and cook, without stirring too much, until golden, about 6 minutes.
Add the garlic and Aleppo pepper and cook for 30 seconds, just until fragrant.
Take the pan off the heat and toss with parsley and a squeeze of lemon.

name: Avocado with lemon, olive oil and oregano
inspiredBy: Spanish and Greek avocado with lemon, olive oil and herbs
about: A whole ripe avocado, halved and dressed with generous olive oil, lemon, oregano and Aleppo pepper. It is simple and creamy, and avocado is a great source of **potassium, folate and fibre**.
steps: Halve the avocado and remove the stone.
Drizzle with the lemon juice and olive oil, then sprinkle over the oregano, Aleppo pepper and a pinch of salt.
Eat it straight from the skin with a spoon.

name: Olive and caper tapenade with cucumber dippers
inspiredBy: Provençal and Ligurian olive tapenade
about: A coarse tapenade of black olives, capers, garlic and lemon, scooped up with crunchy cucumber. The olives and olive oil are the Mediterranean fats at their purest, and they bring **vitamin E**.
steps: Rinse the olives and capers under cold water and pat them dry. Chop them with the garlic and parsley until they make a coarse paste, or pulse them a few times in a food processor.
Stir in the lemon juice, olive oil and pepper.
Cut the cucumber into dippers and serve with the tapenade.

name: Raspberries and walnuts with cinnamon
inspiredBy: Greek fruit and walnuts, without the honey
about: Juicy raspberries with a handful of toasted walnuts and a pinch of cinnamon. It is sweet-tart and crunchy, with plant omega-3 from the walnuts and plenty of **fibre** from the berries.
steps: Toast the walnuts in a dry pan over medium heat until fragrant, about 2 minutes.
Put the raspberries in a bowl, add the warm walnuts and dust with cinnamon.

name: Toasted hazelnuts with rosemary and lemon
inspiredBy: Spanish and Piedmontese toasted hazelnuts
about: Whole hazelnuts toasted in a dry pan until golden and fragrant, then tossed with rosemary, a pinch of salt and a squeeze of lemon. Hazelnuts are grown across Spain and Italy, and a small handful gives you **vitamin E, magnesium and healthy fats** with hardly any carbs.
steps: Toast the hazelnuts in a dry pan over medium heat, shaking now and then, until golden and fragrant, about 4 minutes.
Take the pan off the heat and toss with the olive oil, rosemary and salt.
Add a squeeze of lemon and let them cool for a couple of minutes so they crunch.

name: Avocado filled with tuna and lemon
inspiredBy: Spanish and Italian tuna with avocado and lemon
about: A ripe avocado half filled with flaked tuna, lemon, parsley and a drizzle of olive oil. It is rich, creamy and filling, with **protein and potassium** in one easy bite.
steps: Halve the avocado and remove the stone.
Flake the tuna with the lemon juice, chopped parsley, olive oil, pepper and a pinch of salt.
Pile the tuna into the hollow of the avocado and eat with a spoon.

name: Poached shrimp with lemon and smoked paprika
inspiredBy: Spanish gambas cocidas
about: Shrimp poached in a pot of lemony water for a couple of minutes, then tossed with olive oil, smoked paprika and parsley and eaten cold, like a plate of Spanish gambas cocidas. It is a cold plate of shrimp to pick at, with plenty of **protein** for almost no carbs.
steps: Bring a small pot of salted water to a boil with a squeeze of the lemon.
Add the shrimp and cook until pink and curled, about 2 minutes. Drain and cool under cold water.
Toss with the olive oil, paprika, parsley and the rest of the lemon juice.
tip: Look for shrimp with no added salt or phosphate.

name: Tuna-stuffed eggs with capers and parsley
inspiredBy: Spanish huevos rellenos de atún
about: Hard-boiled egg halves filled with a creamy mash of the yolk, flaked tuna, capers, parsley and lemon, a classic Spanish tapa. It is a small, salty, filling snack, and the egg and tuna bring **choline and protein**.
steps: Lower the egg into boiling water and cook for 9 minutes. Cool it under cold water, then peel and halve lengthwise.
Pop out the yolk and mash it with the drained tuna, chopped capers, parsley, lemon juice and olive oil until creamy.
Spoon the filling back into the whites and dust with the paprika.

name: Marinated olives with oregano, garlic and lemon
inspiredBy: Greek meze marinated olives
about: Black olives tossed with olive oil, a little garlic, oregano and lemon and left to sit for a few minutes, the way every meze table in Greece starts. They are salty, fruity and satisfying, and a handful of olives is a classic Mediterranean source of **healthy fats and vitamin E**.
steps: Rinse the olives under cold water, pat them dry and put them in a small bowl.
Add the olive oil, lemon juice, finely grated garlic, oregano and chopped parsley, and toss well.
Leave them to marinate for 10 minutes if you can, then eat with a fork or toothpicks.

name: Almonds fried in olive oil with pimentón
inspiredBy: Spanish almendras fritas
about: Whole almonds fried in olive oil until golden, then tossed with smoked paprika and a pinch of salt, the kind of snack a Spanish bar puts out with a glass of sherry. They are warm, crunchy and rich, and bring **vitamin E and magnesium**.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a small frying pan over medium heat.
Add the almonds and fry, stirring, for about 3 minutes, until they are golden and smell toasty.
Tip them and the oil onto a plate, toss with the pimentón and salt, and let them cool for a couple of minutes so they crisp up.

name: Shakshuka with kale and parsley, and sliced avocado
inspiredBy: the shakshuka of Tunisia and Libya, now cooked all over the Levant, with kale folded into the sauce and avocado in place of the bread
about: Eggs poached in a cumin and paprika tomato sauce thick with sweet red pepper and a good handful of kale, with cool avocado on the side for the yolk. It is a favourite Middle Eastern breakfast, minus the bread, and the eggs and kale bring **choline, calcium and vitamin K** before nine in the morning.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a wide, deep frying pan over medium heat. Cook the onion and red pepper until soft, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the garlic, cumin, paprika and Aleppo pepper and cook for 30 seconds, until it smells toasty.
Add the tomato, a splash of water, the salt and the pepper. Simmer for 8 to 10 minutes, until the tomato has broken down and the sauce is thick but still saucy.
Stir in the kale and cook until it wilts and turns bright green, about 3 minutes.
Make a dip in the sauce for each egg with the back of a spoon and crack the eggs in. Cover and cook over low heat until the whites are set and the yolks are still a little wobbly, 5 to 6 minutes.
Scatter the parsley over the pan. Slice the avocado alongside and squeeze the lemon over it.
tip: Cook the tomato sauce (without the kale and eggs) in a big batch on Sunday. It keeps for 4 days, and a weekday shakshuka is then ready in 10 minutes.

name: Turkish poached egg on garlic yogurt with Aleppo pepper oil and a crisp cucumber salad
inspiredBy: Turkish çılbır, poached egg on garlicky yogurt, with olive oil in place of the butter and a cucumber salad in place of the bread
about: A soft poached egg on a cool bed of thick garlic yogurt, with a spoonful of warm olive oil blushed red with Aleppo pepper and fresh dill. A crunchy cucumber and radish salad with olives sits alongside. It is ready in 10 minutes, and the egg and thick yogurt bring **protein, choline and calcium**.
steps: Stir the yogurt with the grated garlic and a pinch of the salt. Spread it on a shallow plate and let it come to room temperature while you cook the egg.

Bring a deep pan of water to a bare simmer. Crack each egg into its own cup, swirl the water gently and slide them in one at a time. Poach for 3 minutes, until the whites are set and the yolks are runny.
Meanwhile, toss the cucumber, radish, parsley and olives with the lemon juice and the rest of the salt.
Warm the olive oil in a small pan for about 1 minute, until it shimmers, then take it off the heat and stir in the Aleppo pepper so it turns brick red.
Lift the egg (or eggs) out with a slotted spoon, blot on a towel and set on the yogurt. Spoon the hot pepper oil over, scatter with the dill and serve with the salad.
tip: No Aleppo pepper? A pinch of paprika with a pinch of chili flakes does the same job.

name: Labneh plate with a soft-boiled egg, za'atar oil, olives and cucumber
inspiredBy: the Levantine morning labneh plate, with a soft-boiled egg as on a Turkish kahvaltı table and no bread, with chia stirred through for fibre
about: A thick swoop of labneh under a pool of olive oil and za'atar, with a soft-boiled egg, peppery arugula, cool cucumber and tomato, plenty of olives and fresh mint, with a spoon of chia stirred through the labneh for a little texture. It is how a Lebanese breakfast looks, minus the bread. The egg, labneh and chia bring **choline, calcium and fibre**.
steps: Lower the egg (or eggs) into boiling water and cook for 6 minutes for a jammy yolk. Cool under cold water, then peel.

Stir the chia seeds and a spoonful of water into the labneh and let it stand for 5 minutes, so the seeds soften. (Stir it together the night before if you like it smoother.) Spread it on a plate with the back of a spoon, leaving a little dip in the middle.
Stir the za'atar into the olive oil and pour it into the dip.
Arrange the arugula, cucumber, tomato, radish and olives around it and set the egg halves on the labneh. Scatter with the mint and squeeze the lemon over the vegetables.
tip: Labneh is sold at Middle Eastern shops and many supermarkets. If you can't find it, strain thick plain yogurt in a cloth overnight.

name: Sumac beef on a bread-free fattoush with avocado
inspiredBy: Lebanese fattoush without the fried pita, with seared beef on top
about: Thin slices of seared beef over a big, sharp fattoush of romaine, kale, arugula, cucumber, tomato, radish and mint, dressed with plenty of lemon, olive oil and sumac, with creamy avocado alongside. The crunch comes from the radish and cucumber instead of fried bread. The salad is full of **vitamin C, folate and calcium**.
steps: Toss the sliced beef with half the sumac, a pinch of salt and the pepper. Heat a third of the olive oil in a heavy frying pan over high heat and sear the beef in two batches, about 1 minute per side, until browned but still a little pink inside. Set aside.
For the dressing, whisk the rest of the olive oil with the lemon juice, the rest of the sumac and a pinch of salt.
Rub the kale with a spoonful of the dressing for a minute to soften it. Toss it with the romaine, arugula, cucumber, tomato, radish, parsley and mint and the rest of the dressing.
Pile the salad onto a plate and lay the beef and the avocado cubes over it.
tip: Slicing the beef very thin while it is half frozen is easiest.
ingredients: lean round steak, sliced thin against the grain
stems removed, leaves very thinly sliced

name: Circassian chicken in walnut and garlic sauce, on crisp romaine
inspiredBy: Turkish çerkez tavuğu, poached chicken in a rich walnut sauce, here without the bread that usually thickens it
about: Tender poached chicken breast shredded into a creamy walnut and garlic sauce, served cool over crisp romaine with cucumber and radish and a drizzle of red paprika oil. It is a Turkish and Syrian celebration dish that eats beautifully cold, and it makes two portions. The walnuts bring **plant omega-3, copper and magnesium**.
steps: Put the chicken in a pot with the onion chunk, bay leaf, a pinch of the salt and enough water to cover. Bring to a gentle simmer and poach for 14 to 16 minutes, until cooked through. Lift the chicken out and keep about 1 cup (250 ml) of the broth.

While it cooks, toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 3 minutes, until fragrant. Let them cool, then blitz them in a food processor with the garlic, lemon juice, the rest of the salt then add the warm broth a spoonful at a time until you have a thick, creamy sauce, like hummus.
Shred the chicken into thick pieces with two forks and toss it with about two thirds of the walnut sauce.
Warm the olive oil with the paprika and Aleppo pepper in a small pan for 30 seconds, until it turns a deep red.
Arrange the romaine, cucumber and radish on a plate. Pile the chicken on top, spoon over the rest of the sauce, drizzle with the red oil and scatter with the parsley and the pepper.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. It is meant to be eaten cool or at room temperature, with the greens packed separately.
tip: Cooked chicken keeps well, so you can poach it on Sunday. Save the broth for soup.
ingredients: a chunk, for the poaching water

name: Chicken shawarma lettuce bowls with garlic-tahini sauce, avocado and pickles
inspiredBy: Lebanese and Syrian chicken shawarma, served over crisp romaine with the pickles and garlic sauce but no flatbread
about: Thinly sliced chicken marinated in lemon, garlic and warm spices, roasted until the edges char, then piled over crunchy romaine with cucumber, tomato, pickles, avocado and a punchy garlic and tahini sauce. It makes two portions, so tomorrow's lunch is done. The chicken, tahini and parsley bring **protein, magnesium and calcium**.
steps: Mix the sliced chicken with the olive oil, half the lemon juice, half the garlic (crushed), the baharat, cumin, turmeric, cinnamon, salt and pepper. Marinate for at least 30 minutes, or up to a day in the fridge.

Heat the oven to 230°C (450°F) and line a tray with parchment. Spread the chicken out in one layer and roast for 12 to 15 minutes, turning once, until cooked through and charred at the edges. For a more shawarma-like char, finish it for 2 minutes under the broiler.
Whisk the tahini with the rest of the garlic (crushed), the rest of the lemon and enough cold water to make a pourable sauce. It should look like thin cream. Season with a pinch of salt.
Toss the red onion with the sumac and a pinch of salt and let it sit for a few minutes to soften.
Build the bowls: romaine first, then the cucumber, tomato, pickles and parsley, then the chicken, sumac onions and sliced avocado. Spoon the sauce over.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the sauce, the avocado and the tomato in separate containers. Reheat the chicken in a hot pan for 2 minutes and add the sauce cold.
tip: Slice the breasts thin and don't overcook them. Boneless thighs stay juicier overnight.
ingredients: half for the marinade, half for the sauce

name: Lemon and paprika chicken şiş on cauliflower and kale tabbouleh with lemon-tahini
inspiredBy: Turkish tavuk şiş, the grilled chicken skewers, over a Lebanese-style tabbouleh with finely chopped raw cauliflower and kale in place of the bulgur
about: Juicy chicken marinated in lemon, garlic and paprika, grilled until charred at the edges and set over a bright, mostly-parsley tabbouleh with finely chopped cauliflower and kale for body and a generous ribbon of lemon-tahini. It is a fresh, sharp lunch, and the parsley, kale and cauliflower bring **vitamin C, vitamin K and calcium**.
steps: Mix the chicken with the garlic, half the lemon juice, a third of the olive oil, the paprika, Aleppo pepper, cumin and half the salt. Leave it for 1 hour, or up to a day in the fridge.

Mix the cauliflower, parsley, kale, mint, cucumber and red onion in a bowl. Dress with most of the remaining lemon juice, half the remaining olive oil and the rest of the salt. Leave it for 10 minutes so the cauliflower and kale soften a little.

Thread the chicken onto skewers. Heat a grill or a heavy pan over medium-high heat with the last of the olive oil and cook the skewers for 10 to 12 minutes, turning. Pull them off the heat the moment the juices run clear.
Whisk the tahini with the last of the lemon juice and enough cold water, about 1 tablespoon, to make a pourable sauce.
Spoon the tabbouleh onto a plate, set the chicken on top and drizzle with the tahini sauce.
tip: Cut the cauliflower by pulsing it in a food processor, a few short bursts, so it doesn't turn to mush. For a packed lunch, grill the skewers the night before and keep the tahini sauce separate.
ingredients: boneless, skinless breasts, cut in chunks
half for the marinade, the rest for the tabbouleh and sauce
stems removed, leaves very finely sliced

name: Beef-stuffed eggplant with tomato, peppers and lemony kale
inspiredBy: Turkish karnıyarık, the "split belly" eggplant stuffed with spiced beef, tomato and pepper, with walnuts in the filling as in a Turkish içli köfte, and garlicky greens in place of the pilaf
about: Silky roasted eggplant halves split open and filled with a savoury beef, onion, tomato and pepper mixture with toasted walnuts, baked in a little tomato sauce and served with a pile of garlicky sautéed kale. It is a classic Turkish family dish, and it makes two portions, so tomorrow's lunch is ready. The eggplant and kale bring **fibre, calcium and potassium**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Score the cut side of each eggplant half in a crisscross, brush with about a third of the olive oil and season with salt. Roast cut side up on a lined tray for 25 minutes, until soft and golden.
Meanwhile, toast the walnuts in a dry pan until fragrant, about 3 minutes, and set them aside.
Warm half the remaining olive oil in a large pan and cook the onion and red pepper until soft, about 6 minutes. Add half the garlic, then the beef, and break it up. Brown it well, about 7 minutes.
Stir in the tomato paste, paprika, Aleppo pepper, diced tomato, pepper and a splash of water. Simmer for 5 to 6 minutes, until thick. Stir in the parsley, walnuts and half the lemon juice.

Press the middle of each roasted eggplant half down with a spoon to make a boat. Mound in as much filling as the boats will hold and spoon the rest around them, top each with a slice of tomato and pour about 1/4 cup (60 ml) of water into the tray around them.
Bake for 20 minutes, until the eggplant is meltingly soft and the tops are lightly browned.

While it bakes, warm the last of the olive oil in a wide pan, add the rest of the garlic, sliced, and stir for 30 seconds. Add the kale with a splash of water and a pinch of salt, cover and cook for 5 minutes, until tender. Finish with the rest of the lemon juice.
Serve two eggplant halves and their filling per person with the kale. Keep the second for tomorrow's lunch; it reheats well and keeps for 3 days.
tip: Salting the eggplant isn't necessary. Roasting it face up gives it the soft, sweet texture without extra oil. Roast the eggplant halves on Sunday and the filling comes together in 25 minutes.
ingredients: lean round steak, minced by the butcher or ground in a food processor
1 small, slim eggplant per person (Japanese or Italian), halved lengthwise
diced, with a thin slice kept back for each eggplant half

name: Gulf-style grilled sea bass with spiced cauliflower rice and dakkous
inspiredBy: Gulf grilled fish with baharat, machboos-style spiced rice made from cauliflower, and the tomato-garlic chili sauce called dakkous, finished with toasted nuts the way machboos is
about: Sea bass fillets rubbed with baharat and lemon, grilled until the skin crisps, over cauliflower cooked with cardamom, cinnamon, turmeric and loomi in the style of a machboos, with wilted spinach, toasted hazelnuts and a hot, garlicky tomato dakkous. The fish, cauliflower and spinach bring **selenium, vitamin C and folate**.
steps: Toast the hazelnuts in a dry pan for 3 minutes, until golden, and chop them roughly. Mix a third of the olive oil with half the lemon juice, half the garlic (crushed), the baharat, a pinch of salt and the pepper. Rub it over the fish and leave it for 15 minutes.

Make the dakkous. Chop the tomato, serrano, the rest of the garlic and the cilantro very finely together on a board, or pound them in a mortar, then stir in the cumin, the rest of the lemon juice and a pinch of salt. It should be a coarse, juicy sauce.
Warm half the remaining olive oil in a wide pan and cook the onion until soft, about 4 minutes. Add the cardamom, cinnamon, turmeric and loomi and stir for 20 seconds.
Add the cauliflower and a pinch of salt. Cook, stirring, for 5 to 6 minutes, until just tender but with a little bite. Add the spinach and cook for 1 minute more, until it wilts.
Heat a grill pan, a heavy frying pan or the grill to high. Cook the fish skin side down for 4 to 5 minutes without moving it, until the skin is crisp, then flip for 1 to 2 minutes more.
Serve the fish over the cauliflower rice, scattered with the hazelnuts, with the dakkous, and a small salad of arugula and cucumber dressed with the last of the olive oil and a pinch of salt.
tip: Any firm white fish works: sea bream, snapper or haddock fillets cook the same way.
ingredients: half for the fish, half for the dakkous
ground, or a pinch of crushed dried lime

name: Pan-seared fresh anchovies with sumac onions and a parsley, radish and kale salad
inspiredBy: Turkish hamsi tava, the fresh Black Sea anchovies cooked in a hot pan, with a Levantine sumac onion salad and no cornmeal coating, and the walnut and hazelnut tarator Turkish fish restaurants serve with fried fish
about: Whole fresh anchovies seared in a hot pan until the skins crackle, over a sharp salad of parsley, radish, kale and arugula with thin sumac onions, lemon and a spoonful of rough walnut and hazelnut tarator. Anchovies are the little oily fish people fry all along the Turkish coast. A serving carries **omega-3, calcium and selenium**.
steps: Toast the walnuts and hazelnuts in a dry pan for 3 minutes. Pound them in a mortar, or blitz them in a mini chopper, with a little of the garlic, a squeeze of the lemon, a pinch of salt and a splash of water, into a rough, creamy tarator.
Toss the red onion with the sumac and a pinch of salt and leave it for 5 minutes to soften.
Rub the kale with a pinch of salt and half the garlic for a minute to soften it. Toss it with the parsley, radish, cucumber and arugula, the onions, half the lemon juice and a third of the olive oil.
Pat the anchovies very dry and season them with salt, pepper and the rest of the garlic. Heat the rest of the olive oil in a large non-stick pan over high heat.

Lay the anchovies in the pan in a single layer, in two batches if you need to, and cook for 2 minutes without moving them, until the skins are crisp. Flip and cook for 1 minute more, until just opaque.
Pile the salad on a plate and set the anchovies on top. Spoon the tarator alongside, squeeze over the rest of the lemon and finish with the Aleppo pepper.
tip: Fresh sardines are easier to find in North America and work the same way: scale and gut them, or ask the fishmonger, and cook 2 to 3 minutes a side. Smelt and small mackerel fillets also work.
ingredients: half for the salad, the rest to squeeze over the fish
stems removed, leaves very thinly sliced

name: Sardine, tomato and parsley salad with avocado and lemon-tahini
inspiredBy: Lebanese-style canned sardines with tomato, parsley and lemon, with avocado and a tahini dressing added
about: Canned sardines, soft bones and all, flaked over a bright salad of ripe tomato, cucumber, a big handful of parsley and creamy avocado, with lemon-tahini poured over. It takes 10 minutes and nothing gets cooked. The sardines bring **calcium, omega-3 and vitamin B12**.
steps: Toss the red onion with the sumac and a pinch of salt and leave it for 5 minutes.
Whisk the tahini with the crushed garlic, half the lemon juice and cold water, a teaspoon at a time until pourable.
Toss the romaine, tomato, cucumber, parsley and mint with the olive oil, the rest of the lemon juice, the onions and a pinch of salt and pepper.
Pile the salad onto a plate. Flake the sardines over it in big pieces and add the avocado.
Drizzle the tahini dressing over everything and eat right away.
tip: Buy sardines packed in water or brine, not oil, for a fresher taste. Drain them but keep the soft bones: that is where the calcium is.
ingredients: canned in water or brine, drained, bones in
half for the salad, half for the dressing

name: Lamb and beef kofta platter with baba ghanoush, charred pepper and a sumac arugula salad
inspiredBy: Lebanese kafta mashwiyye, the grilled lamb and beef skewers with parsley, served mezze-style with smoky baba ghanoush
about: Juicy lamb and beef skewers with parsley, scented with baharat and cinnamon, grilled and served on a platter with smoky baba ghanoush, a charred red pepper, a sharp arugula salad with parsley and sumac, and a walnut and tahini tarator. It is the weekend project, and it makes two portions. The meat brings **zinc and iron**, and the eggplant adds potassium and fibre.
steps: Prick the eggplant and char it directly over a gas flame, under a very hot broiler or on the grill for 15 to 20 minutes, turning, until the skin is blackened and the flesh is collapsing. Set it in a bowl and cover it for 10 minutes.

Scoop the soft flesh out, drain off any bitter liquid, and mash it with a third of the tahini, a third of the lemon juice, a little garlic, a drizzle of the olive oil and a pinch of salt. It should be smoky and slightly rough.

Make the kofta mixture. Knead the lamb and beef with the onion, two thirds of the parsley, a spoonful of the olive oil, the baharat, the cinnamon, the salt and the pepper for a full minute, until sticky and well combined. Shape it into long, flat fingers around skewers, or into short ovals if you are using a pan.

Brush the kofta and the pepper strip with some of the olive oil. Grill, broil or pan-sear the kofta for 8 to 10 minutes, turning, until browned and just cooked through. Char the pepper skin side down until blistered, then slice it.

Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 3 minutes. Whisk the rest of the tahini with the rest of the garlic, half the remaining lemon juice, the walnuts and about 2 tablespoons of cold water into a pourable tarator.
Toss the arugula with the rest of the parsley, the sumac, the last of the lemon juice and a drizzle of the remaining olive oil.
Serve the kofta on a platter with the baba ghanoush, pepper, tomato slices and salad, with the tarator spooned over. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Lean lamb can go dry, so don't skip the grated onion, and take the kofta off as soon as they are just cooked through. Reheat leftover kofta in a hot pan for 2 minutes.
ingredients: lean leg, ground twice or minced by the butcher
lean round, ground or minced by the butcher
finely chopped, two thirds for the kofta
a third for the baba ghanoush, the rest for the sauce
toasted and finely chopped, for the sauce
for the baba ghanoush, the sauce and the salad
one wide strip, about a quarter of a pepper, for charring

name: Baked whole trout with a cilantro, walnut and chili sauce, and garlicky kale
inspiredBy: Lebanese samke harra, the baked fish with a spicy cilantro and nut sauce, made with a whole trout and served with Black Sea style sautéed kale
about: A whole trout stuffed with parsley and baked until the skin crisps, under a hot, green sauce of cilantro, garlic, chili, walnuts and lemon, with a pile of garlicky sautéed kale. It is simple enough for a weekend dinner and good enough to be a feast. The trout and walnuts bring **omega-3, B12 and copper**, and the kale adds calcium and vitamin A.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Pat the trout dry and make 3 shallow slashes on each side. Rub the skin and the inside with a little of the olive oil, salt and pepper, and tuck the parsley sprigs into the cavity.
Lay the trout on a lined tray and roast it for 18 to 22 minutes, until the flesh flakes at the thickest part and the skin is crisp.

While it bakes, make the sauce. Blitz the walnuts with the cilantro, most of the garlic, the serrano, half the lemon juice, half the remaining olive oil and a pinch of salt, adding a few tablespoons of water, until you have a thick, spoonable sauce.

Warm the rest of the olive oil in a wide pan over medium heat and add the last of the garlic, sliced. Stir for 30 seconds, then add the kale with a splash of water and a pinch of salt. Cover and cook for 5 to 6 minutes, until tender.

Lift the trout onto a platter, spoon the sauce over and around it, and squeeze over a little of the remaining lemon juice. Dress the kale with the rest of the lemon and the sumac and serve it alongside.
tip: A whole trout gives about two thirds of its weight as fish. Ask the fishmonger to gut and scale it; fillets work too, roasted for 10 to 12 minutes.
ingredients: 1 whole trout, cleaned; buy a fish about half as heavy again as the weight shown
about half for the sauce, the rest for the fish and kale
a few sprigs for the fish

name: Toasted hazelnuts with Aleppo pepper and lemon
inspiredBy: the warm, salted hazelnuts sold in Turkish nut shops (çerez), from the Black Sea hazelnut groves
about: A warm handful of hazelnuts toasted in a dry pan with a little Aleppo pepper, a squeeze of lemon and salt, the way a Turkish nut shop sells them. They are sweet, crunchy and a little hot, and bring **vitamin E, magnesium and healthy fat** with almost no carbs.
steps: Heat a small dry pan over medium heat. Add the hazelnuts and toast, shaking the pan, until they smell nutty and the skins crackle, about 4 minutes.
Tip them into a bowl, rub off any loose skins with a towel if you like, and toss with the Aleppo pepper, lemon juice and salt while they are warm.
tip: Toast a big batch on Sunday and keep it in a jar for the week.

name: Muhammara with cucumber and radish
inspiredBy: Syrian muhammara from Aleppo, the roasted red pepper and walnut dip, made without the breadcrumbs and pomegranate molasses
about: A rich, smoky, slightly hot dip of roasted red pepper and walnuts with a squeeze of lemon, scooped up with cucumber and radish. The walnuts bring **plant omega-3**, and the pepper brings vitamin C.
steps: Use a jarred roasted red pepper, drained and rinsed, or roast a whole pepper under a hot broiler or over a flame until blackened all over, about 15 minutes. Let it steam in a covered bowl, then peel off the skin and remove the seeds.
Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until fragrant.
Blitz the pepper, walnuts, olive oil, lemon juice, garlic, Aleppo pepper, cumin and salt to a thick, slightly coarse paste.
Spoon into a bowl and serve with the cucumber and radish.
tip: It keeps for 5 days in the fridge, so make a double batch.

name: Warm za'atar olives
inspiredBy: Lebanese and Palestinian olives warmed with za'atar and olive oil
about: Rinsed black olives warmed in olive oil with a little za'atar and lemon. It is salty, herby and very satisfying, and the olives bring **vitamin E and healthy fat** with almost no carbs.
steps: Rinse the olives under cold water and pat them dry.
Warm the olive oil in a small pan over low heat. Add the olives and the za'atar and stir for 2 minutes, until warm and fragrant.
Squeeze the lemon over everything and eat warm.
tip: Rinsing cuts the salt on olives noticeably. Leave the pits in for the best flavour, and watch your teeth.

name: Avocado with lemon, za'atar and olive oil
inspiredBy: the way labneh is dressed on a Levantine breakfast table, with olive oil, lemon and za'atar, here on avocado
about: A whole ripe avocado, halved, with a squeeze of lemon, a drizzle of olive oil and a good shake of za'atar. It takes a minute, and the avocado brings **potassium, folate and fibre**.
steps: Halve the avocado and remove the stone.
Squeeze the lemon over the cut face, drizzle with the olive oil and sprinkle with the za'atar and a tiny pinch of salt.
Eat it with a spoon, straight from the skin.
tip: Pick the avocado a couple of days ahead. It should give slightly when pressed.

name: Spiced hazelnuts and walnuts with sumac and Aleppo pepper
inspiredBy: the mixed roasted nuts sold across the Gulf and the Levant, with the Black Sea hazelnuts and the walnuts of the Syrian and Turkish kitchen
about: Hazelnuts and walnuts toasted in a dry pan with sumac, Aleppo pepper and a little salt. It is a crunchy, tangy little handful that brings **vitamin E, plant omega-3 and magnesium**.
steps: Toast the hazelnuts and walnuts in a dry pan over medium heat, shaking now and then, until they smell nutty, about 3 minutes.
Toss with the olive oil, sumac, Aleppo pepper and salt while they are warm.
tip: Make extra and keep it in a jar for up to a week.

name: Olive oil artichoke hearts with dill, lemon and toasted hazelnuts
inspiredBy: Turkish zeytinyağlı enginar, the cold artichoke hearts dressed with olive oil, lemon and dill
about: Tender artichoke hearts dressed with olive oil, lemon and fresh dill, with toasted hazelnuts for crunch. It is a classic Turkish cold meze that takes five minutes from a jar, and the artichokes bring **fibre and folate** for very few carbs.
steps: Toast the hazelnuts in a dry pan over medium heat until golden, about 3 minutes. Tip them out to cool, then chop them roughly.
Drain the artichoke hearts, rinse them well and pat them dry. Halve them if they are large.
Toss them with the olive oil, lemon juice, dill, Aleppo pepper and a tiny pinch of salt.
Pile onto a plate and scatter the hazelnuts over the top.
tip: Choose artichoke hearts packed in brine or water rather than oil, and rinse them.
ingredients: hearts in brine, drained and rinsed

name: Avocado with lemon-tahini, sumac and radish
inspiredBy: the lemon-tahini and sumac that dress hummus on a Levantine table, here spooned over avocado
about: A small ripe avocado, halved, with a ribbon of lemon-tahini, a dusting of sumac, thin radish and a little cilantro. It is creamy and tangy, and the avocado and tahini bring **fibre, potassium and calcium**.
steps: Whisk the tahini with the lemon juice, a pinch of the salt and enough cold water, about 1 tablespoon, to make a pourable sauce.
Set the avocado halves on a plate and spoon the sauce into and over them.
Top with the radish and cilantro and finish with the sumac.
tip: Pick the avocado a couple of days ahead. It should give slightly when pressed.
ingredients: about 1 small avocado, halved and pitted

name: Roasted pumpkin seeds with sumac and Aleppo pepper
inspiredBy: the salted roasted seeds sold at every nut shop in Lebanon, Syria and Turkey, eaten by the handful
about: Pumpkin seeds toasted in a dry pan with sumac, Aleppo pepper and a pinch of salt until they pop and turn golden. They are crunchy, tangy and a little hot, and bring **zinc, magnesium and iron**.
steps: Toast the pumpkin seeds in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring, until they puff and turn golden, about 4 minutes.
Toss with the olive oil, sumac, Aleppo pepper and salt while they are warm.
tip: They keep for 2 weeks in a jar, so toast a bigger batch if you like them.

name: Olive and walnut dip with crisp romaine
inspiredBy: the olive and walnut pastes of Hatay and Gaziantep, served as a meze with raw vegetables
about: A coarse, garlicky paste of rinsed olives, toasted walnuts, parsley and lemon, scooped up with crisp romaine leaves. It is salty, nutty and bright, and the walnuts bring **plant omega-3 and copper**.
steps: Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 2 to 3 minutes, until fragrant.
Pulse the olives, walnuts, garlic, lemon juice, olive oil and parsley in a small processor to a coarse paste, adding a spoonful of water if it is stiff.
Spoon into a bowl, sprinkle with the Aleppo pepper and serve with the romaine leaves for scooping.
tip: It keeps for 4 days in a jar in the fridge.

name: Foul medames with boiled eggs, tahini, raw onion and radish
inspiredBy: Jordanian and Palestinian foul, the breakfast of the foul stands in Amman, with a little chickpea in the pot as Lebanese cooks like it
about: Warm, creamy fava beans and chickpeas mashed with garlic, cumin and lemon, with a swirl of tahini, two boiled eggs and a pile of raw onion, radish, tomato and parsley on top. Scoop it all up with warm whole-wheat pita. The beans bring **fibre, folate and iron**, and the eggs add choline.
steps: Lower the eggs gently into a small pot of boiling water and cook for 8 minutes, then cool them under cold water and peel.

Mash the garlic with the salt into a paste. Warm the fava beans and chickpeas in a small pot with the garlic, the cumin and a splash of water, stirring now and then, until they are steaming hot, about 5 minutes.
Mash roughly with a fork. You want a creamy base with some whole beans left in it. Stir in the lemon juice and half the olive oil.
Stir the tahini with a spoonful of water until it is pourable, like thin cream.
Spoon the beans into a shallow bowl, drizzle with the tahini and the rest of the olive oil, and pile the tomato, onion, radish and parsley on top. Add the halved eggs.
Warm the pita in a dry pan or the toaster, tear it up and use it to scoop.
tip: A 400 g tin of foul makes two portions, so two foul mornings need only one tin. A pinch of chili flakes or a few chopped pickles on top is welcome.
ingredients: from a tin, drained and rinsed

name: Za'atar pita with labneh, olives, egg and cucumber
inspiredBy: the za'atar and olive oil breakfast of Jordan and Lebanon, in the style of a man'oushe
about: Warm pita brushed with za'atar and olive oil, a swirl of labneh, a soft-boiled egg, olives, cucumber and fresh mint. It is the everyday breakfast table in one plate. The labneh and egg bring **protein, calcium and choline**.
steps: Lower the egg gently into a small pot of boiling water and cook for 7 minutes for a jammy yolk. Cool it under cold water, then peel. You can boil a few ahead and keep them in the fridge.
Stir the za'atar into most of the olive oil to make a paste. Spread it over the pita and warm it in a dry pan or a hot oven for a couple of minutes, until it smells toasty.
Stir a pinch of salt into the labneh and swirl it onto a plate. Pour the rest of the olive oil into a little well in the middle.
Halve the egg and arrange it with the olives, sliced cucumber and mint around the labneh. Tear the pita and scoop.
tip: No labneh? Spoon thick Greek yogurt into a sieve lined with a clean cloth the night before, stir in a pinch of salt and let it drain in the fridge.

name: Balila, warm chickpeas with tahini, lemon, cumin and a boiled egg
inspiredBy: Lebanese and Palestinian balila, the warm chickpea breakfast
about: Warm, soft chickpeas in a little of their liquid with lemon, garlic and cumin, finished with a spoon of tahini, parsley and a good pour of olive oil, with a boiled egg alongside. It is simple, savoury and very filling. The chickpeas bring **fibre and protein** and the egg adds choline.
steps: Lower the egg gently into a small pot of boiling water and cook for 8 minutes, then cool it under cold water and peel.
Mash the garlic with the salt into a paste. Warm the chickpeas in a small pot with the garlic, the cumin and a splash of water for 5 minutes, until they are very hot and soft.
Mash a few of them against the side of the pot so the liquid turns creamy, and stir in the lemon juice.
Whisk the tahini with a spoonful of water until pourable.
Spoon the chickpeas and some of their liquid into a bowl. Drizzle over the tahini and the olive oil and scatter with the parsley.
Halve the egg and lay it on top. Warm the pita and serve with the radish on the side.
tip: Add a pinch of chili flakes or a few drops of hot sauce, the way balila is often served in Beirut.

name: Ijjeh, a herb and chard omelette with radish and mint salad
inspiredBy: Levantine ijjeh (eggah), with chard folded in and no flour
about: A thick, green, herby omelette packed with parsley, chard, onion and a little grated halloumi, cut into wedges and eaten with warm pita, crunchy radishes, cucumber and mint. It makes two portions, and the cold wedge is just as good tomorrow morning. The eggs bring **protein and choline**, and the parsley and chard bring vitamin K.
steps: Finely chop the parsley, chard and onion. Keep the chard stems, they stay pleasantly crisp.
Beat the eggs in a bowl with the baharat and half the salt, then stir in the grated halloumi, herbs, chard, onion and walnuts. It should look more green than yellow.

Heat the broiler. Warm half the oil in a medium oven-safe non-stick pan over medium-low heat. Pour in the egg mixture, cover, and cook gently until the edges are set and the top is almost firm, about 8 minutes.
Brush the top with the rest of the oil and slide the pan under the broiler for 2 minutes, until puffed and golden. Cut into wedges.
Slice the radishes and cucumber, toss with the mint, lemon juice and the rest of the salt, and serve beside a wedge with warm pita.
Wrap the second portion for tomorrow. Make a fresh salad then, and eat the wedge cold or tucked into pita.
tip: Leave out the walnuts if you like it softer. A pinch of cinnamon is traditional in some Syrian kitchens.

name: Lamb kafta pita with roasted cauliflower, tarator and tomato
inspiredBy: Lebanese and Palestinian kafta sandwiches, made with lean lamb and finished with tahini sauce and roasted cauliflower, as karnabeet is eaten
about: Finger-shaped patties of lean lamb, parsley and onion with baharat, tucked into warm whole-wheat pita with golden roasted cauliflower, tomato, a sumac onion salad and a lemony tahini sauce. It is street food you can make at home. The lamb brings **iron, zinc and vitamin B12**, and the tahini adds calcium.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C. Toss the cauliflower with half the olive oil and a pinch of salt on a tray and roast until golden at the edges, about 20 minutes.
Pulse the lamb cubes in a food processor, in short bursts with a splash of ice water, until finely ground and sticky. Or ask the butcher to grind lean leg of lamb twice.

Squeeze the grated onion in your hands to get rid of the extra juice. Mix it with the lamb, most of the parsley, the baharat, black pepper and half the salt, kneading for a minute or two. Shape into 3 or 4 fingers about 8 cm long.
Warm the rest of the oil in a non-stick pan over medium-high heat and cook the kafta, turning now and then, until browned all over and cooked through, about 8 minutes.

Make the tarator. Stir the tahini with the lemon juice, the garlic (mashed to a paste), the rest of the salt and 2 to 3 tablespoons of cold water, until pale and pourable. Toss the sliced onion with the rest of the parsley and the sumac.
Warm the pita, fill it with the kafta, cauliflower, sliced tomato and sumac onions, and drizzle with the tarator.
tip: Roast the cauliflower and shape the kafta on Wednesday night while the oven is hot for the salmon. At lunch, fry the kafta and assemble. You can also freeze the shaped raw fingers.
ingredients: most for the kafta, a little for the salad

name: Fattoush with chickpeas and grilled halloumi
inspiredBy: Lebanese fattoush, with chickpeas and halloumi to make it a meal
about: A big, crunchy salad of romaine, radish, cucumber, tomato and mint under shards of toasted pita, with a sumac and pomegranate molasses dressing, spiced chickpeas and slices of golden halloumi. It is sharp, juicy and salty at once. The chickpeas and halloumi bring **protein and calcium**.
steps: Split the pita, tear it into pieces, toss with a little of the oil and toast in a dry pan or a hot oven until golden and crisp, about 5 minutes.
Make the dressing. Mash the garlic with a pinch of salt and whisk it with the lemon juice, pomegranate molasses and the rest of the olive oil.
Toss the chickpeas in a bowl with half the sumac, a pinch of salt and a spoonful of the dressing so they take on some flavour.
Slice the halloumi and cook it in a dry non-stick pan over medium-high heat for about 1 minute per side, until golden.
Chop the romaine, radish, cucumber and tomato into bite-size pieces, tear in the mint and toss with most of the dressing.
Pile on a plate, top with the chickpeas and halloumi, sprinkle with the rest of the sumac and add the pita pieces just before eating.
tip: Grilled chicken or a handful of toasted almonds are good on top too. Use a squeeze of extra lemon if you have no pomegranate molasses.

name: Musakhan-style sumac chicken and onions on pita
inspiredBy: Palestinian musakhan, roasted sumac chicken on bread soaked in onions, made with boneless thighs and a lighter hand with the oil
about: Chicken thighs rubbed with sumac and baharat and roasted until golden, piled on whole-wheat pita with a heap of slowly cooked sumac onions and toasted pine nuts. It is Palestine's best-loved dish, scaled down for a Saturday lunch. The chicken brings **protein and zinc**, and the onions bring plenty of flavour for very little fat.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C. Rub the chicken with half the sumac, the baharat, the black pepper, a third of the oil and half the salt. Spread it on a small tray.
Roast until golden and cooked through, 25 to 30 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook the onions in the rest of the oil with the rest of the salt in a wide pan over medium-low heat, stirring now and then, until completely soft and golden, about 20 minutes, with a splash of water if they start to stick. Stir in the rest of the sumac and the lemon juice for the last minute.
Toast the pine nuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until golden, and watch them closely.
Warm the pita in the oven for the last 5 minutes. Spread the onions over it, lay the chicken on top and scatter with the pine nuts and parsley. Cut it into wedges and eat with your hands.
tip: Serve it with a spoonful of labneh or yogurt on the side if you like. Traditional musakhan is made with much more olive oil, and it is delicious.

name: Adas bi hamod, lemony lentil and chard soup
about: A sunny, sharp Lebanese lentil soup with plenty of chard, finished with crushed garlic and cilantro fried in olive oil and a good squeeze of lemon. It is cosy, hearty and better the next day, so it makes two portions. The lentils and chard bring **iron, folate and fibre**, and the lemon helps your body use that iron.
steps: Soften the onion in half the olive oil in a big pot over medium heat until golden, about 8 minutes.
Add the rinsed lentils and cover with plenty of water, about 4 times their volume. Bring to a boil, then simmer gently until the lentils are nearly tender, about 20 minutes.
Slice the chard stems and add them with a little salt. Cook for 5 minutes, then stir in the leaves and cook until they wilt and soften, about 5 minutes more.

Crush the garlic with a pinch of salt and the cilantro. Warm the rest of the olive oil in a small pan and fry this paste for a minute, until it smells wonderful. Stir it into the soup with the lemon juice.
Taste and add more lemon or salt until it is properly sharp and savoury. Tear the pita into pieces, toast them in a dry pan until crisp and scatter over each bowl.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. The soup thickens as it sits, so loosen it with a splash of water when you reheat it.
tip: For a creamier soup, blitz a ladleful and stir it back in.

name: Shish tawook with parsley tabbouleh and toum-style garlic sauce
inspiredBy: Lebanese shish tawook, with a lighter whipped garlic sauce in place of full toum and a tabbouleh that is mostly parsley
about: Chunks of chicken marinated in yogurt, lemon and garlic and grilled until charred at the edges, with a bright tabbouleh that is mostly parsley and a sharp, punchy garlic sauce. It makes two portions, so tomorrow's lunch is covered. The chicken brings **protein and niacin**, and all that parsley brings vitamins K and C.
steps: Stir the yogurt with a third of the garlic (mashed to a paste), a third of the lemon juice, the baharat, the black pepper and half the salt. Add the chicken and turn to coat. Marinate for at least 30 minutes and up to 6 hours in the fridge.
Cover the bulgur with hot water and leave it for 15 minutes, until tender, then drain well and squeeze out the water.
Mix the bulgur with the parsley, mint, onion, half the remaining lemon juice, half the olive oil and a pinch of salt. Keep the tomato aside and add it at serving, so the tabbouleh stays fresh.
Thread the chicken onto skewers, or spread it on a tray, and grill or broil on high, turning once or twice, until charred at the edges and cooked through, 10 to 12 minutes.

Make the garlic sauce. Pound the rest of the garlic with a pinch of salt, then slowly whisk in the rest of the olive oil and the last squeeze of lemon, a few drops at a time, until it turns thick and creamy. It is a quick toum.
Serve the chicken with the tabbouleh, the tomato, the sauce and the romaine leaves to scoop. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the tomato and sauce in separate containers.
tip: Chicken breast works too, but thighs stay juicier. If the garlic sauce splits, whisk in a teaspoon of cold water.
ingredients: boneless, skinless thighs, cut in 3 cm chunks

name: Samke harra, Lebanese spicy cilantro and walnut baked salmon with tomato bulgur
inspiredBy: Lebanese samke harra from Tripoli, with salmon in place of white fish, baked with a hot cilantro paste and topped with toasted walnuts
about: Salmon fillet rubbed with a fiery paste of cilantro, garlic, chili, cumin and lemon and baked until it flakes, with a tomato bulgur pilaf (burghul bi banadoura) and a handful of toasted walnuts on top. It is the Lebanese coast on a plate. The salmon brings **omega-3 fats and vitamin D**, and the walnuts add crunch.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C. Soften half the onion, diced, in a third of the olive oil in a small pot, about 5 minutes, without browning it. Add half the chopped tomato and cook for 3 minutes, then stir in the bulgur, add double its volume of water and a pinch of salt, cover and simmer on low for 12 minutes. Leave it covered.
Meanwhile, pound or blitz the cilantro, garlic, chili, all the cumin, half the lemon juice, half the remaining oil and a pinch of salt into a rough, spoonable paste.
Rub the paste all over the fish, pressing it in well. Set the fish on a lined tray and bake until it flakes easily with a fork, 12 to 15 minutes.
Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until they smell nutty, and chop them roughly.
Toss the rest of the tomato and the sliced onion with the rest of the lemon juice, the last of the oil and a pinch of salt.
Serve the fish on the bulgur, scattered with the walnuts, with the tomato salad on the side.
tip: Sea bass, grouper, cod or halibut make the traditional version, and trout is lovely too. Use a smaller chili or leave out the seeds if you want less heat.
ingredients: seeded if you like less heat
chopped, half for the pilaf and half for the salad
half diced for the pilaf, half sliced for the salad

name: Mujadara hamra, lentils and bulgur with caramelised onions and malfouf salad
inspiredBy: Lebanese and Palestinian mujadara hamra, the version made with bulgur
about: Brown lentils and bulgur cooked with cumin and baharat and topped with deeply browned onions, with a crunchy mint, lemon and olive oil cabbage and carrot salad on the side. It is humble, filling and very much a Levantine home dinner. The lentils and bulgur bring **iron and fibre**, the carrot brings vitamin A, and it makes two portions for tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Simmer the lentils with the cumin in plenty of water for about 15 minutes, until they are almost tender but still have some bite. Drain, keeping the cooking water.

While they cook, cook the sliced onions in two-thirds of the olive oil with a pinch of salt in a wide pan over medium-low heat, stirring often, until they are deep golden brown and sweet, 30 to 35 minutes. Most of this time is hands-off. Lift out about a third for the top.

Add the lentils, bulgur, baharat and the rest of the salt to the pan with the remaining onions. Pour in enough of the lentil water to cover by about 1 cm, bring to a simmer, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes.
Turn off the heat and leave it covered for 10 minutes so the bulgur finishes steaming, then fluff with a fork.
Make the cabbage salad, salata malfouf. Mash the garlic with a pinch of salt and toss it with the cabbage, carrot, lemon juice, mint and the rest of the olive oil.
Top the mujadara with the caramelised onions and serve with the salad. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the salad dressed fresh. It reheats well, or eat it at room temperature.
tip: Slow, patient onions are the secret. If they start to catch, add a splash of water and keep going.

name: Spicy tomato sardines on toasted pita with parsley and onion salad
inspiredBy: the chili, garlic and tomato fish dishes of the Lebanese and Palestinian coast, made with canned sardines
about: Canned sardines warmed through in a garlicky, chili-spiked tomato sauce and spooned over toasted pita, with a sharp parsley, onion and sumac salad. It is on the table in about 35 minutes. Sardines are one of the best sources of **omega-3, calcium and vitamin D**, because you eat the soft bones.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Cook the diced onion until soft, about 5 minutes, then add the garlic, chili and cumin and stir for a minute, until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and half the salt. Simmer, pressing them down with the back of a spoon, until they collapse into a thick, jammy sauce, 12 to 15 minutes.
Nestle the sardines into the sauce, spoon some over the top and warm them gently for 3 to 4 minutes without stirring, so they stay in nice pieces.
Toss the sliced onion with the parsley, sumac, half the lemon juice and a pinch of salt. Toast the pita until crisp at the edges.
Squeeze the rest of the lemon over the sardines and serve with the pita and the parsley salad.
tip: Fresh sardines or small mackerel, seared and slipped into the sauce, are the classic version if you can find them at a fishmonger or Middle Eastern market. Use about 200 g of cleaned, butterflied fish.

name: Baked kibbeh with spiced lamb and walnut filling and tomato sumac salad
inspiredBy: Lebanese and Syrian kibbeh bil sanieh, made with lean lamb and plenty of bulgur
about: A tender layer of spiced lamb and bulgur dough over a savoury filling of onion, spiced lamb and walnuts, baked until the top is crisp and golden, with a tomato, onion and sumac salad. It is the weekend project dish. Lamb and bulgur bring **iron, zinc and B vitamins**, and it makes two portions.
steps: Rinse the bulgur, cover it with cold water and leave it for 20 minutes, then squeeze it very dry. Heat the oven to 200 C and brush a 20 cm square baking dish with a little of the oil.
Pulse the lamb cubes in a food processor, in short bursts, until finely ground. Or ask the butcher to grind lean leg of lamb twice. Set a third aside for the filling.

Make the filling. Soften half the kibbeh onion, finely chopped, in a spoonful of the oil. Add the reserved lamb and cook, breaking it up, until browned, about 5 minutes. Stir in the walnuts, a third of the baharat and a pinch of salt. Set aside to cool slightly.

Make the dough. Grate or blitz the other half of the kibbeh onion. Put the rest of the lamb, the squeezed bulgur, the grated onion, the rest of the baharat, the black pepper and the salt in the food processor and pulse in short bursts, adding a spoonful of ice water, until it is a smooth, sticky paste. Chill it for 15 minutes if it feels too soft.
With wet hands, press half the dough into the dish in a flat, even layer. Spread the filling over it, then pat the rest of the dough over the top, smoothing it to seal in the filling.
Score the top in diamonds with a wet knife, drizzle with the rest of the oil and bake until deep golden brown and crisp at the edges, 35 to 40 minutes. Rest for 10 minutes before cutting.
Meanwhile, slice the tomato and the salad onion very thinly, and toss with the parsley, sumac, lemon juice and a pinch of salt. Serve a portion with the salad.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. Reheat the kibbeh in a hot oven and make a fresh salad.
tip: Keep the dough and the knife wet, it is what makes the top smooth. Kibbeh freezes very well, baked or unbaked.
ingredients: most for the kibbeh, a little for the salad

name: Baked mackerel on collapsed eggplant with tarator
inspiredBy: the Levantine pairing of fish with tarator, the tahini and lemon sauce, served over silky roasted eggplant
about: Mackerel fillets roasted over eggplant that has collapsed into a soft, silky bed with lemon, garlic and parsley, drizzled with a creamy tahini tarator. It is bold, rich and ready in about an hour, mostly in the oven. Mackerel is one of the richest sources of **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the tahini adds calcium.
steps: Heat the oven to 230 C. Score the cut side of the eggplant halves in a diamond pattern, brush with half the olive oil and sprinkle with half the salt and the cumin. Roast cut side down on a tray until completely soft and collapsing, about 30 minutes.
Mash half the garlic with a pinch of salt. Mix it with a third of the lemon juice and a little of the olive oil, and chop most of the parsley into it.

Turn the eggplant cut side up and scoop and mash the flesh roughly with a fork on the tray. Spoon over the dressing, tuck the tomato halves around it and lay the mackerel on top, skin side up. Brush the fish with the rest of the olive oil.
Roast for 10 to 12 minutes more, until the fish flakes easily and the skin is crisp.
Make the tarator. Stir the tahini with the rest of the garlic, the rest of the lemon juice, a pinch of salt and 3 to 4 tablespoons of cold water until pale and pourable.
Serve the fish on the eggplant, drizzled with the tarator and the rest of the parsley, with warm pita.
tip: Any oily fish works here. The roasted eggplant keeps well, so roast extra for a baba ghanoush-style spread.

name: Silky hummus with radish and cucumber sticks
about: A proper creamy hummus made from a tin of chickpeas, with plenty of tahini and lemon, served with crunchy radishes and cucumber. Make the batch once and it covers both hummus snacks, with some left for the table. The chickpeas and tahini bring **fibre, protein and calcium**.
steps: Make a batch of 4 portions: blitz 1 tin of chickpeas (about 240 g drained) with 4 tablespoons of tahini, the juice of 1 lemon, 2 cloves of garlic, a pinch of cumin, a good pinch of salt and 4 to 6 tablespoons of ice-cold water for 3 to 4 minutes, until pale and silky. Keep it in the fridge for up to 4 days.
Spoon one portion (about a quarter of the batch) into a bowl, make a well in the middle and drizzle with the olive oil. Serve with the radish and cucumber sticks.
tip: Ice-cold water and a long blitz are the secret to a smooth, pale hummus. Rubbing the skins off the chickpeas makes it even silkier.

name: Dried figs and almonds
about: Chewy dried figs and a small handful of almonds, a pairing found on every Levantine market stall. It is sweet, crunchy and easy to carry. The figs bring **calcium and fibre** and the almonds bring vitamin E.
steps: Put the figs and almonds in a small bowl or a bag and eat together.
tip: In fig season, two or three fresh figs or a bunch of grapes are lovely in place of the dried figs.

name: Pomegranate seeds with toasted almonds
about: Juicy pomegranate seeds with a small handful of toasted almonds, sweet-sour with a crunch. It is bright, cool and a little festive. The almonds bring **vitamin E and protein** and the pomegranate brings fibre and vitamin C.
steps: Tip the pomegranate seeds into a small bowl.
Scatter with the toasted almonds and eat with a spoon.
tip: Pomegranates are in season in the fall. The rest of the year, buy a tub of seeds, or use fresh figs or grapes in season.

name: Grilled halloumi, cucumber and mint in pita
about: A few slices of golden grilled halloumi tucked into warm whole-wheat pita with cool cucumber and fresh mint, the way it is eaten in Lebanon and Jordan. It is salty, chewy and fresh. The halloumi brings **calcium and protein**.
steps: Slice the halloumi and cook it in a dry non-stick pan over medium-high heat for about 1 minute per side, until golden.
Warm the pita, tuck in the halloumi, sliced cucumber and mint, and add a squeeze of lemon.

name: Pomegranate seeds with walnuts
inspiredBy: the pomegranate and walnut pairing of Levantine muhammara
about: Juicy pomegranate seeds with a handful of walnuts, sweet and sour with a crunch, like the flavours of a muhammara dip. The walnuts bring **omega-3 fats** and the pomegranate brings vitamin C and fibre.
steps: Tip the pomegranate seeds into a small bowl.
Scatter with the walnuts and eat with a spoon.

name: Pita with tahini and dried figs
inspiredBy: tahini with date or grape molasses, a Levantine breakfast sweet, made with figs
about: Warm whole-wheat pita spread with tahini and topped with chopped dried figs, nutty and sweet. It is a good, filling snack. The tahini and figs bring **calcium and copper**.
steps: Warm the pita in a dry pan or the toaster.
Spread with the tahini, scatter over the chopped figs and fold.

name: Pomegranate bowl with mint and lemon
about: Juicy pomegranate seeds with torn mint and a squeeze of lemon, sweet, sour and very refreshing. It is a light bowl after a rich meal. The pomegranate brings **vitamin C and fibre**.
steps: Tip the pomegranate seeds into a bowl.
Tear over the mint and squeeze over the lemon juice.
tip: Pomegranates are in season in the fall. The rest of the year, buy a tub of seeds.

name: Za'atar pita with olives
inspiredBy: the zeit w za'atar plate of Jordan and Lebanon
about: Warm whole-wheat pita brushed with olive oil and za'atar, with a few olives on the side. It is a simple snack from a Levantine breakfast table. The whole-wheat pita brings **fibre and B vitamins**.
steps: Stir the za'atar into the olive oil and brush it over the pita.
Warm the pita in a dry pan or a hot oven for 2 minutes and serve with the olives.

name: Dried figs stuffed with walnuts
inspiredBy: the figs and walnuts of Levantine sweet trays
about: Soft dried figs with a walnut half tucked into each one, chewy and nutty. They taste like a sweet from a Levantine tray but are made of just two ingredients. The walnuts bring **omega-3 fats** and the figs bring calcium and fibre.
steps: Snip the stems off the figs and slit each one open.
Tuck a walnut half into each fig and eat the rest of the walnuts alongside.
tip: In fig season, use fresh figs or a bunch of grapes with the walnuts.

name: Yogurt with chopped figs and toasted almonds
about: Thick, cool yogurt with chopped dried figs for sweetness and crunchy toasted almonds on top. It is creamy, a little sweet and very quick. The yogurt brings **calcium and protein**, and the figs add more calcium.
steps: Stir most of the chopped figs into the yogurt.
Spoon into a bowl and top with the rest of the figs and the almonds.

name: Pita with olives, cucumber and mint
about: Warm whole-wheat pita with crunchy cucumber, a few olives and torn mint, the kind of plate you might pick at on a Levantine afternoon. It is fresh and filling. The cucumber and mint bring **vitamin K and potassium**.
steps: Slice the cucumber and toss it with the olives, mint, olive oil and salt.
Warm the pita and eat it with the salad, tucked inside or on the side.

name: Labneh, olive and mint pita roll
inspiredBy: the labneh sandwiches of Lebanese bakeries
about: Warm whole-wheat pita spread with labneh, olive oil and chopped olives, rolled up with fresh mint. It is a quick, filling snack. The labneh brings **protein and calcium**.
steps: Warm the pita in a dry pan or the toaster.
Spread it with the labneh, drizzle with the olive oil, scatter over the olives and mint, and roll it up.

name: Greek yogurt with strawberries, walnuts and toasted oats
inspiredBy: Greek yiaourti me karydia, the everyday bowl of thick yogurt and walnuts, without the honey
about: Thick Greek yogurt with sliced strawberries, chopped walnuts and a crunch of toasted oats. It is how plenty of Greek kitchens start the day, minus the honey. The **protein, fibre and walnut fat** all arrive together, so the fruit digests more slowly.
steps: Toast the oats in a dry pan over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, shaking now and then, until they smell nutty. Tip them onto a plate to cool.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl and pile the strawberries on top.
Scatter on the walnuts and the warm oats, then dust with cinnamon.
tip: Toast a jar of oats on Sunday and breakfast takes two minutes. In winter, frozen berries thawed overnight in the fridge work well and leave a lovely juice to swirl through.

name: Tostada con tomate and soft eggs with an orange
inspiredBy: Spanish tostada con tomate, the garlic and tomato toast every bar serves in the morning
about: Rye toast rubbed with garlic and ripe grated tomato, topped with two soft eggs, with an orange on the side. It is a thin slice of bread and mostly tomato and egg. The **eggs bring protein and choline**, and the orange adds vitamin C.
steps: Cut the tomato in half and grate it on the large holes of a box grater into a bowl, leaving the skin behind. Stir in a pinch of salt and half the olive oil.
Toast the rye until crisp and rub the cut side of the garlic over it.
Fry the eggs in the rest of the olive oil in a nonstick pan over medium heat for about 3 minutes, until the whites are set and the yolks are still soft.
Spoon the tomato onto the toast, top with the eggs and a pinch of salt, and serve with the orange.
tip: Grate the tomato the night before and keep it in a jar in the fridge, and breakfast takes 5 minutes. Rubbing a little garlic on the toast is the whole secret.

name: Spinach, mushroom and red pepper frittata with a slice of rye
inspiredBy: Italian frittata di spinaci, the thick open omelette that is just as good cold
about: A thick, golden frittata with spinach, mushrooms, soft onion and sweet red pepper, with a handful of parsley and a slice of rye. It makes two portions, and the second is a fine cold breakfast the next morning. The **eggs and spinach** bring protein, choline and folate with very little starch.
steps: Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Warm the olive oil in an ovenproof nonstick pan over medium heat and cook the onion, pepper strips and mushrooms until soft and the pan is dry, about 8 minutes.
Add the spinach and stir until it has wilted and the pan is nearly dry, about 2 minutes.
Beat the eggs with the salt, pepper, nutmeg and parsley. Pour them over the spinach and cook without stirring for 3 minutes, until the edges are set.
Slide the pan into the oven for about 8 minutes, until the top is set and lightly golden. Let it rest for 5 minutes, then cut it in half.
Serve one half with the rye, toasted. Pack the other half for tomorrow morning, cold or warmed.
tip: The frittata is happy cold, so slip a wedge into a lunchbox. A spoonful of crumbled feta on top before it goes in the oven is lovely too.

name: Fakes salata: Greek lentil salad with feta, cucumber and olives
inspiredBy: the lentil salads of Greek tavernas, with the lentils dressed while they are still warm
about: Green lentils tossed warm with red wine vinegar and olive oil, then cooled and mixed with carrot, cucumber, tomato, red onion and parsley, over a bed of arugula and topped with feta and olives. It is a cold salad you would find on a Greek table. The lentils carry plenty of **fibre and slow-digesting protein**, so this is a lunch that holds you.
steps: Rinse the lentils and simmer them with the bay leaf in plenty of unsalted water for about 20 minutes, until tender but still holding their shape. Drain well.
While they are still warm, toss the lentils with the vinegar, half the olive oil and the salt, and let them cool for 10 minutes.
Fold in the carrot, cucumber, tomato, onion, parsley and dried dill.
Pile the arugula on a plate, spoon the lentils over it, and finish with the feta, olives, oregano, pepper and the rest of the olive oil.
tip: Cook the lentils on Sunday evening and keep them in the fridge (they last 4 days), and this lunch takes 10 minutes. Fold the cucumber in just before eating so it stays crisp.

name: Pasta e ceci with more ceci than pasta
inspiredBy: Roman and southern Italian pasta e ceci, with the chickpeas doing most of the work
about: A thick, rosemary-scented chickpea and tomato soup with a little whole-wheat pasta and plenty of broccoli cooked soft right in the pot, in the southern Italian way. There is far more chickpea than pasta. The **chickpeas bring fibre and protein** so the little bit of pasta digests more slowly.
steps: Warm most of the olive oil in a pot over medium heat and cook the onion and carrot for about 7 minutes, until soft and sweet. Add the garlic and rosemary and stir for 1 minute.
Add the crushed tomatoes and the chickpeas with enough water to just cover them. Simmer for 10 minutes, then mash about a third of the chickpeas against the side of the pot so the soup turns creamy.

Add the broccoli with enough hot water to just cover it and simmer for 5 minutes. Add the pasta and cook for 8 to 10 minutes more, stirring often, until the pasta is tender with a little bite and the broccoli is soft enough to break up into the soup. Add water a splash at a time if it gets too thick.
Season with salt and pepper, and finish with the Parmesan, parsley and a drizzle of olive oil.
tip: To make it a quick lunch, cook the soup base (steps 1 and 2) on Sunday and keep it in the fridge. On the day, add the pasta and broccoli, and it is ready in about 20 minutes. It thickens as it sits, so loosen it with a splash of water.
ingredients: whole-wheat, broken spaghetti or any small shape
small florets, plus the peeled stalk, chopped (about half a head)

name: Cretan dakos-style salad with chickpeas, tomato and feta
inspiredBy: Cretan dakos, where a barley rusk is topped with grated tomato and soft cheese, here with rye toast and chickpeas
about: Crisp rye toast pieces topped with juicy grated tomato, cucumber, chickpeas, feta and olives, finished with a few walnuts, oregano and olive oil. It is inspired by the dakos of Crete, with chickpeas for protein and just a thin slice of bread. The **chickpeas and feta** make it a full lunch, and the tomato juice softens the toast just enough.
steps: Toast the rye until it is dry and crisp, then break it into rough pieces and put them in a shallow bowl.
Grate the tomato on a box grater, leaving the skin behind, and stir in the salt. Spoon it over the toast pieces and let them soak for a minute.
Toss the chickpeas with the cucumber and onion and spoon them over the top.
Crumble on the feta, scatter on the olives, walnuts and oregano, and finish with the olive oil.
tip: Toast the bread until it is really dry, like a rusk. If your toast is soft, leave it in a 160°C (325°F) oven for 10 minutes first.
ingredients: a small, thin slice, toasted hard

name: Barley risotto with chicken, mushrooms, broccoli and cannellini
inspiredBy: Italian orzotto from Friuli and Veneto, where pearl barley is cooked the way risotto is
about: Pearl barley simmered slowly with onion and garlic until creamy, with broccoli cooked right in the pot, then stirred together with browned chicken and mushrooms, cannellini beans and spinach. Parmesan goes in at the end and toasted hazelnuts on top. A small portion of barley goes a long way when the **chicken, beans and vegetables** do most of the work, and a lemony arugula salad sits beside it.
steps: Toast the hazelnuts in a dry pan for 3 minutes and chop them roughly. Warm a third of the olive oil in a wide pot over medium heat and cook the onion for about 5 minutes, until soft. Stir in the garlic and thyme for 1 minute.

Stir in the barley for a minute, then add hot water a ladleful at a time, keeping the barley just covered. Simmer, stirring now and then, for 25 minutes, then drop the broccoli florets on top and keep simmering for 8 to 10 minutes, until the barley is tender with a little bite, the broccoli is soft and the pot is creamy.

While the barley simmers, warm another third of the olive oil in a wide pan over medium-high heat and brown the chicken for 4 to 5 minutes. Add the mushrooms in a single layer and cook for 7 to 8 minutes more, stirring only now and then, until they are golden and the liquid has cooked off.

Stir the chicken and mushrooms into the barley with the beans and spinach, and cook for 2 minutes, until the spinach has wilted and the chicken is cooked through. Stir in the Parmesan, half the lemon juice, salt, pepper and the parsley, and scatter the toasted hazelnuts on top.
Toss the arugula with the rest of the lemon juice, the last of the olive oil and a pinch of salt, and serve it beside the orzotto. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: It thickens as it sits, so loosen the leftover portion with a splash of water or stock when you reheat it.
ingredients: boneless skinless thighs, in small pieces

name: Grilled sardines on a white bean, tomato and arugula salad
inspiredBy: Italian sarde alla griglia, served the Tuscan way on a lemony white bean salad
about: Fresh sardines grilled until the skin blisters, laid over cannellini beans tossed with tomato, grated carrot, onion, parsley and red wine vinegar, on a bed of arugula. It is simple, bright and ready in about 25 minutes. The sardines are the **omega-3 and calcium** hero of the week, and the soft bones are edible.
steps: Toss the beans with the tomato, carrot, onion, parsley, garlic, vinegar, half the olive oil and a pinch of salt. Let them sit for 10 minutes so the flavours settle.
Heat the broiler on high and line a tray with foil. Pat the sardines dry and rub them with a little olive oil, salt, pepper and oregano.
Broil the sardines on the tray for 3 to 4 minutes a side, until the skin is blistered and the flesh flakes easily.
Spread the arugula on a plate, spoon the beans over it and lay the sardines on top. Squeeze over the lemon juice and drizzle with the rest of the olive oil.
tip: A grill pan works too but it smokes, so open a window. Ask the fishmonger to scale and gut the sardines and you save 10 minutes. Frozen sardines work well: thaw them in the fridge overnight, and cook them the same day.

name: Chicken souvlaki with horiatiki salad and tzatziki
inspiredBy: Greek souvlaki with the village salad, the plate a taverna brings without asking
about: Lemony, oregano-scented chicken skewers with a chunky village salad of tomato, cucumber, pepper, olives and feta, a spoonful of garlicky tzatziki and a few bites of warm pita. The salad is half the plate and goes first. The **chicken and yogurt carry the protein**, so the pita can stay small.
steps: Mix the chicken with the lemon juice, half the garlic, a little of the olive oil, half the oregano, salt and pepper. Marinate for at least 20 minutes, or a few hours in the fridge.
Make the tzatziki: grate a third of the cucumber, squeeze out the water and stir it into the yogurt with the rest of the garlic, the dried dill and a pinch of salt.
Thread the chicken onto skewers, or leave it loose for a pan. Cook in a hot grill pan or skillet for 10 to 12 minutes, turning, until browned at the edges and cooked through.
Toss the tomato, the rest of the cucumber, the pepper, onion and olives with a little salt. Set the feta on top and drizzle with the rest of the olive oil and the remaining oregano.

Warm the pita in the pan for a minute. Eat the salad first, then the chicken with the tzatziki and a few bites of pita. Pack the second portion, with the salad and tzatziki in separate containers, for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: For the leftover lunch, eat the chicken cold on the salad, or warm it for a minute and tuck it into the pita.
ingredients: boneless skinless thighs, cut in 3 cm cubes

name: Spanish lentil stew with chorizo, carrot and spinach
inspiredBy: Spanish lentejas estofadas, the lentil pot that turns up in homes across Spain
about: A thick lentil stew with smoky paprika, a little chorizo, carrot and a whole bag of spinach wilted in, brightened with a splash of vinegar at the end. A small amount of chorizo flavours the whole pot. The **lentils bring iron, folate and fibre**, so it is a full bowl on its own.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a pot over medium heat and cook the chorizo for 3 minutes, until it has given up its orange oil. Add the onion and carrot and cook for 7 minutes, until soft.
Stir in the garlic and smoked paprika for 30 seconds, then add the crushed tomatoes, lentils, bay leaf and enough water to cover everything by about 3 cm.
Bring to a boil, then simmer gently for 30 to 35 minutes, until the lentils are tender and the stew is thick. Add a splash of water if it gets dry.
Stir in the spinach a few handfuls at a time, letting each lot wilt before adding the next, then add half the vinegar, and season with salt and pepper. Take out the bay leaf.
Serve the stew in bowls with the parsley and a splash of the rest of the vinegar. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Lentejas are even better the next day. Swap the chorizo for a spoonful of extra smoked paprika for a fully vegetarian pot.
ingredients: Spanish cured chorizo (the hard kind, not fresh Mexican), diced

name: Baked salmon with tomatoes, broccoli, zucchini and olives over a little farro
inspiredBy: Greek psari plaki, fish baked with tomato, onion and garlic, here as a tray bake with a spoonful of farro
about: Salmon baked on a tray with juicy tomatoes, broccoli, zucchini, onion and olives, then spooned over a small portion of nutty farro.
