tip: Ghee is the traditional fat for the taqliya, and a teaspoon of it is delicious here if you have some. Molokhia freezes well, so a double batch makes a quick dinner later.
ingredients: frozen minced molokhia, or fresh, or dried
quartered, plus a little thinly sliced

name: Koshari with lentils, chickpeas and a little pasta
inspiredBy: Cairo koshari, reimagined with brown rice and lentils doing most of the work, and a small handful of whole-wheat pasta
about: The Cairo street classic: lentils, rice, pasta and chickpeas under a spiced tomato sauce, crisp onions and a sharp garlic and vinegar splash. Here it leans on lentils and chickpeas for **fibre, iron and slow carbs**, with less rice and pasta than the street version.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the sliced onions with most of the oil and a pinch of salt and spread them in a single layer over two trays. Roast for 25 to 30 minutes, flipping once, until deep golden. They crisp up as they cool.
Simmer the brown rice alone in plenty of water for 10 minutes. Add the lentils and half the cumin and simmer for about 22 minutes more, until both are tender. Drain and season with a pinch of salt.
Cook the pasta in boiling salted water until just al dente, then drain.

For the sauce, warm the rest of the oil and half the garlic (finely chopped) over low heat for 1 minute. Stir in the tomato paste, the crushed tomato, the rest of the cumin, the coriander, cinnamon and salt. Simmer for 12 minutes until thick, then stir in the chickpeas to warm through.
Crush the remaining garlic and stir it into the vinegar with a splash of water. This is the daqqa.

Pile the lentils and rice into bowls, top with the pasta, the saucy chickpeas and the crispy onions. Spoon over the garlic vinegar, scatter with parsley and add a spoonful of shatta at the table. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the onions in a separate container.
tip: Cook the lentil and rice base on Sunday and keep it in the fridge, then koshari is a 25-minute job. Re-crisp the leftover onions in a dry pan before you eat them.

name: Alexandrian grilled sardines with cumin and lemon, tahini sauce and baladi salad
inspiredBy: the grilled sardines of Alexandria's fish markets, rubbed with cumin and garlic
about: Fresh sardines rubbed with garlic, cumin and lemon, grilled until the skin blisters, with a lemony tahini sauce, a crunchy tomato, cucumber, carrot and parsley salad and warm bread. The sardines bring **omega-3, vitamin D, B12 and calcium**.
steps: Mash half the garlic with the salt, then stir in the cumin, paprika, chili, half the oil and half the lemon juice. Rub this all over the sardines, inside and out, and leave them for 15 minutes.
Heat the broiler (or a grill pan or barbecue) as hot as it goes. Cook the sardines for 3 to 4 minutes on each side, until the skin is blistered and the flesh flakes off the bone.
Make the tahini sauce. Mash the rest of the garlic, stir in the tahini and half the remaining lemon juice, and thin with water until it pours like cream.
Toss the tomato, cucumber, carrot, onion and parsley with the rest of the lemon juice and oil and a pinch of salt.
Serve the sardines hot with the salad, the tahini sauce and warm bread.
tip: Ask the fishmonger to gut and scale the sardines. If you cannot find fresh ones, mackerel fillets work the same way.

name: Bamia bil lahma, okra and beef in garlicky tomato, with brown rice
inspiredBy: Egyptian bamia, the okra and meat stew every Cairo family makes, with a garlic and coriander taqliya
about: Tender okra and small chunks of beef simmered in a thick tomato sauce, finished with a sizzle of garlic and coriander, over brown rice. Okra is **rich in fibre, folate and vitamin K**, and the garlic and tomato make it taste like Friday lunch.
steps: Brown the beef in half the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat, about 5 minutes. Add the onion and cook until golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the tomato paste, the crushed tomato, the bay leaf, the pepper, half the salt and 250 ml of water. Cover and simmer gently for about 55 minutes, until the beef is nearly tender.
Start the rice in a separate pot with twice its volume of water about 35 minutes before the end, and cook until fluffy.
Add the okra whole, trimming only the stems, and simmer for another 15 minutes, until tender. Do not stir too much, it will turn slimy. Shake the pot instead.
Fry the sliced garlic with the ground coriander in the rest of the oil until golden, about 1 minute, then tip the sizzling taqliya into the pot with the lemon juice.
Serve over the rice, scattered with parsley. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: A pressure cooker cuts the beef to about 20 minutes, which makes this a weeknight dish. Cut the okra without piercing the pods and do not soak it, so it stays firm.
ingredients: small whole pods, frozen is fine

name: Sudanese chicken and peanut mullah with spinach, sorghum asida and rocket
inspiredBy: Sudanese mullah dakwa, the peanut and tomato stew, with asida made from sorghum
about: Chicken simmered with onion, tomato, ginger and ground roasted peanuts into a thick, rich stew with spinach folded in, mounded around a soft sorghum asida with a peppery rocket salad. The chicken, peanuts and spinach bring **protein, vitamin E, magnesium and folate**.
steps: Grind the peanuts with a splash of water in a mortar or small blender until they make a coarse paste. This is the dakwa.

Brown the chicken in the olive oil for 4 to 5 minutes. Lift it out. In the same pot, cook the onion until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic, baharat, cumin, ginger and chili and stir for 1 minute.
Stir in the tomato paste, then the crushed tomato and salt. Simmer for 5 minutes, then return the chicken with 300 ml of water. Cover and simmer for 20 minutes.

Stir a ladle of the sauce into the peanut paste to loosen it, then stir it all into the pot. Simmer uncovered for 10 minutes more, until thick and the oil shines at the edges. Fold in the spinach for the last 2 minutes and add the lemon juice.

Meanwhile, make the asida for tonight only. Whisk all the sorghum flour with twice its weight of cold water until smooth. Bring another twice its weight of salted water to a boil, pour in the paste while whisking, then switch to a wooden spoon and beat hard over low heat for 6 to 8 minutes, until stiff, smooth and glossy. Shape into a mound in a bowl and make a well.

Spoon the mullah into the well and serve the rocket dressed with a squeeze of lemon alongside. Asida is best fresh, so pack the second portion of mullah, with its rocket in a separate box, for tomorrow's lunch with warm pita or rice.
tip: A tablespoon of natural peanut butter stands in for the ground peanuts. Ghee is the traditional fat in Sudan and is delicious here.
ingredients: baladi bread or whole-wheat pita, for tomorrow's portion

name: Alexandrian sayadeya, spiced mackerel over caramelized onion and cumin brown rice
inspiredBy: Alexandria's sayadeya, the fisherman's rice, made with brown rice and baked mackerel instead of fried fish
about: Deeply caramelized onions and cumin cooked into brown rice, topped with spice-rubbed mackerel, sweet browned onions and a few toasted almonds, with a bright tomato and parsley relish. It is Alexandria's weekend dish. The mackerel brings **omega-3 and B12**, and the almonds add vitamin E.
steps: Cook the onions in half the oil in a wide, heavy pot over medium-low heat, stirring often, for 25 to 30 minutes, until deep brown and sweet. Add a splash of water if they start to catch. Set a third of them aside for the top.

Add half the garlic and most of the cumin to the pot, then the rice. Stir for 1 minute, then add about 2.2 times the rice's volume of boiling water and half the salt. Cover and cook on low for 35 to 40 minutes, until the rice is tender. Rest, covered, for 5 minutes.
Heat the oven to 230°C (450°F). Mash the rest of the garlic with the remaining cumin, the chili, a little of the lemon juice and the rest of the oil, and rub it all over the mackerel.
Roast the mackerel skin-side up for 10 to 12 minutes, until the skin crackles and the flesh flakes.
Toss the tomato with the parsley, the rest of the lemon juice and a pinch of salt.
Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes.

Spoon the rice onto plates, top with the mackerel, the reserved onions and the almonds, and serve the relish beside it. Keep the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the fish, rice and relish in separate containers. Reheat the rice with a splash of water. The fish is good cold or warm.
tip: Make the onions the day before, they are the slow part, and the whole dinner comes together in 45 minutes. Mullet or sea bass is what Alexandrians use, and either works here too.

name: Kebda Iskandarani, chicken liver with garlic, cumin and sweet pepper in baladi bread
inspiredBy: Alexandria's street-corner liver, a favourite sandwich in Egypt's port city, made with chicken liver
about: Quick-seared chicken liver with plenty of garlic, cumin and red pepper, finished with lemon, stuffed in warm bread with tomato and a garlicky yogurt sauce, with roasted sweet potato wedges and crisp chickpeas on the side. Liver is one of the richest foods for **iron, B12 and vitamin A**, and a small portion once a week is plenty. Skip it if you are pregnant or planning to be.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the sweet potato wedges and the chickpeas with a third of the oil, half the cumin and half the salt on a tray and roast for 30 minutes, turning once, until the wedges are golden and soft and the chickpeas are a little crisp.
Stir a little crushed garlic and a pinch of salt into the yogurt and set aside. Crush the rest of the garlic with the remaining salt and cumin.

Pat the liver dry. Heat the rest of the oil in a wide pan until very hot. Add the liver in one layer, then the red pepper and the garlic mix, and cook, tossing, for about 4 minutes in all, until the liver is browned and no pink remains. Overcooked liver goes dry, so do not go much past that.
Squeeze over the lemon juice and stir in the parsley.

Split the warm bread, spread a spoonful of the garlic yogurt inside and tuck in the tomato and liver. Serve the rest of the yogurt as a dip for the wedges and chickpeas, with the shatta for those who want it.
tip: Soaking the liver in milk or lemon water for 15 minutes mellows the flavour if you are new to liver. In Alexandria it is often served with tahini too.

name: Hummus el-sham, warm cumin chickpeas with lemon
inspiredBy: hummus el-sham, the warm chickpeas sold in paper cups on Cairo street corners
about: Chickpeas warmed with cumin, olive oil and a squeeze of lemon, like the cups sold at Cairo street corners. A bowl brings **plant protein and fibre**.
steps: Warm the chickpeas with the olive oil, cumin and a splash of the tin's liquid in a small pan or the microwave for 2 to 3 minutes.
Add the lemon juice, salt and pepper, and eat warm.

name: Termis (lupini beans) with lemon and cumin
inspiredBy: termis, the lupini beans sold from Egyptian street carts
about: Firm, salty lupini beans tossed with lemon and cumin, a famous Egyptian street snack. They bring **plant protein and fibre** for very few calories.
steps: Rinse the lupini and toss with the lemon, cumin and salt.
Squeeze each bean out of its skin with your fingers and eat the soft inside, or eat them whole.

name: Sardines with tomato and shatta on baladi bread
inspiredBy: sardin ala el-eish, tinned sardines mashed onto warm bread with a kick of shatta, a quick Cairo bite
about: Tinned sardines mashed with lemon and a spoonful of shatta, piled onto warm bread and topped with sliced tomato. The soft sardine bones bring **calcium and omega-3**.
steps: Warm the bread in a dry pan or the toaster.
Mash the sardines with the lemon, shatta and pepper, pile onto the bread and lay the tomato on top.
ingredients: tinned in water or brine, drained

name: Carrot, orange and almond smoothie
inspiredBy: carrot and orange juice from Cairo juice bars, thickened with almonds as in a koktail
about: Carrots and an orange blended into a sweet, golden drink with a few almonds for body, like the corner juice stands in Cairo. The carrots bring **a full day of vitamin A**, and the almonds and orange bring vitamin E and vitamin C. Keep the pulp in for fibre.
steps: Soak the almonds in warm water for 10 minutes, then drain. Grate the carrots.
Blend the carrots, orange, almonds and about 100 ml of cold water for 2 minutes, until as smooth as it will go.
Add the lemon juice, taste, and serve over ice. Add a little more water if it is too thick.

name: Roasted sweet potato with cinnamon and a squeeze of lemon
inspiredBy: batata, the roasted sweet potato sold from carts on winter streets in Cairo
about: A hot roasted sweet potato with a pinch of cinnamon and a squeeze of lemon, like the carts on Cairo corners in winter. It brings **vitamin A and fibre**.
steps: Prick the sweet potato and microwave it for 8 minutes, or roast at 200°C (400°F) for about 45 minutes for the best flavour, until it is soft and collapses when squeezed.
Split it open and sprinkle with the cinnamon, lemon juice and salt.
tip: Roast it on Tuesday next to the koshari onions, since the oven is already hot, and rewarm it on Wednesday.

name: Zabadi with chopped dates and cinnamon
inspiredBy: plain yogurt with dates, the way a Nile Valley kitchen would sweeten it
about: Plain yogurt with chopped dates and cinnamon, sweetened by the fruit. The yogurt brings **protein and calcium**.
steps: Stir the chopped date into the yogurt, then sprinkle with the cinnamon.
ingredients: ½ medjool or 2 small dates, chopped

name: Dates stuffed with almonds
inspiredBy: the almond-stuffed dates of Egyptian and Sudanese tea tables
about: Soft dates stuffed with whole almonds, served with tea in many Nile Valley homes. The almonds bring **vitamin E and magnesium**.
steps: Slit the dates and remove the pits. Tuck an almond into each date, and eat the rest of the almonds alongside.

name: Dates with tahini
inspiredBy: dates and tahini, a sweet, nutty pairing from the Egyptian breakfast table
about: Soft dates filled with a little tahini and a pinch of cinnamon, rich and sweet. The tahini brings **calcium, copper and vitamin E**, and the dates bring potassium.
steps: Slit the dates and remove the pits. Spoon a little tahini into each and eat.
ingredients: 1½ medjool or 3 small Egyptian dates, pitted

name: Gebna beida, olives and mint in baladi bread
inspiredBy: the Egyptian white cheese sandwich, with olives and dried mint
about: A simple Egyptian sandwich of salty white cheese, black olives and dried mint in a small pita. It brings **calcium and protein**.
steps: Split the pita and fill with the white cheese and olives. Rub the dried mint between your fingers over the top. Eat right away.

name: Zabadi bil khiar, yogurt with cucumber, garlic and mint
inspiredBy: the cool yogurt and cucumber salad on Egyptian tables, eaten with bread
about: Cool plain yogurt with grated cucumber, a little garlic and dried mint, scooped up with a few bites of bread. The yogurt brings **protein and calcium**.
steps: Squeeze the grated cucumber lightly in your hand. Stir it into the yogurt with the crushed garlic, dried mint and salt.
Eat with torn pieces of bread.
ingredients: baladi bread or whole-wheat pita, torn for scooping

name: Baladi bread with olive oil and dukkah
inspiredBy: the Egyptian snack of bread dipped in olive oil, then in dukkah
about: Warm bread, a little olive oil and a spoon of dukkah, the Egyptian mix of toasted hazelnut, sesame, coriander and cumin. It brings **vitamin E and healthy fats**.
steps: Warm the bread in a dry pan. Tear it up, dip each piece in the oil and then in the dukkah.

name: Orange with dates
inspiredBy: a Nile Valley fruit plate of oranges and dates
about: A juicy orange with a soft date alongside. The orange brings **vitamin C**, and the date adds sweetness and potassium.
steps: Peel the orange and break it into segments. Eat it with the date.

name: Oat and rye porridge with lingonberry jam and hazelnuts
inspiredBy: Swedish havregrynsgröt and Finnish ruisputro, with rye flakes half and half with oats and lingonberries on top
about: Creamy porridge of oats and rye flakes cooked in milk, with a cool spoonful of skyr, tart lingonberry jam and chopped hazelnuts on top. The oats, rye and hazelnuts bring **steady-release fibre, magnesium and vitamin E**, and the skyr adds protein.
steps: Put the oats, the rye flakes, the milk and the salt in a small pot over medium heat. Stir often until it bubbles gently and turns thick and creamy, about 8 minutes. Add a splash of water only if it thickens too fast.
While it cooks, toast the hazelnuts in a small dry pan until they smell nutty, about 3 minutes, then chop them roughly.
Spoon the porridge into a bowl and top with the skyr, the lingonberry jam and a pinch of cinnamon. Scatter with the hazelnuts.
tip: Lingonberry jam is tart on purpose, a bit like cranberry sauce with more perfume. If you can't find it, a spoon of cranberry sauce or frozen blueberries works. No rye flakes? Use all oats.
ingredients: the kind that is mostly berries

name: Skyr with blueberries, toasted oats and hazelnuts
inspiredBy: Icelandic skyr with berries, with toasted oats and hazelnuts for crunch
about: Thick, cool skyr with juicy blueberries and a crunchy mix of toasted oats and hazelnuts. It is an Icelandic way of eating skyr, and it is **ready in under ten minutes**. The skyr brings plenty of protein and calcium, and the hazelnuts bring vitamin E.
steps: Toast the oats in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring, until they smell nutty and look a shade darker, about 4 minutes. Add the hazelnuts for the last minute so they warm through.
Tip both onto a plate to cool for a minute, then roughly chop the hazelnuts.
Spoon the skyr into a bowl and tumble the blueberries over it. Scatter on the oats and hazelnuts. The berries are usually sweet enough.
tip: Toast a whole jar of oats and hazelnuts on Sunday and it keeps all week. Loosen the skyr with a splash of milk, as Icelanders do, which matters most in a big bowl. Frozen blueberries work well too, just thaw them first.

name: Open-faced rye with egg, shrimp and dill
inspiredBy: Danish smørrebrød with egg and shrimp, with skyr standing in for the mayonnaise
about: Dark rye bread with butter, radishes, sliced egg and a pile of little shrimp, with a lemony skyr and dill spoonful on top. It is a Danish smørrebrød, and a breakfast to eat slowly. The shrimp and egg bring **protein, choline and iodine**, and the rye brings fibre.
steps: Lower the egg gently into boiling water and cook for 8 minutes. Cool it under cold water, then peel and slice it.
Stir the skyr with the lemon juice, half the dill, finely chopped, and a pinch of white pepper until it is smooth and loose enough to spoon.
Butter the rye all the way to the edges. Layer on thin slices of radish, then the egg.
Spoon over the skyr, pile on the shrimp and finish with the rest of the dill. Eat it with a knife and fork, like they do in Denmark.
tip: Boil the egg the night before and this takes five minutes on a weekday morning. Dense rye is closest to Danish rugbrød, so look for German-style whole rye or pumpernickel in the bakery or packaged aisle.

name: Pickled herring on rye with egg, beets and dill
inspiredBy: Swedish sillmacka and Danish sild på rugbrød
about: Buttered dark rye topped with sweet-sour pickled herring, ruby beets, sliced egg, thin onion and a generous spoon of skyr and dill. It is a classic Nordic lunch plate that needs **almost no cooking**. The herring brings omega-3 and vitamin D, the egg adds choline, and the beets and rye bring fibre.
steps: Lower the egg gently into boiling water and cook for 8 minutes. Cool it under cold water, then peel and slice it.
Drain the herring and pat it dry. If the pieces are large, cut them into bite-size strips.
Slice the onion as thin as you can and let it sit in cold water for 5 minutes to take the edge off, then drain. Stir the skyr with half the dill, finely chopped, and a pinch of white pepper.
Butter the rye all the way to the edges. Lay on the beets and the egg, then the herring.
Spoon the skyr over, top with the onion and the rest of the dill, and eat it with a knife and fork.
tip: Boil an egg or two on Sunday night and this is a five-minute lunch. Pickled herring is salty, so a quick rinse before you pat it dry takes the edge off. Look for the plain wine or mustard kinds in the fridge section. Dense rye is closest to Danish rugbrød, so look for German-style whole rye or pumpernickel in the bakery or packaged aisle.

name: Pytt i panna with ham, a fried egg and pickled beets
about: Crisp little cubes of potato and mushroom fried with onion and smoky ham, with a fried egg on top, pickled beets on the side and a spoon of mustard. It is the Swedish "bits in a pan" supper, and a fine use of a Saturday lunch hour. The egg and ham bring protein and choline, and UV-exposed mushrooms add **a good dose of vitamin D**.
steps: Boil the potato cubes in a pot of water for 5 minutes, until they are just tender at the edges. Drain well and let them steam dry for a couple of minutes, which is what makes them crisp.
Warm most of the oil in a big non-stick pan over medium-high heat. Add the potatoes and fry, turning only now and then, until golden and crisp at the edges, about 12 minutes.

Add the mushrooms, the onion and the ham and cook until the water from the mushrooms has cooked off, the onion is soft and the ham has a few browned edges, about 6 minutes. Season with the pepper and a tiny pinch of salt, since the ham is already salty.
Push everything to one side, add the rest of the oil and fry the egg until the white is set and the yolk is still runny.
Slide the hash onto a plate with the egg on top. Serve with the pickled beets, a spoonful of mustard and a scatter of parsley.
tip: This is a great way to use up leftover boiled potatoes. Skip the boiling step and go straight to the pan.
ingredients: vitamin D mushrooms if you can find them, cut in small cubes
from the deli counter, cut in small cubes

name: Swedish-style meatballs with potatoes, creamed spinach and lingonberries
inspiredBy: Swedish köttbullar with stuvad spenat, made lean with oats soaked in milk and a light gravy
about: Small, tender meatballs with allspice and onion, a light creamy gravy, boiled potatoes, soft creamed spinach, a spoon of lingonberry jam and crisp cucumber. It makes two portions, so **tomorrow's lunch is done**. The beef brings iron, zinc and B12, and the spinach brings folate and vitamin K.
steps: Stir the oats into a little of the milk, about a third of it, and leave them for 10 minutes to swell. Meanwhile, put the potatoes on to boil in lightly salted water, about 20 minutes.
Grate the onion into a bowl. Add the beef, the soaked oats, the allspice, white pepper, a little nutmeg and most of the salt. Mix with a fork until just combined, since overworking makes them tough.
With wet hands, roll the mixture into small balls, about the size of a walnut. Chill them for 10 minutes if you have time, so they hold their shape.
Warm the oil in a large non-stick skillet over medium heat. Brown the meatballs in batches, shaking the pan to roll them, until golden all over and cooked through, about 8 minutes. Lift them out.

Mash one hot boiled potato chunk into most of the remaining milk with a splash of the potato water until smooth. Leave the empty pan on the heat for a moment so the bits on the bottom turn a shade darker, then pour in the milk slowly, scraping them up so the gravy takes their colour. Simmer for 2 or 3 minutes until it coats a spoon. Season with a pinch of salt and pepper, then slide the meatballs back in.

Wilt the spinach in a dry pot over medium heat, a big handful at a time, until soft. Squeeze out the extra water, chop it, then stir in a spoon of that gravy, a pinch of nutmeg and a pinch of salt and warm through. Dress the sliced cucumber with a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of salt.

Toss the potatoes with the chopped parsley. Serve the meatballs and gravy with the potatoes, spinach, a spoon of lingonberry jam and the cucumber. Pack the second portion, with its gravy, for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: The meatballs freeze beautifully. Cook a double batch of just the meatballs and pull a few out on a busy night. Reheat them gently in the gravy with a splash of water.
ingredients: a third for soaking the oats, the rest for the gravy and the spinach

name: Norwegian-style lapskaus with beef, rutabaga, barley and kale
inspiredBy: Norwegian lapskaus and Swedish kalops, with pearl barley and kale added
about: A thick, comforting stew of lean beef, rutabaga, carrot and potato with allspice and bay, pearl barley for chew and kale stirred in at the end. Pickled beets and a little mustard bring the acid. It makes two portions, and the **kale and carrot bring vitamins A and K** while the beef brings iron and zinc.
steps: Pat the beef dry. Warm half the oil in a large heavy pot over medium-high heat and brown the beef in two batches until deeply golden, about 5 minutes per batch. Lift it out.
Lower the heat, add the rest of the oil and the chopped onion and cook until soft and sweet, about 5 minutes. Stir in the allspice and thyme for a minute.

Return the beef to the pot with the barley, the bay leaves and the salt. Add enough water to cover everything by about 2 cm, bring to a boil, then turn the heat down and simmer gently, partly covered, for 40 minutes.

Add the rutabaga, carrot and potato in 2 cm cubes. Simmer for another 20 to 25 minutes, until everything is tender and the stew has thickened, since the edges of the potato melt into it. Top up with water if the barley has drunk it all.
Stir in the kale and cook for 5 minutes, until bright green and soft. Take out the bay leaves, stir in the mustard and most of the parsley, and taste for salt.

Serve with the pickled beets alongside and the rest of the parsley scattered over. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. The barley drinks up liquid overnight, so add a splash of water when you reheat it.
tip: A pressure cooker makes this a 40-minute dinner: brown the beef, then cook everything but the kale for 25 minutes. It also holds well in a slow cooker while you're out.

name: Lohikeitto, Finnish salmon and potato soup, with rye bread
inspiredBy: Finnish lohikeitto, made with milk in place of the cream
about: Chunks of salmon poached in a creamy, dill-flecked soup of potato and leek, with allspice and a squeeze of lemon, and buttered dark rye on the side. It is the soup Finns make on a cold night, and it makes two portions. The salmon brings **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, and the potato and leek bring potassium.
steps: Warm the oil in a pot over medium heat and cook the leek, stirring, until it is glossy and soft but not browned, about 5 minutes.
Add the potato in 2 cm cubes, the allspice, the bay leaves and the salt, with enough water to just cover. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 12 to 15 minutes until the potatoes are tender.
Cut the salmon into 3 cm chunks. Turn the heat to low, slip them in and poach gently for 3 to 4 minutes, until just opaque. Don't stir hard, or they'll break up.
Stir in the milk and warm it through without letting it boil. Add the dill, the lemon juice and the white pepper, and fish out the bay leaves.
Serve in wide bowls with the rye and a little butter. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, and reheat it gently so the salmon stays tender.
tip: A spoonful of crème fraîche on top is lovely if you have some. If you like it thicker, mash a few potato cubes against the side of the pot.

name: Ärtsoppa, Swedish yellow pea soup with pork, mustard and oat pancakes
inspiredBy: Swedish ärtsoppa with plättar, the Thursday soup, with lean pork shoulder and pancakes made from oats
about: A thick, savoury soup of whole yellow peas simmered with a piece of lean pork, onion, carrot and marjoram, served with a good spoon of mustard, then little oat pancakes with lingonberry jam. It is the Thursday supper of Swedish tradition and makes two portions. The peas bring **iron, folate and fibre**, and the pancakes bring an egg's worth of choline.
steps: The night before, cover the yellow peas with plenty of cold water and leave them to soak. Drain and rinse them in the morning.

Warm half the oil in a big pot and soften the onion, roughly chopped, for 5 minutes. Add the drained peas and the pork in one piece, cover with fresh water by about 3 cm and bring to a boil. Skim off the foam that rises.

Turn the heat down, add the carrot in small cubes, and simmer gently, partly covered, for 1 to 1½ hours, stirring now and then and skimming off any loose pea skins that float up, until the peas have fallen apart and the pork is tender.
Lift out the pork, cut it into bite-size pieces and stir it back in. Add the marjoram, thyme and salt, and mash a few peas against the pot. Add a splash of water if it is thicker than you like.

While the soup finishes, blitz the oats to a fine flour in a blender. Add the eggs and blitz again, then blitz in water a little at a time, no more than about ⅓ cup, until the batter pours like cream. Let it rest 10 minutes.
Brush a non-stick pan with a little of the rest of the oil over medium heat. Pour in small rounds of batter and cook until golden underneath and set on top, about 1 minute on each side.

Serve the soup with a spoon of mustard stirred into each bowl and a scatter of parsley, then the pancakes with the lingonberry jam. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. The soup thickens a lot, so loosen it with water when you reheat it.
tip: Split yellow peas cook in 45 minutes with no soak if you cannot find whole ones. A piece of smoked pork shoulder is the classic. In a pressure cooker, soaked whole peas and pork are done in 25 minutes. The pancakes keep in the fridge a day, and are good cold, rolled up around the jam.
ingredients: half for the soup, half for the pancakes
blitzed to a flour, for the pancakes

name: Danish-style cod fishcakes with kale and apple slaw, rye and cucumber skyr
inspiredBy: Danish fiskefrikadeller and Norwegian fiskekaker, with a New Nordic kale slaw and a light stand-in for remoulade
about: Light, springy fishcakes of fresh cod with onion, dill and a hint of nutmeg, pan-fried until golden and served with dark rye, a crunchy kale and apple slaw with sunflower seeds and a cool skyr and cucumber sauce. **Cod is one of the leanest proteins**, and it brings iodine and selenium.
steps: Cut the cod into chunks and put it in a food processor with the egg, the oats, the onion, half the dill, the salt, the white pepper and the nutmeg. Pulse into a coarse, sticky paste, then pulse in the milk a little at a time, stopping when the paste is soft but still holds its shape on a spoon. Chill it for 15 minutes so it firms up.

Massage the sliced kale with a pinch of salt for a minute until it darkens and softens. Toss it with the grated apple, half the lemon juice and a few drops of the oil, and leave it to soften while you cook. Toast the sunflower seeds in a dry pan for 2 minutes.
Stir the skyr with the diced cucumber, the rest of the dill, chopped, and the rest of the lemon juice until it makes a loose, cool sauce.
Warm the rest of the oil in a non-stick pan over medium heat. Shape the cod mixture with two wet spoons into ovals about as thick as your thumb, as the Danes do.
Fry the fishcakes for about 4 minutes on each side, until golden outside and just springy in the middle.
Scatter the sunflower seeds over the slaw and serve the fishcakes with the rye, the slaw and the cucumber skyr.
tip: Fresh cod is best, but thawed frozen cod or haddock works too. Pat it very dry first. Make a double batch if you like: cold fishcakes on buttered rye are a proper Danish lunch.
ingredients: blitzed with the cod as a binder

name: Hønsekødssuppe, Danish chicken and root vegetable soup with barley and horseradish
inspiredBy: Danish hønsekødssuppe, with pearl barley standing in for the usual small dumplings and kale and spinach for extra greens
about: A gentle chicken soup with leek, rutabaga, carrot, pearl barley, kale and a handful of spinach, finished with parsley and a spoonful of sharp horseradish stirred in at the table, with rye bread on the side. It makes two portions, and **the chicken brings protein and niacin** while the vegetables bring vitamins A, C and K.
steps: Warm the oil in a big pot and soften the leek for 4 minutes. Add the chicken, the bay leaves, the pepper and about 6 cups of cold water. Bring slowly to a simmer, skim off the foam, and simmer the chicken a full 30 minutes before the vegetables go in, since boneless thigh makes a thin broth.
Add the barley and the rutabaga and carrot in chunky cubes. Simmer for 30 minutes, until the barley is plump and the vegetables are tender.
Lift the chicken out, shred or cut it into bite-size pieces and stir it back into the soup.
Add the kale and spinach and cook for 4 minutes, until the kale is tender and bright, then stir in most of the parsley and fish out the bay leaves. Add the salt now and taste.

Ladle into wide bowls, stir a little horseradish into each one and scatter with the rest of the parsley. Serve with the rye. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. The barley drinks the broth overnight, so loosen it with water when you reheat it.
tip: Bone-in thighs with the skin off make a richer broth. Go easy on the horseradish the first time, since a little goes a long way.
ingredients: for stirring in at the table

name: Gravlax-style cured salmon with dill potatoes and mustard sauce
inspiredBy: Swedish gravlax with hovmästarsås, with a lighter cure than the traditional one
about: Salmon given a gentle, sweet cure of salt, sugar, white pepper and plenty of dill until silky, then sliced thin and served with buttery dill potatoes, a sweet-sharp Swedish mustard and skyr sauce, cucumber and crispbread. The curing is **mostly waiting**, so it's the weekend project. Salmon brings omega-3, vitamin D and B12, and the potatoes bring potassium.
steps: Start this the day before, ideally in the morning. Mix most of the salt (keep a pinch for the potatoes), most of the sugar (keep a little back for the sauce) and the white pepper with half the dill, chopped. Rub it all over the salmon, then lay the fish skin-side down in a dish.

Wrap the dish tightly with plastic and set something small and heavy on top, like a can of beans. Chill for 24 to 36 hours, turning the salmon once. A little liquid will collect, and that is exactly what should happen.
Unwrap the salmon, scrape off the dill and cure and pat it dry. Slice it thinly on the diagonal, working away from the skin and leaving the skin behind.
Boil the potatoes until a knife slides in, about 15 to 20 minutes. Drain, then toss with the butter, a big handful of the chopped dill and the pinch of salt you kept back.

Whisk the mustard, the skyr, the rest of the sugar, the oil, half the lemon juice and a little chopped dill into a smooth sauce. Slice the cucumber very thin and dress it with the rest of the lemon juice and a pinch of dill.
Fan the gravlax onto a plate with the potatoes, the cucumber and the sauce, with the crispbread alongside.
tip: This is a gentler cure than a classic gravlax, so the salmon is lightly seasoned and silky rather than firm and salty. Eat it within 2 days. Most salmon sold here has been frozen already, which is what you want for a raw cure.
ingredients: skin-on, centre-cut piece, previously frozen, as most is
most for the cure, a pinch for the potatoes
most for the cure, a little for the sauce
half for the cure, half for the potatoes and sauce
small new potatoes if you can find them, scrubbed

name: Crispbread with aged cheese and apple
about: Thin slices of nutty aged cheese on crunchy rye crispbread, with crisp apple wedges alongside. It is the everyday Swedish **ostmacka**, with calcium from the cheese and fibre from the apple and the rye.
steps: Slice the cheese thinly with a cheese slicer and lay it on the crispbread. Cut the apple into wedges and eat them on the side.
tip: Jarlsberg, Herrgård or an aged gouda all work.

name: Crispbread with aged cheese and cucumber
about: Thin slices of nutty aged cheese on crunchy rye crispbread, with cool cucumber slices and a little dill. It is a classic Swedish **ostmacka**, with calcium from the cheese and a fresh crunch.
steps: Slice the cheese thinly with a cheese slicer and lay it on the crispbread.
Top with thin slices of cucumber and a little chopped dill.
tip: Jarlsberg, Herrgård or an aged gouda all work.

name: Kefir with blueberries
inspiredBy: Swedish filmjölk with blueberries, with kefir as the nearest thing in most shops
about: A glass of cold, tangy kefir with a handful of blueberries stirred in. It is a Nordic cultured-milk snack in the spirit of Swedish filmjölk, with **protein, calcium and live cultures**.
steps: Pour the kefir into a glass or bowl and stir in the blueberries. Eat with a spoon, or blitz it into a smoothie.
tip: Scatter a spoon of the toasted oats and hazelnuts from the skyr jar on top for crunch.

name: Carrot and sunflower seed salad with lemon and dill
about: Shredded raw carrot with toasted sunflower seeds, lemon, a little oil and dill. It is a **crunchy, sweet-sharp snack** with beta-carotene from the carrot and vitamin E from the seeds.
steps: Toast the sunflower seeds in a dry pan until they smell nutty, about 2 minutes.
Grate the carrot coarsely and toss it with the lemon juice, the oil, the dill and a pinch of salt. Scatter the seeds on top.
tip: Make a bigger bowl and it keeps two days in the fridge.

name: Pickled beet and apple salad with sunflower seeds
about: Sweet-sour pickled beet with crisp apple, toasted sunflower seeds, lemon and a little dill. It is a **bright, crunchy snack in the Nordic pickle tradition**, with fibre from the beets and apple, and vitamin E from the seeds.
steps: Toast the sunflower seeds in a dry pan until they smell nutty, about 2 minutes.
Cut the beets and the apple into small cubes, keeping the apple's skin on for colour.
Toss them together with the lemon juice and the chopped dill, and scatter with the seeds.

name: Shrimp and dill on crispbread
inspiredBy: Swedish räkmacka
about: Little cooked shrimp tossed with lemon and plenty of dill, piled on crunchy rye crispbread, with peppery radish slices. It is a light take on the Swedish shrimp sandwich, and it is **high in protein, choline and iodine**.
steps: Toss the shrimp with the lemon juice, the chopped dill and a pinch of white pepper.

Spread the butter on the crispbread and lay on a few thin slices of radish. Pile the shrimp on top, or serve it on the side if it will not stack, since a big spoonful of shrimp won't all fit on the crispbread.

name: Apple and hazelnuts
about: A crisp apple with a handful of lightly toasted hazelnuts. It is a **sweet, crunchy autumn snack** in Denmark and Sweden, and the hazelnuts bring vitamin E and magnesium.
steps: Toast the hazelnuts in a dry pan until they smell nutty, about 3 minutes, then eat them with the apple cut in wedges.

name: Golden mushrooms on crispbread with parsley and lemon
inspiredBy: Swedish svampmacka, with rye crispbread in place of toasted rye bread
about: Mushrooms fried until golden in a little rapeseed oil, piled on crunchy rye crispbread with parsley, lemon and white pepper. It is a crispbread take on the Swedish svampmacka, a savoury, meaty snack. UV-exposed mushrooms bring **most of a day's vitamin D** in one plate (check the label), along with B vitamins.
steps: Warm the oil in a pan over medium-high heat and add the mushrooms. Cook, stirring now and then, until the water has cooked off and they are golden, about 6 minutes.

Season with the white pepper and a pinch of salt, stir in the lemon juice and most of the parsley, and scatter with the rest of the parsley. Spoon the mushrooms onto the crispbread just before eating, or the crispbread goes soft.
tip: Regular white or cremini mushrooms work too, but they bring almost no vitamin D. Spread sliced mushrooms in one layer in the midday sun for 15 to 30 minutes first and they make some.
ingredients: vitamin D mushrooms if you can find them, sliced

name: Steel-cut oats with blueberries, walnuts and maple
inspiredBy: a Canadian and New England porridge, with steel-cut oats, blueberries and real maple
about: Chewy, nutty steel-cut oats simmered in milk and water, then piled with juicy blueberries, toasted walnuts and sunflower seeds and a drizzle of real maple. A pot made ahead keeps for days, so weekday mornings take two minutes. The oats and blueberries bring **fibre**, and the walnuts add plant omega-3.
steps: Toast the oats in a dry pot over medium heat for about 2 minutes, stirring, until they smell nutty. Toast the walnuts and sunflower seeds in a small dry pan at the same time, about 3 minutes, and chop the walnuts.
Pour in the milk and about the same amount of water, add the cinnamon and salt, and bring to a boil. Turn the heat down so it just bubbles.
Cook uncovered, stirring now and then, until the oats are tender and creamy but still a little chewy, 20 to 25 minutes.
Spoon into a bowl and top with the blueberries, walnuts, sunflower seeds and maple.
tip: Cook a pot for three mornings at once: multiply the oats and liquid, cool it, and keep it covered in the fridge for up to 5 days. Warm a portion with a splash of milk. Frozen blueberries work just as well as fresh.

name: Egg and veggie breakfast muffins with whole-wheat toast and an orange
about: Fluffy little egg muffins baked in a tin with spinach, red pepper, scallion and sharp cheddar. One tin makes breakfast for two mornings, and they reheat in 45 seconds, with toast and a juicy orange on the side. The eggs bring **protein and choline**, and the orange adds vitamin C.
steps: Heat the oven to 180°C (350°F) and brush the cups of a muffin tin lightly with the oil.
Divide the spinach, red pepper, scallion and most of the cheddar between 4 muffin cups.
Whisk the eggs with the salt and pepper until no streaks of white are left, then pour over the vegetables, filling each cup about three quarters full. Sprinkle the last of the cheddar on top.
Bake until puffed, golden at the edges and set in the middle, about 20 minutes. Let them cool for 5 minutes, then run a knife around each one to loosen it.
Serve two warm muffins with the toast and the orange, peeled and cut into wedges.
Pack the other two muffins for tomorrow's breakfast. Cool them completely, keep them in a covered container in the fridge, and warm them in the microwave for about 45 seconds.
tip: Press the chopped spinach dry in a clean towel first, so the muffins don't weep. Bake a double tin on Sunday and freeze the extras, then pull a few out the night before.
ingredients: chopped small and pressed dry in a towel

name: Egg, back bacon and cheddar breakfast sandwich on whole-wheat toast
inspiredBy: the Canadian peameal bacon sandwich and the diner egg sandwich, on whole-wheat toast with extra spinach and tomato
about: A proper diner-style breakfast sandwich: a soft-yolk fried egg, seared Canadian back bacon, melted sharp cheddar, ripe tomato and fresh spinach on toasted whole-wheat bread, with orange wedges on the side. It is quick enough for a weekday morning and sturdy enough to eat on the way out the door. The egg and bacon bring **protein and choline**, and the whole-wheat toast adds fibre.
steps: Brush a nonstick pan with half the oil and sear the back bacon over medium-high heat for about 1 minute per side, until it has golden edges. It is ready to eat, so it only needs to brown. Move it to a plate.
Wipe the pan, add the rest of the oil and crack in the egg. Cook until the white is set and the yolk is still a little soft, about 3 minutes, flipping at the end if you like it over-easy.
Toast the bread. Lay the cheddar on the hot toast so it softens. Spread the other slice with the Dijon and layer on the spinach, tomato, bacon and egg. Add a grind of pepper and close the sandwich.
Peel the orange, cut it into wedges and serve it alongside.
tip: At the Light size, serve it open-faced on one slice. It's Canadian bacon in the US, and back bacon or peameal in Canada. Packaged back bacon is ready to eat, so 1 minute a side is plenty. Raw peameal needs 3 to 4 minutes a side. Cook the egg all the way through if you plan to wrap the sandwich for later.
ingredients: cut in wedges, on the side

name: Bison burger on a whole-wheat bun with cider slaw and pickled onion
about: A juicy, lean bison patty on a toasted whole-wheat bun with a crunchy cider slaw, ripe tomato, crisp romaine and quick-pickled onion. Bison is rich in flavour and lean, so it tastes like a great burger without the grease. The bison brings **iron, zinc and protein**, and the slaw adds crunch and vitamin C.
steps: Put the sliced onion in a small bowl with half the cider vinegar and a pinch of the salt, and stir now and then. It turns bright and tangy in about 15 minutes.
Toss the cabbage with the rest of the vinegar, half the Dijon, half the oil and a pinch of salt. Let it sit while you cook the burger so it softens a little.
Mix the bison gently with the smoked paprika, garlic powder, pepper and the rest of the salt, and shape it into a patty a little wider than the bun. Don't overwork it, or it turns tough.
Heat the rest of the oil in a heavy pan over medium-high heat. Cook the patty until it is browned and cooked through, about 4 minutes per side. Bison is lean and dries out fast, so don't overcook it.
Toast the bun in the same pan for a minute. Spread it with the rest of the Dijon, then build the burger with the romaine, patty, tomato, pickled onion and a pile of slaw.
tip: At the Light size, serve it open-faced on one bun half. Ground turkey or lean beef works if you can't find bison. Make the slaw and pickled onion on Sunday and Monday lunch is ready in 15 minutes.

name: Big chopped Cobb-style salad with blackened chicken
inspiredBy: the Brown Derby Cobb salad, with Louisiana-style blackened chicken thigh in place of poached breast, no blue cheese, and a lighter dressing
about: Crisp chopped romaine topped with rows of juicy blackened chicken, chewy browned back bacon, a hard-boiled egg, ripe tomato and creamy avocado, in a mustardy vinaigrette. The Cajun-spiced chicken gives it a Southern kick. The chicken and egg bring **protein and choline**, and the avocado adds healthy fats and potassium.
steps: Flatten the chicken with the heel of your hand or a pan, so it is an even thickness. Rub it all over with the Cajun spice and the salt.

Heat the canola oil in a heavy pan, cast iron if you have it, over medium-high heat, and turn on the fan, since the spices smoke. Sear the chicken until it is deeply browned and there is no pink in the middle, about 5 minutes per side. Let it rest for 5 minutes, then chop it. Cool it if you are making it ahead.
Lower the egg into a pot of simmering water and boil for 10 minutes. Cool it in cold water, then peel and chop.

Sear the back bacon in a dry pan over medium-high heat for about 1 minute per side, until browned and chewy. It will not go crisp, and that is fine. Chop it. Toast the bread and cut it into small croutons.
Whisk the olive oil, cider vinegar, Dijon and pepper in the bottom of a big bowl or on a platter.
Pile the romaine on top. Arrange the chicken, bacon, egg, avocado, tomato and croutons in rows. Toss it all at the table, so it stays crisp until you eat.
tip: Sear the chicken and boil the egg the night before and this is a 10 minute lunch. Crumbled blue cheese is the traditional topping if you have it. Use a mild blend for kids.
ingredients: toasted and cut in small croutons

name: Turkey and bean chili with sweet potato and spinach
about: A thick, smoky chili with lean ground turkey, kidney beans, sweet potato and a big handful of spinach wilted in at the end. A splash of cider vinegar at the finish keeps it bright. The beans and spinach bring **fibre and iron**, and the sweet potato adds vitamin A.
steps: Warm the oil in a big pot over medium heat. Cook the onion and red pepper until soft, about 7 minutes. Add the garlic, chili powder, cumin, smoked paprika and oregano and stir for 30 seconds, until fragrant.
Add the turkey and break it up with a spoon. Cook until it is no longer pink, about 6 minutes.

Stir in the crushed tomatoes, sweet potato, beans, salt and about 1 cup (250 mL) of water for the two portions. Bring to a boil, then simmer partly covered, stirring now and then, until the sweet potato is tender and the chili is thick, about 25 minutes.
Stir in the spinach and cook until it wilts, about 2 minutes. Finish with the cider vinegar and taste for salt.
Ladle into bowls and scatter with the scallion. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. It thickens overnight, so loosen it with a splash of water when you reheat.
tip: A spoonful of Greek yogurt or a little grated cheddar on top is the classic finish. Chili freezes beautifully, so double the pot if you like.

name: Sheet-pan chicken thighs with carrots, squash and apples
inspiredBy: a New England autumn roast, with the cider vinegar and mustard glaze that goes so well with chicken
about: Juicy chicken thighs roasted on one pan with sweet carrots, butternut squash, onion and apple wedges, all coated in a cider vinegar and mustard glaze, with kale crisped at the end. It is a New England autumn supper with almost no cleanup. The vegetables bring **vitamin A and fibre**, and the chicken brings protein.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Line a large sheet pan, or two if it is crowded, with parchment.

Whisk the oil, cider vinegar, Dijon, garlic, thyme, sage, salt and pepper in a big bowl. Toss the squash, carrots and onion with half of it, spread them on the pan, and roast for 15 minutes on their own. They need a head start.
Toss the chicken in the rest of the glaze and nestle it in among the vegetables. Roast for 7 minutes.

Tuck the apple wedges in among everything, stir once, and roast another 10 minutes. Scatter the kale on top and roast the last 5 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through and the vegetables are browned at the edges.
Spoon the pan juices over everything. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. It reheats well in a hot oven, a skillet or the microwave.
tip: Parsnips or small potatoes can replace the squash. If you only have bone-in thighs, give them 10 more minutes.

name: Québec-style split pea soup with back bacon and whole-wheat toast
inspiredBy: Québec soupe aux pois, with lean back bacon in place of a ham hock and kale stirred in
about: A thick, comforting split pea soup, the soupe aux pois of Québec kitchens, with carrot, celery, onion, a little smoky back bacon and the summer savory Québec cooks love, finished with kale and a splash of cider vinegar. Split peas need no soaking and melt into a spoon-coating soup. The peas bring **fibre, iron and folate**, and the kale adds calcium and vitamin C.
steps: Warm the oil in a big pot over medium heat. Cook the onion, carrot and celery until the onion is soft and starting to colour, about 8 minutes. Add the bacon and garlic and cook 2 more minutes.
Add the split peas, thyme, summer savory, bay leaf and pepper, and pour in about 5 cups (1.25 L) of water for the two portions. Bring to a boil, then turn it down to a gentle simmer.
Cook partly covered, stirring now and then so nothing sticks, until the peas have broken down into a thick soup, 50 to 60 minutes. Add a splash of water if it gets too thick.
Fish out the bay leaf. Press a few spoonfuls of the soup against the side of the pot to thicken it, then stir in the kale, cider vinegar and salt. Cook about 5 minutes, until the kale is tender.
Serve with the toast. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. It thickens in the fridge, so loosen it with water when you reheat.
tip: Yellow split peas are traditional in Québec, and green ones work too. Short on time? A pressure cooker does it in 15 minutes at high pressure. A dash of hot sauce at the table is very good.

name: Wild rice and mushroom hotdish with bison, cranberries and walnuts
inspiredBy: Midwestern hotdish, made with wild rice, mushrooms and bison, with no canned soup and no tater tots
about: A Minnesota-style hotdish built on nutty wild rice, a creamy mushroom sauce, lean ground bison, onion and celery, with a handful of spinach, tart cranberries and crunchy toasted walnuts on top. Wild rice, the manoomin that Ojibwe families have harvested for centuries, and cranberries are Great Lakes classics, and the oven does most of the work. The bison and mushrooms bring **B vitamins and iron**, and UV-treated mushrooms, if you can find them, add some vitamin D.
steps: Heat the oven to 180°C (350°F). Rinse the wild rice in a sieve.
Warm the oil in a large ovenproof pot over medium-high heat. Brown the bison, breaking it into crumbles, about 5 minutes. Add the onion and celery and cook until soft, about 5 minutes.

Add the mushrooms and cook, stirring now and then, until their water has cooked off and they are golden, about 8 minutes. Splash in the cider vinegar and scrape up the browned bits from the bottom of the pot. Stir in the garlic, thyme, sage and pepper.

Scoop about a third of the mushrooms into a blender with a ladle of hot water and blend until smooth and creamy. Stir it back into the pot with the wild rice, the salt, and about 2 cups (500 mL) of hot water for the two portions.
Cover and bake until the rice has split open and is tender and the sauce is thick, 60 to 70 minutes, or about 40 minutes if you soaked the rice in the morning.

Stir in the spinach and cranberries, cover again for 5 minutes, then taste for salt. Toast the walnuts in a dry pan until they smell nutty, about 3 minutes, and scatter them on top. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Rinse and soak the wild rice in the morning and it cooks in about 40 minutes. Ground turkey or lean beef works in place of the bison.
ingredients: toasted and chopped, for crunch on top

name: Maritime salmon cakes with sweet potato wedges and dill slaw
inspiredBy: Maritime salmon cakes, made from a tin of salmon and bound here with breadcrumbs instead of mashed potato, with sweet potato wedges on the side
about: Golden pan-seared salmon cakes made with canned pink salmon, egg, scallion and celery, with sweet potato wedges and a crunchy dill slaw. Mashing in the soft canned salmon bones is where the calcium comes from, and you will never notice them. The salmon brings **omega-3 and vitamin D**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the sweet potato wedges with a quarter of the oil and a pinch of the salt, spread them on a tray, and roast until browned and tender, about 30 minutes, turning once.

Drain the salmon into a bowl and flake it with a fork, mashing in the soft bones. Add the egg, scallion, celery, half the Dijon, half the dill, the pepper and the breadcrumbs, and mix until it holds together when squeezed. Shape into two plump patties and chill them for 10 minutes.
Toss the cabbage, kale and carrot with the cider vinegar, a drizzle of the oil, the rest of the Dijon and dill, and a pinch of salt for the slaw. Let it sit while the cakes cook.
Heat the rest of the oil in a nonstick pan over medium heat. Cook the cakes until deeply golden and hot through, about 4 minutes per side.
Serve the cakes on the slaw with the sweet potato wedges on the side.
tip: Make the patties in the morning and keep them chilled, and dinner is 10 minutes. A squeeze of lemon, if you have one, finishes them nicely.

name: Maple baked beans with wilted kale on whole-wheat toast
inspiredBy: Québec fèves au lard and Boston baked beans, simmered on the stove with maple and smoked paprika in place of salt pork
about: Creamy white beans simmered on the stove in a sweet and tangy tomato, maple and mustard sauce with smoked paprika, piled on whole-wheat toast with kale wilted in at the end. It tastes like a Saturday supper in a Maritime kitchen, with a fraction of the sugar. The beans bring **fibre, iron and folate**, and the kale adds calcium.
steps: Warm the oil in a saucepan over medium heat. Cook the onion until soft and golden, about 6 minutes. Stir in the garlic, smoked paprika and thyme for 30 seconds.

Add the beans, crushed tomatoes, maple, Dijon, half the cider vinegar, pepper, salt and about 1 cup (250 mL) of water. Bring to a boil, then simmer uncovered, stirring now and then and mashing a few beans against the pan, until the sauce is thick and glossy, about 25 minutes.
Stir in the kale for the last 5 minutes, until it wilts and turns bright green. Finish with the rest of the vinegar.
Toast the bread and pile the beans on top. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. The flavour deepens overnight.
tip: For the classic smoky taste, stir a few chopped slices of back bacon in with the onion. The beans keep 5 days in the fridge.

name: Maple-mustard roasted salmon with squash and Brussels sprouts
inspiredBy: Pacific Northwest cedar-plank salmon, roasted here on a sheet pan, with a plank if you own one
about: A tender salmon fillet glazed with maple and Dijon, roasted until just flaking, with caramelized butternut squash, crisp Brussels sprouts and quick-pickled onion on top. It is the weekend dinner that tastes like the Pacific Northwest. The salmon brings **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the squash and Brussels sprouts add vitamins A and C.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the squash and Brussels sprouts with the oil and half the salt on a large sheet pan. Roast for 20 minutes, until the squash is starting to brown.

While they roast, make the quick pickle: pack the sliced onion into a small bowl with half the cider vinegar, a little of the maple and a pinch of salt. Stir now and then, and leave it for at least 20 minutes.
Stir together the rest of the maple and vinegar with the Dijon, garlic, pepper and the rest of the salt for the glaze.

Push the vegetables to one side of the pan. Lay the salmon skin side down on a sheet of parchment, or on a soaked cedar plank, and brush it generously with the glaze. Roast until the salmon just flakes in the thickest part, 10 to 12 minutes.
Pile the pickled onion on the salmon and serve with the roasted vegetables, spooning any glaze left on the parchment over the salmon.
tip: Atlantic or coho salmon work as well as sockeye. Add about 2 minutes for a thicker, fattier fillet. For the full cedar-plank effect, soak a plank in water for an hour, set the salmon on it and roast it on the oven rack, or grill it with the lid closed.

name: Blueberry yogurt parfait with sunflower seeds and maple
about: Thick Greek yogurt layered with juicy blueberries, crunchy sunflower seeds and a drizzle of maple. It is a snack that tastes like dessert and keeps you full. The yogurt brings **protein and calcium**, and the sunflower seeds add vitamin E.
steps: Spoon half the yogurt into a glass or jar and top with half the blueberries.
Add the rest of the yogurt and blueberries, then finish with the sunflower seeds, maple and a pinch of cinnamon.

name: Cranberry and toasted sunflower seed mix
about: A handful of tart dried cranberries and crunchy toasted sunflower seeds. It fits in a pocket and is just right for a fall walk. The sunflower seeds bring **vitamin E and magnesium**.
steps: Toast the sunflower seeds in a dry pan for 3 minutes, until they smell nutty, and let them cool.
Toss them with the cranberries in a small bowl or a bag.

name: Veggie sticks with yogurt ranch dip
inspiredBy: ranch dip, made with Greek yogurt in place of mayonnaise and buttermilk
about: Crunchy carrot, celery and red pepper sticks with a creamy dill and garlic yogurt dip that tastes like ranch. It is a good-for-you snack that is genuinely fun to eat. The vegetables bring **vitamins A and C**.
steps: Stir the yogurt with the dill, garlic powder, salt and pepper, and let it sit for a few minutes.
Cut the carrot, celery and red pepper into sticks and serve them with the dip.

name: Avocado and tomato toast
about: Creamy avocado mashed onto crunchy whole-wheat toast with juicy tomato, black pepper and a pinch of smoked paprika. It is a snack that is somewhere between breakfast and lunch. The avocado brings **healthy fats and potassium**.
steps: Toast the bread until golden and crisp.
Mash the avocado with the salt and pepper and spread it on the toast. Top with the tomato slices, a pinch of smoked paprika and another grind of pepper.

name: Baked cinnamon apple with walnuts and maple
about: A warm apple with the core scooped out, filled with chopped walnuts, maple and cinnamon and baked until soft. It tastes like apple pie without the crust. The apple and walnuts bring **fibre and plant omega-3**.
steps: Heat the oven to 190°C (375°F). Scoop the core out of the apple, leaving the bottom intact, and set it in a small baking dish.
Mix the walnuts, maple and cinnamon and spoon the mixture into the apple.
Pour a splash of water around the apple and bake until it is soft but still holding its shape, about 25 minutes. Eat it warm.
tip: No oven? Microwave it for 3 to 4 minutes, until soft.

name: Juicy orange wedges
about: A big, juicy orange cut into wedges. It is the simplest snack there is, and it keeps in a lunch bag. The orange brings **vitamin C** and a little fibre.
steps: Peel the orange and break it into segments, or cut it into wedges with the peel on and eat them straight off the rind.

name: Blueberry and spinach milk smoothie
about: A cold blender smoothie of milk, blueberries and a handful of spinach with a touch of maple. You taste the blueberries, not the spinach. The milk brings **protein and calcium**.
steps: Put the milk, blueberries, spinach and maple in a blender.
Blend until completely smooth, about 1 minute, and drink right away.

name: Apple slices with sharp cheddar
about: Crisp apple slices with a few slabs of sharp cheddar. It is a New England classic, sweet, salty, crunchy and creamy in one bite. The cheddar brings **protein and calcium**.
steps: Slice the apple into wedges.
Cut the cheddar into slabs and eat them together.

name: Crispy roasted white beans with smoked paprika
about: White beans roasted until crunchy outside and creamy inside, tossed with olive oil, smoked paprika and salt. It is a high-protein snack you can eat by the handful. The beans bring **protein, fibre and iron**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Pat the beans very dry with a clean towel, so they crisp instead of steaming.
Toss them with the olive oil, smoked paprika and salt, and spread them on a tray in a single layer.
Roast, shaking the tray every 10 minutes, until the beans are crisp and golden, 30 to 35 minutes. Let them cool for 5 minutes, since they crisp up more as they cool.
tip: They are best the day they are made. Roast them on a lower rack alongside Monday's chicken or Friday's sweet potato wedges, since the oven is already at 220°C. A double batch keeps in an open container at room temperature for a day.
ingredients: canned, drained, rinsed and patted very dry

name: Greek yogurt with apple, toasted walnuts and cinnamon
about: Thick Greek yogurt topped with diced apple, warm toasted walnuts and a dusting of cinnamon. It is a creamy, crunchy snack that feels like a treat. The yogurt brings **protein and calcium**, and the walnuts add plant omega-3.
steps: Toast the walnuts in a dry pan over medium heat until they smell nutty, about 3 minutes, and chop them roughly.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl and top with the diced apple, the walnuts and the cinnamon.

name: Maple-cinnamon roasted sweet potato rounds
about: Thick rounds of sweet potato roasted until caramelized at the edges, with a little maple and cinnamon. They are soft inside, sweet, and easy to eat with your hands. The sweet potato brings **vitamin A and potassium**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Cut the sweet potato into rounds about 1 centimetre thick and toss them with the oil and salt.
Spread them on a tray and roast, turning once, until soft and browned at the edges, about 25 minutes.
Drizzle with the maple, dust with the cinnamon and eat warm.

name: Egg besan chilla with fresh methi and peanut-green chutney
inspiredBy: Punjabi methi besan cheela, with eggs in the batter (anda chilla)
about: Thin, savoury chickpea-flour pancakes with egg, onion, fresh fenugreek leaves and ajwain, served hot with a green chutney thickened with roasted peanuts. A quick breakfast with **protein, choline and folate** in every bite. Anda chilla is a home twist on the classic besan cheela, a little closer to a spiced omelette.
steps: Whisk the besan with the turmeric, hing, half the salt and a few spoonfuls of cold water until completely smooth. Rub the ajwain between your palms to wake it up, then add it. Beat in the eggs and stir in the onion, fenugreek leaves and half the green chili. The batter should pour like thin pancake batter, so add a splash more water if it is thick.

Toast the peanuts in a dry pan for 3 to 4 minutes, until golden. Make the chutney: blitz them with all the cilantro and the rest of the green chili, the ginger, lemon juice, a pinch of salt and a splash of water until it is a thick green sauce.

Warm a non-stick pan over medium heat and wipe it with a little of the oil. Pour in half the batter and spread it thin with the back of the ladle. Cook until the top looks set and the underside is golden with brown spots, about 3 minutes.
Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edge, flip and cook 1 minute more. Repeat with the rest of the batter and eat the chillas hot with the green chutney.
tip: Frozen methi from a South Asian grocery works when fresh is hard to find. Serve with a spoonful of lime pickle if you have a jar. If a chilla sticks or tears, the pan is too cool or the batter too thick.
ingredients: leaves picked off the stems, finely chopped
half chopped, half for the chutney

name: Egg and paneer bhurji with spinach and a hot roti
inspiredBy: Punjabi and Delhi dhaba-style anda bhurji, with paneer folded in
about: Soft, spiced scrambled eggs and crumbled paneer with golden onion, tomato, spinach and ginger, scooped up with a fresh whole-wheat roti. It is the dhaba breakfast of Punjab and Delhi. The eggs and paneer bring **protein, choline and calcium**.
steps: Mix the atta with a pinch of the salt and enough warm water to make a soft dough. Knead for a minute, cover it and let it rest. Squeeze the chopped spinach dry in your fist or a clean towel, so it does not water down the eggs.

Warm the oil in a non-stick pan over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and let them sizzle for about 10 seconds until they smell toasty. This is a tadka: whole spices bloomed in hot oil, which flavours everything that goes in next.

Add the onion, ginger and green chili and cook until the onion is soft and golden, about 5 minutes. While it cooks, roll the dough into a thin round and cook it in a hot, dry pan for about a minute on each side, until it puffs and has brown spots. Wrap it in a clean towel.
Stir the turmeric, Kashmiri chili and tomato into the onion and cook until the tomato breaks down into a thick paste, about 3 minutes. Add the spinach and stir for 1 minute.

Beat the eggs with the rest of the salt and pour them in, then crumble in the paneer. Stir slowly, folding from the edges, until the eggs are softly set and still glossy, about 2 minutes. Off the heat, crush the kasuri methi over the top. Serve with the warm roti.
tip: To make this a 10-minute breakfast, knead the dough the night before (it keeps two days in a covered bowl in the fridge), or warm a store-bought whole-wheat roti in a dry pan.

name: Vegetable daliya with masoor dal and a boiled egg
inspiredBy: Punjabi daliya, the savoury cracked-wheat porridge
about: Cracked wheat simmered with red lentils, cauliflower, tomato and green peas into a savoury, spiced porridge, finished with a cumin and hing tadka and a boiled egg on top. Daliya is a comforting Punjabi breakfast that keeps you full all morning. The wheat and lentils bring **fibre, iron and folate**.
steps: Lower the egg into a small pot of boiling water and cook for 9 minutes. Cool under cold water and peel. Rinse the lentils and the cracked wheat together in a sieve and drain.

Warm the oil in a heavy pot over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and the hing and let them sizzle for about 10 seconds. This is the tadka: whole spices bloomed in hot fat. Add the onion, ginger and green chili and cook until the onion is soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the turmeric and tomato and cook until the tomato turns soft and jammy, about 3 minutes.

Add the wheat, lentils, cauliflower and salt, and pour in about 3 times as much water as the wheat and lentils together. Bring to a boil, then turn the heat down, cover and simmer, stirring now and then, until everything is soft and the porridge is thick, about 20 minutes. Stir in the peas for the last 5 minutes.
Spoon into a bowl and serve with the halved egg on top.
tip: Make it the night before and reheat with a splash of water, or use a pressure cooker and have it ready in 10 minutes.
ingredients: coarse bulgur, or daliya from a South Asian grocery

name: Methi missi paratha with boiled eggs and dahi
inspiredBy: Punjabi missi roti and methi paratha, in one
about: Soft whole-wheat parathas made with a little besan, fresh fenugreek leaves and ajwain, cooked on a hot pan with a brush of ghee and served with boiled eggs and cold yogurt. Missi paratha is a Punjabi favourite, and the besan and methi **add protein, iron and calcium** to ordinary paratha dough. It is the slow, relaxed breakfast for the weekend.
steps: Lower the eggs into a pot of boiling water and cook for 9 minutes. Cool them under cold water and peel.

In a large bowl, mix the atta, besan, fenugreek leaves, cilantro, cumin seeds, hing, Kashmiri chili, amchur and salt. Rub the ajwain between your palms and add it too, since it is what makes missi roti taste like missi roti. Add warm water a splash at a time and knead into a soft, slightly tacky dough, about 3 minutes. Go easy on the water, because the fresh leaves give some off. Cover and rest for 15 minutes.
Divide the dough into 1 or 2 balls, depending on how hungry you are. Dust with a little atta and roll each into a thin round, about 15 cm (6 in) across.

Heat a dry pan or tawa over medium-high heat. Cook a paratha for 30 seconds, flip it and brush the top with a little ghee. Flip again, brush the other side with ghee and cook until golden with brown spots, about 1 minute more. Wrap the first paratha in a clean towel to keep it soft while you cook the second.
Serve the parathas hot with the boiled eggs, halved and sprinkled with a pinch of salt and black pepper, and a bowl of cold dahi.
tip: Frozen methi works too. A spoonful of lime or mango pickle next to the dahi is how many Punjabi homes serve it.
ingredients: leaves picked off the stems, finely chopped

name: Chicken tikka and chana chaat
inspiredBy: Lahore chicken tikka chaat and Delhi chana chaat, as a full lunch
about: Yogurt-marinated chicken seared until charred at the edges, tossed with chickpeas, onion and tomato, then finished with a cilantro, chili and lemon chutney, chaat masala and a cool spoon of dahi. Half of the chickpeas are crisped in the pan for crunch. It is a Lahore and Delhi street-food lunch with **plenty of protein and fibre**.
steps: Toast the cumin seeds in a dry pan for 30 seconds until fragrant, then crush them. Stir a third of the yogurt with the Kashmiri chili, half the lemon juice, half the crushed cumin and a pinch of the chaat masala and black salt. Add the chicken, stir to coat and leave it for 15 minutes.
Make the chutney: blitz the cilantro and green chili with the rest of the lemon juice, a pinch of black salt and a splash of water, until it is a loose green sauce.

Warm the oil in a pan over medium-high heat. Cook the chicken, turning it now and then, until it is browned and cooked through, about 6 minutes. Tip it into a bowl. In the same pan, fry half the chickpeas with half the chaat masala for about 4 minutes, shaking the pan, until they are crisp at the edges.
Add the rest of the chickpeas, the tomato, onion and the remaining cumin, chaat masala and black salt to the chicken and toss.
Spoon it onto a plate, drizzle with the chutney, add the rest of the yogurt and scatter the crisp chickpeas and the pomegranate seeds over the top. Eat right away.
tip: For a Monday lunch, marinate and cook the chicken and crisp the chickpeas on Sunday night. Keep the chutney and yogurt in separate containers and assemble at lunch. Leave out the green chili if you like it mild.
ingredients: a third for the marinade, the rest on top

name: Rajma masala with brown basmati rice
inspiredBy: Punjabi and Delhi rajma chawal, made with canned beans
about: Red kidney beans simmered in a thick, gingery onion and tomato gravy with a bloom of bay leaf and cumin, served over brown basmati with raw onion rings and a spoon of cold dahi. It is the great everyday comfort food of Punjab and Delhi. The beans bring **iron, folate and plenty of fibre**.
steps: Rinse the rice and simmer it in a pot with plenty of boiling water, partly covered, until tender, about 25 minutes. Drain it like pasta.

While the rice cooks, warm the oil in a pan over medium heat. Add the bay leaf and cumin seeds and let them sizzle and darken a shade, about 15 seconds. Add the chopped onion and cook until deep golden, about 8 minutes.

Add the ginger and garlic and stir for 1 minute. Stir in the crushed coriander, Kashmiri chili and the tomato and cook, pressing with the spoon, until the tomato turns into a thick, jammy paste that leaves the oil at the edges, about 6 minutes.
Add the kidney beans, the salt and about a cup of water. Simmer for 15 minutes, mashing a few beans against the side of the pan so the gravy thickens. Stir in the garam masala.

Spoon the rajma over the rice, pile the raw onion rings on top with a pinch of salt and serve with the cold dahi. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, and keep the onion rings and dahi fresh.
tip: The beans and rice both freeze well in portions. Cook the rice while the masala simmers and both are ready together.
ingredients: 60 g chopped for the gravy, the rest sliced into rings

name: Masoor dal khichdi with cauliflower and a ghee tadka
inspiredBy: Punjabi dal khichdi, made with brown basmati and cauliflower
about: Red lentils and brown basmati simmered together with cauliflower, tomato and ginger into a soft, comforting khichdi, topped with a sizzling ghee tadka of cumin, garlic and dried red chili, with a spoon of cold dahi. Khichdi and dahi is the classic easy weekend meal across Punjab, Delhi and Lahore. The lentils bring **iron, folate and fibre**.
steps: Rinse the lentils and rice together in a bowl of water until it runs mostly clear, then drain.

Put them in a heavy pot with the cauliflower, tomato, ginger, turmeric, salt and about 5 times as much water as the rice and lentils together. Bring to a boil, then turn the heat down, partly cover and simmer, stirring now and then, until the rice and lentils are completely soft and the khichdi is thick like porridge, about 40 minutes. Add a little hot water if it gets too stiff. Stir in the spinach for the last 2 minutes.

Now the tadka. Warm the ghee in a small pan until it shimmers. Add the cumin seeds and hing, and as soon as the seeds sizzle, add the garlic and the dried red chili. Fry for 30 seconds, until the garlic is just golden, then pour the sizzling ghee over the khichdi.
Spoon the khichdi into a bowl and serve with the cold dahi alongside.
tip: A pressure cooker makes this in 15 minutes. Khichdi thickens as it sits, so loosen it with hot water if you eat it later.

name: Dal palak tadka with brown basmati and cucumber raita
inspiredBy: Punjabi dhaba dal tadka, made with masoor and spinach
about: Creamy red lentil dal with spinach, finished with a sizzling tadka of ghee, cumin, hing, garlic and dried red chili and a squeeze of lemon, over brown basmati with a cool cucumber raita. It is the dal you find on every Punjabi table, and it gives you **lentil protein, iron and folate**. It makes two portions, and the second one is tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Rinse the lentils until the water runs mostly clear. Put them in a large pot with the turmeric, half the salt and about 4 times the volume of water. Bring to a boil, then simmer, partly covered, until the lentils are completely soft and falling apart, about 20 minutes. Skim off any foam, and whisk briefly so the dal turns creamy.
While the dal cooks, rinse the rice and simmer it in a pot with plenty of boiling water, partly covered, until tender, about 25 minutes. Drain it like pasta.

In a small pan, warm a third of the ghee over medium heat and cook the chopped onion until golden, about 7 minutes. Stir it into the dal with the rest of the salt, add the spinach and simmer for 5 minutes, until the spinach has wilted into the dal.

Now the tadka, the sizzling finish. Warm the rest of the ghee in a small pan until it shimmers. Add the cumin seeds and hing, and as soon as the seeds sizzle and darken a shade, about 15 seconds, add the garlic and the dried red chili. Fry for 30 seconds, until the garlic is just golden, then pour the whole sizzling pan over the dal. Squeeze over the lemon juice.
Squeeze the grated cucumber dry and stir it into the yogurt with the rest of the onion, finely chopped, and a pinch of salt for a quick cucumber raita.
Serve the dal over the rice with the raita alongside. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the raita in a small container. The dal and the rice reheat well with a splash of water.
tip: Toor dal works too: soak it for 30 minutes and cook it for 35 to 40 minutes, or 15 minutes in a pressure cooker.
ingredients: 40 g chopped for the dal, the rest for the raita

name: Chicken karahi with whole-wheat roti
inspiredBy: Lahori chicken karahi, with less oil and a roti on the side
about: Chicken seared in a hot pan, then cooked down in its own tomato juices with plenty of fresh ginger, black pepper and green chili until the sauce clings. This is the way Lahore does it, with no onion and no cream. The chicken gives **lean protein and B vitamins**, and tomorrow's lunch is already made.
steps: Mix the atta with warm water into a soft dough, knead for a minute, cover and rest it.

Warm the oil in a wide, heavy pan or karahi over high heat. Add the chicken and sear it, stirring often, until it loses its pink colour and starts to brown, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and the grated ginger and stir for 30 seconds.

Add the tomato, black pepper, crushed coriander and cumin, half the green chili and the salt. Turn the heat to medium-high and cook, pressing the tomatoes with the back of the spoon, until they collapse and oil shines around the edges of the sauce, about 15 minutes. Add a splash of water only if it starts to stick.
Take the pan off the heat. Beat the yogurt until smooth and stir it in constantly so it does not split. Return to a low heat and simmer 3 to 5 minutes, until the sauce is thick and coats the chicken.
Finish with the lemon juice, the ginger matchsticks, the rest of the green chili and the cilantro.
While the tomatoes cook down, roll thin rounds from the rested dough and cook them in a hot, dry pan for about a minute on each side until they puff and have brown spots. Wrap them in a clean towel.
Serve the karahi hot with the rotis. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with its rotis wrapped in foil.
