tip: Warmed store-bought whole-wheat rotis save ten minutes. Chicken thighs stay juicy when reheated, so they are better than breast here.
ingredients: half grated, half cut into thin matchsticks

name: Sarson da saag with paneer, roti and salted lassi
inspiredBy: Punjabi sarson da saag, with paneer
about: Mustard greens cooked down with ginger and garlic, thickened with a spoonful of cornmeal, finished with a sizzling ghee, garlic and chili tarka, with soft paneer folded in. A warm roti and a glass of salted lassi finish it. The greens give you **vitamin K, folate and calcium**, and it is the heart of a Punjabi winter table.
steps: Mix the atta with warm water into a soft dough, knead for a minute, cover and rest it.

Put the mustard greens in a large pot with a splash of water, cover and cook for 18 to 20 minutes, until they are completely soft. Let it cool a little, then blend or mash it with the grated garlic and the ginger into a thick, slightly coarse purée.
Warm half of the ghee in a wide pot over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds, and when they sizzle, add the onion. Cook until the onion is deep golden, about 8 minutes.
Stir in the green purée, the cornmeal and the salt. Simmer on low for 15 minutes, stirring often, until thick and glossy. Add a splash of water if it gets too dry.
Fold in the paneer, crush the kasuri methi over the top and simmer 3 minutes, just until the paneer is warm through.
While the saag simmers, roll thin rounds from the rested dough and cook them in a hot, dry pan for about a minute on each side until they puff and have brown spots. Wrap them in a clean towel.
Now the tarka. Warm the rest of the ghee in a small pan, add the sliced garlic, hing and dried red chili and fry for 30 seconds, until the garlic is golden. Pour it over the saag.

Whisk the yogurt with ¾ cup of cold water and a pinch of salt into a thin, drinkable lassi. Serve the saag with the rotis and a glass of lassi. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with its rotis wrapped in foil and the lassi in a jar.
tip: Warmed store-bought whole-wheat rotis save time. Any plain dahi works for the lassi: thin Greek yogurt with water to match. The saag freezes well without the rotis.
ingredients: 4 g grated, the rest sliced for the tarka
cornmeal, also sold as makki atta

name: Mackerel curry with mustard seed, ginger and tomato
inspiredBy: Punjabi machhi curry and Karachi machli salan, with Atlantic mackerel
about: Chunks of Atlantic mackerel simmered in an onion and tomato masala with ginger, brown mustard seeds, Kashmiri chili and amchur, finished with cilantro and served with a warm roti. The rich fish stands up to the spices, and it is one of the best sources of **omega-3 and vitamin D** you can buy.
steps: Rub the mackerel with the turmeric, a pinch of the salt and a good pinch of the amchur and let it sit for 10 minutes. The sour spice tames the strong fish smell.
Mix the atta with warm water into a soft dough, knead for a minute and rest it.
Warm the oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Add the mustard seeds and let them pop for about 15 seconds, then add the onion and cook until golden, about 8 minutes.
Add the ginger, garlic, Kashmiri chili and crushed coriander and stir for 1 minute. Add the tomato and the rest of the salt and cook until it collapses into a thick paste, about 8 minutes.

Pour in a cup of water, stir in the rest of the amchur and bring to a simmer. Lay in the fish pieces, cover and cook gently for 8 to 10 minutes, until the fish is opaque and flakes easily. Shake the pan rather than stirring so the pieces stay whole. Scatter the cilantro on top.
Roll the dough into thin rounds and cook them in a hot, dry pan for about a minute on each side until they puff and have brown spots. Serve the curry with the rotis.
tip: Frozen Atlantic mackerel fillets work well. Trout or arctic char also work, with a little less cooking time.
ingredients: fillets or steaks, cut into thick pieces, bones in or out
brown mustard seeds (rai) if you have them

name: Nihari-inspired goat stew with whole-wheat roti
inspiredBy: Nihari from Old Delhi, Lucknow and Lahore, which normally cooks overnight on bone-in shank
about: Bone-in goat shoulder simmered until it falls off the bone in a deep, golden gravy of browned onion, ginger, black pepper, cardamom, cinnamon and cloves, thickened with a little atta and finished with fresh ginger and lemon. Real nihari cooks overnight, so this is a faster home version of the Old Delhi, Lucknow and Lahore classic. Goat is lean and high in **iron, zinc and B12**.
steps: Mix the Kashmiri chili, black pepper, dry ginger, cardamom, cinnamon and cloves in a small bowl. This is the nihari spice mix.
Warm the oil in a heavy pot over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring often, until it is deep golden brown, about 15 minutes. Stir in the grated ginger and garlic for 1 minute.
Add the goat, with the bones, and brown it on all sides for about 8 minutes. Stir in the spice mix and the salt and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.

Pour in enough water to cover the meat by about 2 cm (1 in) and bring to a boil. Cover, turn the heat to very low and cook for 2 to 2½ hours, until the goat is tender and falling off the bone. Top up with hot water if the pot gets dry.

Whisk 15 g of the atta (about 2 tablespoons) with cold water until smooth. Stir it into the stew and simmer for the last 15 minutes, stirring, so the flour cooks out and the gravy turns thick and glossy.
Mix the rest of the atta with warm water into a soft dough, rest it, then roll small, thin rounds and cook them in a hot, dry pan for about a minute on each side until they puff and have brown spots.
Ladle the nihari into bowls and top with the ginger matchsticks and a squeeze of lemon. Eat it with the rotis. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with its rotis wrapped in foil.
tip: A pressure cooker makes the goat tender in 45 minutes. Bone-in lamb shoulder works too if goat is hard to find. A ready nihari masala box from a South Asian grocery can stand in for the spices.
ingredients: boneless weight. Buy about 235 g of bone-in curry-cut shoulder and keep the bones in the pot
15 g thickens the stew, the rest is for small rotis
half grated, half cut into thin matchsticks

name: Tandoori-spiced salmon with roasted cauliflower and okra, mint raita and roti
inspiredBy: Punjabi fish tikka and tandoori gobi, roasted on one tray
about: Salmon in a tangy yogurt, ginger and ajwain marinade, roasted on one tray with cauliflower and okra under the broiler, then finished with chaat masala and served with a cool mint raita and a warm roti. It has the char and tang of tandoori fish and needs only your oven. The salmon brings **omega-3 and vitamin D**.
steps: Mix the atta with warm water into a soft dough, knead for a minute, cover and rest it. Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F).

In a bowl, mix a third of the yogurt with the lemon juice, ginger, garlic, ajwain (rubbed between your palms), Kashmiri chili and half the salt. Coat the salmon in this marinade, cover and chill for 30 minutes, no longer than 2 hours.
Toss the cauliflower and okra on a baking tray with the oil and the rest of the salt. Roast for 15 minutes, turning once, until they are browned in spots.

Push the vegetables to one side, lay the salmon on the tray and roast for 10 to 12 minutes, until it flakes easily and the marinade has browned at the edges. Finish with a minute under the broiler if you want more char.

While it roasts, make the raita. Stir the mint into the rest of the yogurt with a pinch of salt and a splash of cold water. Roll thin rounds from the rested dough and cook them in a hot, dry pan for about a minute on each side until they puff and have brown spots.
Sprinkle the vegetables and salmon with the chaat masala and serve with the raita and the rotis.
tip: Trout or arctic char work as well as salmon.
ingredients: a third for the marinade, the rest for the raita

name: Masala chaas with almonds
inspiredBy: Punjabi spiced chaas
about: A cold, thin spiced yogurt drink with roasted cumin, mint and chaat masala, with a handful of almonds on the side. It is the Punjabi way to cool down and settle a heavy meal. It gives **protein and calcium** with very little sugar.
steps: Toast the cumin seeds in a dry pan for 30 seconds until fragrant, then crush them.
Whisk the yogurt with about a cup of cold water, the crushed cumin, mint, chaat masala and black salt until it is frothy and thin enough to drink.
Pour it over ice and drink it cold, with the almonds on the side.
tip: Any plain dahi works: thin Greek yogurt with water to match.

name: Pomegranate raita with almonds
about: Cold, thick yogurt with sparkling pomegranate seeds, roasted cumin and chaat masala, with a few toasted almonds on top. It is a raita you can eat with a spoon. It is **high in calcium and protein**, and the almonds add vitamin E.
steps: Toast the cumin seeds in a dry pan for 30 seconds until fragrant, then crush them. Toast the almonds in the pan for 3 to 4 minutes, until golden, and chop them.
Stir the yogurt with the crushed cumin, chaat masala and black salt. Spoon into a bowl and scatter the pomegranate seeds and almonds on top.

name: Fruit chaat with apple, guava and orange
inspiredBy: Pakistani and Delhi street-style fruit chaat
about: Chopped apple, guava and orange segments tossed with lemon, chaat masala and a little black pepper, the way fruit chaat is sold on the street in Lahore and Delhi. It is sweet, sour and a little salty. Guava and orange **bring vitamin C and fibre**.
steps: Toss the apple, guava and orange with the lemon juice, chaat masala and black salt and black pepper.
Let it sit for a few minutes so the fruit gets juicy, and eat it.
tip: If guava is hard to find or rock-hard, use more apple and a pear.

name: Guava with chaat masala
inspiredBy: Street-style masala guava
about: A ripe guava cut into wedges and sprinkled with lemon and chaat masala, the way it is sold on the street in Lahore and Delhi. It is sweet, sour and salty, with **more vitamin C than an orange** and plenty of fibre.
steps: Arrange the guava on a plate, squeeze over the lemon juice and sprinkle with the chaat masala and black salt and black pepper.
tip: Ripe guava gives a little when pressed. If it is hard, leave it on the counter for a few days.

name: Guava lassi
inspiredBy: Punjabi fruit lassi
about: Ripe guava blended with cold yogurt and a pinch of black pepper into a fragrant lassi and strained smooth. It is creamy and lightly sweet, with **protein and vitamin C**.
steps: Put the guava, yogurt, black pepper, salt and about three quarters of a cup of cold water in a blender.
Blend until completely smooth, then strain through a sieve to catch the seeds. Pour over ice and drink it cold.
tip: Frozen guava pulp from a Latin or South Asian grocery needs no straining.

name: Masala roasted chickpeas
inspiredBy: Roasted chana, a common North Indian tea-time snack
about: Chickpeas roasted until crisp and tossed with cumin, amchur and chaat masala. They are a crunchy, tangy snack with **protein and fibre** that keeps you going until dinner.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Pat the chickpeas completely dry with a clean towel, because dry chickpeas turn crisp.
Toss them with the oil and the Kashmiri chili on a baking tray in a single layer. Roast for 20 minutes, shaking the tray halfway.
Add the cumin seeds and roast 5 to 8 minutes more, until the chickpeas are golden and crunchy. Toss with the amchur and chaat masala and black salt while they are hot.
tip: Make a big tray on Sunday and keep it in a jar. They soften after a few days.

name: Apple and almonds
about: A crisp apple with a handful of almonds. It is simple and sweet, and the almonds bring **vitamin E and crunch**.
steps: Slice the apple and eat it with the almonds.

name: Pomegranate and almonds
about: A bowl of ruby pomegranate seeds with a handful of almonds, juicy and crunchy. Pomegranate brings **vitamin C and fibre**, and the almonds add vitamin E.
steps: Scoop the seeds out of the pomegranate into a bowl and eat them with the almonds.

name: Apple chaat
about: Crisp apple wedges tossed with lemon, chaat masala and black pepper. It is a fast, sour and salty snack and a good way to eat an apple. The skin keeps the **fibre** in.
steps: Toss the apple wedges with the lemon juice, chaat masala and black salt and black pepper, and eat right away.

name: Peanut chaat with kachumber
inspiredBy: Moongphali chaat
about: Crunchy cucumber, tomato and onion, the cooling salad served beside every Punjabi meal, dressed with lemon and chaat masala and topped with warm toasted peanuts. It is a moongphali chaat, a street snack in Delhi and Lahore. It is fresh, sour and crunchy, with **niacin and vitamin E** from the peanuts.
steps: Toast the peanuts in a dry pan for 3 to 4 minutes, shaking often, until golden.
Toss the cucumber, tomato and onion with the lemon juice and chaat masala and black salt, and scatter the warm peanuts over the top.

name: Haldi doodh with almonds
inspiredBy: Punjabi haldi doodh
about: Warm milk simmered with turmeric, a pinch of black pepper and a little fresh ginger, with a few almonds alongside. Haldi doodh is the golden milk that Punjabi families drink in the evening. A glass has **calcium, vitamin D and B12**, and the pepper helps your body use the turmeric.
steps: Pour the milk into a small pot and add the turmeric, black pepper and ginger. Warm over medium-low heat, stirring now and then, until it is steaming and just starting to bubble at the edges, about 5 minutes.
Strain it into a mug and drink it warm with the almonds on the side.
tip: A teaspoon of honey makes it softer and sweeter.

name: Masala peanuts
inspiredBy: Roadside masala moongfali
about: Raw peanuts toasted in a dry pan until golden, then tossed with a little onion, tomato, lemon and chaat masala. It is the crunchy moongfali masala sold at roadside stalls in Delhi and Lahore. Peanuts bring **niacin, vitamin E and plant protein**.
steps: Toast the peanuts in a dry pan over medium heat, shaking often, until they are golden and smell nutty, about 4 minutes. Let them cool for a minute.
Toss the warm peanuts with the onion, tomato, cilantro, lemon juice, chaat masala and black salt and salt, and eat right away while they are still crunchy.

name: Pomegranate chaat
about: Ruby pomegranate seeds tossed with lemon, chaat masala and a little black pepper. It is a sweet, sour and salty snack, and the seeds bring **vitamin C and fibre**.
steps: Scoop the seeds out of the pomegranate into a bowl.
Toss them with the lemon juice, chaat masala and black salt and black pepper and eat right away.

name: Cucumber with chaat masala
inspiredBy: Street-cart cucumber chaat
about: Cold cucumber spears sprinkled with lemon, chaat masala and a pinch of black salt, the way they are sold from street carts across Punjab and Delhi. It is crisp, sour and salty, and very light. The cucumber brings **water, crunch and a little vitamin K**.
steps: Arrange the cucumber on a plate.
Squeeze over the lemon juice and sprinkle with the chaat masala and black salt. Eat right away.

name: Menemen with white cheese, Turkish eggs with tomato and pepper
about: Turkey's favourite scramble: tomatoes and green pepper cooked down until jammy, then softly set eggs and a little crumbled white cheese stirred through, with Aleppo pepper. You eat it straight from the pan, scooping it up with warm lavash. The eggs and tomatoes bring **protein, choline and lycopene** for a morning that lasts.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a small, wide pan over medium heat. Add the onion and green pepper and cook until soft but not browned, about 4 minutes.
Add the tomato with the Aleppo pepper, black pepper and salt. Cook, stirring and mashing now and then, until it breaks down into a thick, jammy sauce, about 5 minutes.

Crack the eggs straight into the pan, scatter over the feta and stir it all gently through the tomatoes. Take the pan off the heat while the eggs still look a little wet, because they keep cooking in the hot pan. Scatter with the parsley.
Bring the pan to the table with the warm lavash and scoop it up. Mopping the pan with the bread is the whole point.
tip: Turkish cooks argue about whether the onion belongs, so leave it out if you are on the other side. Leave the cheese out for a plain menemen.
ingredients: Turkish sivri or any mild green pepper, sliced

name: Nan-o-panir-o-sabzi with walnuts, a boiled egg and fresh herbs
about: The classic Persian breakfast plate: warm lavash, salty feta, walnut halves and a soft-boiled egg, with a heap of fresh herbs and cucumber to roll up into little bites. Nothing to cook but an egg. The herbs bring **vitamin K and folate**, and the walnuts add plant omega-3.
steps: Lower the egg gently into a small pot of boiling water and cook for 6 minutes for a jammy yolk. Cool it under cold water and peel.
Wash the herbs and scallion and shake them dry. Leave the mint and parsley as whole sprigs, which is how they are served.
Slice the cucumber and arrange it on a plate with the herbs and scallion. Sprinkle the cucumber with a pinch of salt.
Put the feta and walnut halves on the side of the plate with the halved egg. Warm the lavash in a dry pan or the toaster.
Tear off a piece of bread, wrap a little feta, a walnut and a few herb leaves inside, and eat it as a small roll (this is called a loghmeh). Keep going until the plate is empty.
tip: Persian breakfast comes with sweet black tea. Boil the egg the night before and this takes 5 minutes. Fresh tarragon or basil on the plate is lovely if you find it.

name: Kuku sabzi, Persian herb frittata with barberries and yogurt
about: A thick, deep-green frittata packed with parsley, cilantro, dill, scallion and spinach, with dried fenugreek and tart barberries running through it. It is a Nowruz classic, and it makes two portions, so tomorrow's breakfast is cold wedges tucked into bread. The herbs bring **vitamin K, folate and iron** in a single sitting.
steps: Chop the parsley, cilantro, dill, scallion and spinach very finely. A few pulses in a food processor does it, and the pile should look like a lot more green than you expect.
Beat the eggs in a big bowl with the fenugreek, turmeric, pepper and salt. Fold in all the herbs and the drained barberries. It should be thick, more green than yellow.

Warm half the olive oil in a 20 to 22 cm non-stick, oven-safe pan over medium heat. Pour in the mixture, flatten the top and cover. Cook covered over low heat for 15 minutes, until the edges pull away from the pan and the top is almost set.
Heat the broiler. Brush the top with the rest of the oil and slide the pan under for 3 to 4 minutes, until the top is set and just golden. You can flip it with a plate instead if you prefer.
Let it cool for 5 minutes, then cut into wedges. Serve one portion warm with the yogurt and lavash.
Wrap the second portion for tomorrow. Cold kuku in lavash with a spoonful of yogurt is a very good breakfast sandwich.
tip: A handful of chopped walnuts folded in is traditional if you like crunch. If you cannot find barberries, a few chopped dried cranberries give a similar tang.
ingredients: green and white parts, finely chopped
rinsed, soaked in water for 5 minutes and drained

name: Antalya-style piyaz, white bean salad with egg and tahini
inspiredBy: Turkish piyaz, the white bean salad served with köfte, here as a lunch with a boiled egg and the tahini-lemon dressing they make in Antalya
about: Creamy white beans, juicy tomato and a lot of parsley under a lemony tahini dressing, with sumac onions and a halved boiled egg on top. It is a Turkish meze turned into lunch, and it is better after it sits for 10 minutes. The beans bring **fibre, folate and iron**, and the egg adds choline.
steps: Lower the egg into a small pot of boiling water and cook for 8 minutes, then cool it under cold water and peel.
Toss the sliced red onion with the sumac and a pinch of the salt, squeezing it with your fingers for a minute until it softens and turns pink. Leave it for 10 minutes.
Mash the garlic with the rest of the salt, then whisk it with the tahini, lemon juice, adding cold water a teaspoon at a time until it is pale and pourable like thin cream. Whisk in the olive oil.
Toss the white beans gently with the dressing and most of the parsley. Spread them on a plate.
Pile the tomato and sumac onions on top, add the halved egg, sprinkle with the Aleppo pepper and the rest of the parsley, and eat with the toasted lavash.
tip: Cooked from dried beans (about 70 g dry), it tastes even better. Flaked tinned tuna instead of the egg is a Turkish favourite too.
ingredients: from a tin, drained and rinsed

name: Mercimek çorbası, Turkish red lentil soup with mint and Aleppo oil
about: The soup every Turkish kitchen starts a meal with: red lentils, carrot, potato and onion blended silky smooth, with a lemon squeeze and a spoonful of sizzling olive oil, dried mint and Aleppo pepper on top. A peppery arugula (roka) salad and toasted bread make it lunch. The lentils bring **iron, folate and plant protein**, and the lemon helps you take up that iron.
steps: Warm half the olive oil in a medium pot over medium heat and soften the onion and carrot for 5 minutes. Stir in the cumin and a pinch of paprika for 30 seconds.
Add the lentils, potato, salt and about 600 ml (2½ cups) of water. Bring to a boil, skim off any foam, then simmer gently until everything is very soft, about 20 minutes.
Blend the soup smooth with an immersion blender (or in batches in a blender, leaving the lid vent open). If it is too thick, loosen it with hot water. Stir in half the lemon juice and taste for salt.
Warm the rest of the olive oil in a small pan with the dried mint and Aleppo pepper until it sizzles and turns red, 30 seconds. Spoon it over the soup.
Serve with the toasted lavash and the arugula, with the rest of the lemon squeezed over the leaves.
tip: Double or triple the soup and freeze the rest in single portions for up to 3 months.
ingredients: rinsed until the water runs clearer

name: Lahmacun-style flatbread with spiced beef, parsley salad and ayran
inspiredBy: Turkish lahmacun, with a whole-wheat lavash standing in for the thin dough so it takes 25 minutes
about: Whole-wheat lavash spread thin with a spiced beef, tomato and pepper topping and baked until crisp at the edges and still bendy in the middle, then rolled up with a handful of parsley, sumac onions and lemon, with a cold glass of ayran, as it is eaten in Turkey. The beef brings **iron, zinc and vitamin B12**, and the yogurt in the ayran brings calcium.
steps: Cut the beef into small cubes and pulse it in a food processor in short bursts until finely ground, or ask the butcher to grind it. Heat the oven to 230 C.
Chop the tomato, green pepper, onion and garlic, and blend or finely chop with the pepper paste into a thick, rough paste. Drain off any extra liquid so the lavash does not turn soggy.
Mix the paste with the beef, half the parsley (finely chopped), the Aleppo pepper, paprika, cumin, black pepper and most of the salt until it is sticky and well combined.
Cut the lavash in half if it is large, brush the tops lightly with water, then with half the oil, and spread the beef mixture over it in a thin, even layer, right out to the edges.
Bake on a tray for 6 to 8 minutes, until the edges are crisp and the meat is cooked through, but the middle is still bendy enough to roll.

Meanwhile toss the sliced red onion with the sumac, a pinch of salt, the rest of the parsley, the rest of the oil and half the lemon juice. Pile it on the hot lavash, squeeze over the rest of the lemon, roll up and eat with your hands.
Whisk the yogurt with 150 ml of cold water and a pinch of salt for the ayran, and pour it over ice.
tip: Blend the topping on Friday night and keep it covered in the fridge. On Saturday it is 10 minutes in the oven.
ingredients: half for the topping, half for the salad

name: Ghormeh sabzi, Persian herb stew with beef and kidney beans, with brown basmati
about: Iran's national stew: a deep green, savoury-sour pot of parsley, cilantro, scallion and spinach fried until dark with fenugreek (shanbalileh), with tender beef, kidney beans and a dried lime (limoo amani) for the sour note. It makes two portions, and it is even better tomorrow. The herbs and beans bring **iron, folate and vitamin K**, and the lime and lemon help you take up the iron.
steps: Warm a third of the olive oil in a heavy pot over medium heat. Cook the onion until golden, about 8 minutes, then stir in the turmeric, add the beef and brown it for 5 minutes.
Pour in enough water to cover the beef by 2 cm (about 3 cups for two portions). Add the pierced dried lime, the salt and pepper. Bring to a boil, cover and simmer gently for 1 hour.

While the beef simmers, warm the rest of the oil in a wide pan over medium-low heat. Fry the parsley, cilantro, scallion and spinach, stirring often, until they turn dark green and smell toasty, about 20 minutes. Stir in the fenugreek for the last 2 minutes. This slow frying is where the flavour comes from.

Tip the fried herbs and the kidney beans into the pot. Simmer uncovered for 25 to 30 minutes, until the beef is very tender and the sauce is thick and glossy. Taste, and add the lemon juice and a little salt until it is pleasantly sour.

For the rice, rinse the brown basmati and simmer it in a big pot of salted boiling water for 25 minutes, like pasta, then drain. Return it to the pot, wrap the lid in a clean tea towel and leave it for 10 minutes to steam and fluff up. Cook enough for both portions.
Serve the stew over the rice. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. The dried lime stays in the pot, and you can press it with a spoon on the plate for more sourness.
tip: Short on time? In a pressure cooker, cook the beef for 20 minutes, then add the herbs and beans and simmer for 10 minutes. You can also fry the herbs the night before.
ingredients: from a tin, drained and rinsed
one whole dried lime serves two portions, pierced a few times

name: Chicken köfte with bulgur pilav and çoban salatası
inspiredBy: Adana and Urfa köfte, which are lamb, made here with chicken thighs and a little bulgur pilav on the side
about: Garlicky, spiced chicken köfte shaped on skewers and cooked until browned, with a nutty bulgur pilav and a crunchy shepherd's salad of tomato, cucumber and pepper. It makes two portions, so tomorrow's lunch is already cooked. The chicken and bulgur bring **protein, niacin and fibre**, and the salad brings vitamin C.
steps: Cut the chicken into small cubes and pulse in a food processor in short bursts until finely ground and sticky, or ask the butcher to grind it. Squeeze the grated onion lightly, leaving it moist.

Mix the chicken with the onion, garlic, parsley, pepper paste, Aleppo pepper, cumin, sumac, black pepper and half the salt. Knead for 2 minutes, until sticky. Chill for at least 20 minutes, or up to a day.

For the pilav, warm a third of the oil in a small pot and toast the bulgur for 1 minute. Add the rest of the salt and 1.5 times its volume in hot water. Cover and simmer gently for 12 minutes, then leave it off the heat, covered, for 10 minutes. Make enough for both portions.
With wet hands, mould the chicken around skewers or into long fingers about 2 cm thick. Heat half the remaining oil in a non-stick pan over medium-high heat, or heat the broiler.
Cook the köfte, turning now and then, until browned all over and cooked through with no pink in the middle, 8 to 10 minutes.
For the çoban salatası, chop the tomato, cucumber, green pepper and red onion into small, even pieces. Toss with the rest of the oil, the lemon juice, a pinch of salt and a little chopped parsley.
Serve the köfte on the pilav with the salad. Pack the second portion of köfte and pilav for tomorrow, and chop the salad fresh then.
tip: Warm the leftover köfte and pilav in a pan with a splash of water. A spoonful of yogurt on the side is lovely if you have it.
ingredients: finely chopped, some for the salad

name: Cornmeal and hazelnut sardines with Black Sea kale and lemon potatoes
inspiredBy: Black Sea hamsi tava, fried fresh anchovies in cornmeal, made with sardines or fresh anchovies, a little of the region's hazelnut and karalahana (Black Sea kale)
about: Fresh sardines rolled in cornmeal and a little ground hazelnut, then pan-fried until golden and crisp, the way people on the Black Sea coast fry their anchovies, with garlicky kale and parsley-lemon potatoes. It is quick and punchy. The sardines bring **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, and the kale and hazelnuts bring calcium and vitamin E.
steps: Put the potatoes in a pot of cold salted water, bring to a boil and cook until just tender, about 12 to 15 minutes. Drain, then toss with half the lemon juice and the parsley.

While they cook, warm a third of the oil in a wide pan over medium heat and soften the onion for 5 minutes. Add the garlic and Aleppo pepper for 30 seconds, then the kale with a splash of water. Cover and cook until the kale is tender and bright, 8 to 10 minutes. Season with salt.
Pat the sardines very dry with paper towels and season with salt and pepper. Mix the cornmeal with the ground hazelnuts on a plate, roll the sardines in it and pat off the excess.

Warm the rest of the oil in a large non-stick pan over medium heat. Fry the sardines for 3 minutes a side, keeping the heat at medium because the ground hazelnut scorches, until the coating is golden and crisp and the flesh flakes.
Serve the sardines on the kale with the potatoes beside them and the rest of the lemon squeezed over everything.
tip: Fresh sardines are scarce. Whole frozen ones, thawed and patted dry, work. Ask the fishmonger to scale and gut them. They are small, so you will want 5 or 6.
ingredients: fresh, cleaned and gutted, heads off. Fresh anchovies work too
leaves stripped from the stems, sliced

name: Etli kuru fasulye, Turkish white bean stew with beef, kale and bulgur pilav
inspiredBy: Turkish etli kuru fasulye, with some Black Sea karalahana kale stirred in
about: Turkey's favourite home stew: tender white beans in a thick, savoury red pepper sauce with Aleppo pepper, a little beef and a handful of kale, served with bulgur pilav and a sumac onion salad on the side. It makes two portions, and it is even better the next day. The beans and kale bring **fibre, folate, iron and calcium**.
steps: Soak the beans in plenty of water overnight, or cover them with boiling water for 1 hour if you forgot. Drain them.

Warm half the oil in a heavy pot over medium heat and brown the beef for 5 minutes. Add the onion and carrot and cook until soft, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic, pepper paste and Aleppo pepper and stir for 2 minutes, until it darkens.

Add the beans with enough hot water to cover them by 3 cm, about 3 cups for two portions. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer gently for about 1 hour, until the beans are creamy and the beef is tender. Add the salt and pepper when the beans are nearly done.
Stir in the kale for the last 10 minutes and let the sauce reduce until thick.

For the pilav, warm the rest of the oil in a small pot, toast the bulgur for 1 minute, then add 1.5 times its volume in hot water and a pinch of salt. Cover and cook gently for 12 minutes, then leave it covered for 10 minutes. Make enough for both portions.
Toss the red onion with the sumac, the lemon juice and half the parsley and squeeze it with your fingers to soften. Serve the beans over the pilav with the onion salad and the rest of the parsley.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. It thickens overnight, so add a splash of water when you reheat.
tip: Short on time? In a pressure cooker, the soaked beans take about 25 minutes. Two 400 g tins of white beans work too, simmered for just 25 minutes. For a vegetarian version, leave out the beef.
ingredients: leaves stripped from the stems, sliced

name: Saffron salmon with sabzi polo style herb rice and grilled tomatoes
inspiredBy: Persian sabzi polo ba mahi, the Nowruz herb rice with fish, made with brown basmati and a baked salmon fillet
about: A saffron and lemon salmon fillet, baked until just flaky, on a bed of brown basmati rice steamed through with a mountain of parsley, dill, cilantro and scallion. Grilled tomatoes alongside, as in a Persian kebab house. The salmon brings **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, and the herb rice is a big hit of vitamin K.
steps: Rinse the rice and simmer it in plenty of salted boiling water for 25 minutes, like pasta. Drain it, return it to the pot, cover with a tea towel under the lid and leave it for 10 minutes to steam. If you have time, soak the rinsed rice for 30 minutes first.

Mash the garlic with a little of the salt. Mix it with the steeped saffron and its water, half the lemon juice, the turmeric, pepper and a teaspoon of the oil. Coat the salmon and leave it for 15 minutes.

Heat the oven to 220 C. Put the salmon skin-side down on a tray with the halved tomatoes, cut-sides up. Drizzle the tomatoes with a little oil and a pinch of salt. Roast for 10 to 12 minutes, until the salmon flakes and the tomato edges are charred.

Warm the rest of the oil in a small pan, stir in the fenugreek for 20 seconds, and fold it through the hot rice with the parsley, dill, cilantro and scallion and a pinch of salt. Return the rice to the pot, cover with the towel lid and steam on the lowest heat for 5 minutes, so the herbs wilt into the rice and it turns bright green.
Serve the salmon on the herb rice with the tomatoes and the rest of the lemon.
tip: Cook extra brown basmati the tea-towel way and keep it for 4 to 5 days in the fridge, or freeze it in portions.
ingredients: ground and steeped in 1 tbsp hot water

name: Fesenjan-inspired chicken with walnut and pomegranate, with brown basmati
inspiredBy: Persian fesenjan from Gilan, with a lighter hand with the walnuts and a brown basmati base
about: Chicken thighs slowly simmered in a rich, dark sauce of ground toasted walnuts and sweet-sour pomegranate molasses, with turmeric and cinnamon, and finished with fresh pomegranate seeds. It is the Persian celebration stew, and it is even better the next day. The walnuts bring **plant omega-3, magnesium and copper**.
steps: Toast the walnuts in a dry pan over medium heat for 4 minutes, until they smell nutty. Cool them, then grind to a coarse, damp-sand texture in a food processor, in short pulses so they do not turn to paste.
Warm the oil in a heavy pot over medium heat and cook the onion until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Stir in the turmeric, add the chicken and turn it for 3 minutes, until it just loses its pink.

Stir in the ground walnuts, the cinnamon, salt, pepper and just enough water to cover the chicken. Bring to a gentle simmer, cover with the lid slightly ajar, and cook for 40 minutes, stirring often so it does not catch. The sauce will darken and thicken.

Stir in the pomegranate molasses and the saffron water, and simmer for 20 minutes more, until the oil from the walnuts rises to the top and the chicken is very tender. Taste: it should be sour first, then sweet. Add a little more water if it has thickened too far.

For the rice, rinse the brown basmati and simmer it in plenty of salted boiling water for 25 minutes, then drain. Return it to the pot, wrap the lid in a tea towel and let it steam for 10 minutes. Make enough for both portions.
Serve the chicken over the rice, scattered with the pomegranate seeds. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. Warm it gently with a splash of water, because the sauce thickens overnight.
tip: Like most Persian stews it is even better made a day ahead. Pomegranate molasses varies by brand, so taste first. If it is too sharp, a small spoon of pekmez rounds it out.
ingredients: boneless, skinless thighs, cut in 4 cm pieces
ground and steeped in 1 tbsp hot water

name: Grilled mackerel (uskumru) with tahini sauce, sumac onions and arugula
inspiredBy: Turkish grilled mackerel, with a Hatay-style tahini tarator
about: A fat, oily mackerel fillet seared until the skin is crisp, then served the Turkish coastal way, with sumac onions, peppery arugula, tomato and warm lavash to tuck it into, plus a lemony tahini sauce borrowed from Hatay and the Levant. It takes 20 minutes. The mackerel brings **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, and the tahini and arugula add calcium.
steps: Toss the sliced red onion with the sumac, half the parsley, a pinch of salt and a third of the lemon juice. Squeeze it with your fingers until it softens and turns pink. Leave it while you cook.
Mash the garlic with a pinch of salt and whisk it with the tahini, half the remaining lemon juice and 2 to 3 tablespoons of cold water, until pale and pourable like thin cream.
Pat the mackerel dry and season both sides with salt, pepper and the Aleppo pepper. Rub the skin with a little of the oil.
Heat a heavy pan or the broiler on high. Cook the fillets skin-side down for 4 minutes without moving them, until the skin is crisp, then flip for 1 to 2 minutes, until just cooked through.
Dress the arugula and sliced tomato with the rest of the lemon juice, the rest of the oil and a pinch of salt.
Serve the mackerel on the sumac onions with the salad, a spoonful of the tahini sauce and the rest of the parsley, and the warm lavash alongside. Tuck some into a piece of bread if you like.
tip: Mackerel is strongly flavoured, so do not skip the lemon and the sumac onions. If you cannot find fresh mackerel, use sardines or trout.

name: Medjool dates stuffed with walnuts and hazelnuts
about: Soft dates stuffed with walnut halves and a hazelnut, the sweet nibble Persian and Turkish families serve with tea. The walnuts bring **plant omega-3 and magnesium**, the hazelnuts bring vitamin E, and the dates bring potassium.
steps: Slit the dates open, take out the pits and press a walnut half and a hazelnut or two into each date. Serve with a cup of tea.

name: Ayran with cucumber sticks
about: The salty, frothy Turkish yogurt drink, with dried mint and cucumber sticks on the side. It is **calcium and protein** in a glass.
steps: Whisk the yogurt with 130 ml of cold water, the salt and the dried mint until frothy, and serve over ice if you like.
Eat the cucumber sticks alongside.

name: A Medjool date stuffed with walnut and hazelnut
about: One soft date stuffed with a walnut half and a hazelnut, the small sweet bite that goes with a cup of tea. The walnut brings **plant omega-3**, the hazelnut brings vitamin E, and the date brings potassium.
steps: Slit the date open, take out the pit and press a walnut half and a hazelnut or two into it. Serve with a cup of tea.

name: Mast-o-khiar, cucumber yogurt with dill and mint
inspiredBy: Persian mast-o-khiar, with a little lavash to scoop
about: Cool, thick yogurt with grated cucumber, fresh dill and mint, with torn lavash for scooping. It is the Iranian answer to a hot afternoon. The yogurt brings **calcium and protein**, and the cucumber keeps it light.
steps: Squeeze the grated cucumber lightly. Stir it into the yogurt with the dill, mint and salt, and loosen with a spoonful of cold water.
Serve in a bowl with the torn lavash for scooping.

name: Yogurt with pekmez and dried figs
inspiredBy: Pekmezli yoğurt, the Turkish afternoon bowl, with Aegean dried figs
about: Thick yogurt with a drizzle of dark grape molasses (pekmez) and chopped dried figs, a simple Turkish afternoon treat. The yogurt brings **calcium and protein**, and the figs add fibre.
steps: Spoon the yogurt into a bowl, drizzle with the pekmez and scatter over the chopped figs.

name: Roasted chickpeas, leblebi style
inspiredBy: Turkish leblebi, the roasted chickpeas sold at every market, made from tinned chickpeas in the oven
about: Crunchy oven-roasted chickpeas with cumin, Aleppo pepper and lemon, in the style of the leblebi sold at Turkish nut shops. They bring **plant protein, fibre and folate**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C. Pat the chickpeas very dry and toss with the oil, cumin, Aleppo pepper and salt on a tray.
Roast for 25 to 30 minutes, shaking the tray halfway, until golden and crunchy. Squeeze over the lemon while they are hot. They crisp further as they cool.
tip: Roast a fresh tray on the day. They lose their crunch after 3 days in a jar.
ingredients: from a tin, drained and rinsed

name: Dried figs with hazelnuts
about: Aegean dried figs with hazelnuts from the Black Sea coast, a sweet and nutty Turkish tea-time plate. The hazelnuts bring **vitamin E and magnesium**, and the figs bring fibre and a little calcium.
steps: Serve the figs and hazelnuts together on a small plate. Toast the hazelnuts in a dry pan for 3 minutes first if you like.

name: Orange slices with cinnamon
about: Sliced orange with a pinch of cinnamon, a Persian-style fruit plate. The orange brings **vitamin C and folate**.
steps: Peel the orange and slice it into rounds. Sprinkle with the cinnamon and chill for 10 minutes if you have time.

name: Tahini and pekmez on warm lavash
inspiredBy: Turkish tahin-pekmez, tahini swirled with grape molasses
about: A thick swirl of tahini and pekmez (grape molasses) on warm whole-wheat lavash, a very Turkish sweet snack. The tahini brings **calcium, copper and healthy fats**.
steps: Warm the lavash. Spread the tahini over it, then drizzle with the pekmez and swirl them together with a knife. Fold and eat.

name: Dried figs with walnuts and hazelnuts
inspiredBy: Turkish incir ve ceviz, the classic pairing, with a few Black Sea hazelnuts
about: Chewy dried figs with walnut halves and a few hazelnuts, a classic Turkish and Persian pairing. The figs bring **fibre and a little calcium**, the walnuts bring plant omega-3, and the hazelnuts bring vitamin E.
steps: Tuck a walnut half into each fig, or serve them side by side on a plate with the hazelnuts.

name: Pomegranate seeds with walnuts
inspiredBy: the pomegranate and walnut pairing of fesenjan, as a snack
about: Ruby pomegranate seeds with a handful of walnut halves, the sweet-tart and rich pairing that Persian cooks love. The walnuts bring **plant omega-3 and magnesium**, and the pomegranate brings vitamin C.
steps: Tip the pomegranate seeds into a bowl and eat them with the walnut halves, a spoonful of each at a time.

name: Orange with toasted hazelnuts
about: Mediterranean oranges with toasted Black Sea hazelnuts, a simple Turkish pairing. The hazelnuts bring **vitamin E and magnesium** and the orange brings vitamin C.
steps: Toast the hazelnuts in a dry pan for 3 minutes, until fragrant. Peel and slice the orange and eat it with the nuts.

name: Huevos pericos with arepa de choclo and hot chocolate
inspiredBy: Colombian huevos pericos, with the arepa made from frozen corn and whole-grain cornmeal instead of precooked white flour
about: Soft scrambled eggs cooked with tomato and scallion, the everyday Bogotá breakfast, served with a sweet, golden arepa de choclo, a few slices of avocado and a mug of hot chocolate made with evaporated milk. The arepa is blended from sweet corn and whole-grain cornmeal, so it has a soft middle and a toasty crust. The eggs and avocado bring **protein, choline and vitamin E**, and the milk adds calcium.
steps: Blend the corn with a splash of water, about a tablespoon, until it is mostly smooth but still a little pebbly. Stir in the cornmeal and half the salt. Let the batter sit for 10 minutes while the cornmeal drinks up the corn juice and thickens to a thick pancake batter. If it looks loose, stir in another spoon of cornmeal.
Make the chocolate caliente: warm the evaporated milk with the same amount of water in a small pot, whisk in the cocoa and cinnamon, and simmer for 2 minutes until smooth. Keep it warm.
Dice the tomato and slice the scallion, keeping the white and green parts separate.

Brush a non-stick pan with a little of the oil over medium heat. Spoon in the batter in one or two mounds and flatten each to about 1 cm thick. Cook until the bottoms are golden, about 4 minutes, then flip and cook 3 to 4 minutes more, until they feel firm and smell like toasted corn.
Wipe the pan, warm the rest of the oil and soften the scallion whites and tomato with a pinch of salt until the juices mostly cook off, about 4 minutes.
Beat the eggs, pour them in and stir gently with a spatula until they are just set and still creamy, about 1 minute. Stir through the green scallion.
Serve the eggs with the arepas, the sliced avocado and the hot chocolate.
tip: Blend the arepa batter the night before and keep it in the fridge; stir in a spoon of water in the morning and breakfast takes 10 minutes. A few cubes of cheese inside the arepa are classic if you want them.
ingredients: evaporated milk, thinned with an equal amount of water

name: Cuscuz de milho with fried egg, grilled coalho and papaya
inspiredBy: Cuscuz nordestino from northeast Brazil, steamed cornmeal with egg and grilled queijo coalho, made with coarse whole-grain cornmeal in place of flocão
about: Fluffy steamed cornmeal, the breakfast of Brazil's northeast, topped with a fried egg, golden-brown queijo coalho and juicy tomato, with sweet papaya and a mug of chocolate quente made with evaporated milk on the side. It needs no flour and no tapioca, only cornmeal, water and a steamer. The whole-grain corn and egg bring **fibre, protein and choline**, and the cheese and milk bring calcium.
steps: Stir the cornmeal with half the salt in a bowl. Sprinkle over water a spoonful at a time, tossing with a fork, until the meal looks like damp sand. Let it rest 15 minutes, so the coarse grains soften.
Make the chocolate quente: warm the evaporated milk with the same amount of water in a small pot, whisk in the cocoa, and simmer for 2 minutes until smooth. Keep it warm.

Steam the damp meal in a steamer basket or fine sieve lined with a damp cloth, set over simmering water and covered, for about 20 minutes, until tender and fluffy. Fluff it with a fork halfway through.
While it steams, slice the tomato and toss it with half the lime juice, a pinch of salt and the cilantro. Cube the papaya and squeeze the rest of the lime over it.
Brown the coalho slices in a dry non-stick pan, about 1 to 2 minutes per side, until golden and a little crusty. Lift them out.
Warm the oil in the same pan and fry the eggs, sunny side up, until the whites are set and the yolks are still soft.
Pack the cuscuz into a bowl or plate, top with the eggs and cheese, and serve with the tomato, the papaya and the hot chocolate.
tip: Steam it the night before, then warm it covered with a spoon of water for 1 minute in the morning. Flocão (coarse flaked cornmeal) is the traditional meal and is sold at Latin and Brazilian shops. Queijo coalho grills without melting; queso panela, halloumi or paneer will do if you cannot find it.
ingredients: evaporated milk, thinned with an equal amount of water

name: Quinua con leche with banana and a little cocoa
inspiredBy: Peruvian quinua con leche, the warm quinoa and milk breakfast drink sold from street carts, thickened into a spoonable porridge
about: Quinoa simmered in evaporated milk with cinnamon, clove and a little cocoa until it turns creamy, then stirred with ripe banana. It is the warm, comforting breakfast of the Andes, with a chocolate hint. The quinoa brings **iron, magnesium and protein**, and the milk adds calcium.
steps: Rinse the quinoa in a fine sieve under cold running water for a full minute, until the water runs clear. This washes off the bitter coating.

Put the quinoa, the evaporated milk, about three times the quinoa's volume of water, the cocoa, the cinnamon and the clove in a small pot, and whisk so the cocoa dissolves. Bring to a gentle simmer, then cook on low, stirring now and then, until the grains are tender with a little white tail, about 18 minutes.
Mash half the banana into the porridge and cook 3 minutes more, until it is thick, glossy and creamy. The banana is the only sweetener, so add a little honey or sugar if you like.
Spoon into a bowl and top with the sliced banana. Add a splash of hot milk if you like it looser.
tip: Cook a double batch the night before and keep it covered in the fridge for up to 3 days; reheat with a splash of water. Ripe papaya can stand in for the banana.
ingredients: evaporated milk, thinned with an equal amount of water

name: Ceviche-style cooked cod with camote and corn
inspiredBy: Peruvian ceviche, with the cod lightly poached first, served with sweet potato and corn in the classic way
about: Tender cubes of cod in a sharp lime, ají amarillo and cilantro marinade, with sweet potato, sweet corn and crisp red onion. The cod is lightly poached so it is cooked through, and the lime marinade still makes it taste like ceviche. Cod brings **lean protein and iodine**, and the lime, cilantro and onion keep it zingy.
steps: Boil the sweet potato chunks in salted water for about 8 minutes, add the corn kernels, and boil 4 minutes more, until the sweet potato is just tender when poked with a fork. Drain and let them cool.
Soak the sliced red onion in a bowl of ice-cold water for 5 minutes to take the sting out, then drain well.

Bring a small pot of salted water to a simmer, slip in the cod cubes and poach for about 90 seconds, until just opaque. Drain well, spread on a plate and chill in the fridge for 5 minutes, so they do not keep cooking.
In a bowl, stir the lime juice with the ají amarillo paste, the grated garlic, half the cilantro and the salt. Add the cod and turn it gently. Let it sit for 10 minutes, so it soaks up the marinade.
Serve the cod with its marinade, the onion, the sweet potato and the corn, with the rest of the cilantro on top. Eat right away.
tip: Ají amarillo paste is sold at Latin grocers and online. Use any firm, mild white fish. Poach the cod and boil the camote and corn on Sunday night, then marinate for 10 minutes at lunch.

name: Quinoa solterito with black beans, corn and queijo coalho
inspiredBy: Peruvian and Bolivian solterito, the bean, corn and cheese salad, with quinoa and black beans making it a full meal, and red pepper in place of rocoto
about: Fluffy quinoa tossed with black beans, sweet corn, tomato, red pepper, red onion, avocado and diced queijo coalho in a lime, oregano and olive oil dressing. It is the kind of salad that sits happily in a lunchbox. The quinoa and beans together bring **iron, folate and protein**, and the lime helps your body use that iron.
steps: Rinse the quinoa and simmer it in twice its volume of water with a pinch of salt until the grains are tender and have popped their little white tails, about 15 minutes. Drain if needed, fluff and let cool.
Use black beans from your Sunday pot (see the plan notes), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed.
Whisk the lime juice, olive oil, oregano and a pinch of salt in a large bowl.
Add the quinoa, beans, corn, tomato, red pepper and onion and toss well. Fold in the cilantro and top with the avocado and the diced coalho.
tip: Make a double batch of the salad base without the avocado and cheese; it keeps 3 days. Add them just before you eat.

name: Pollo a la parrilla with chimichurri, roasted sweet potato and ensalada criolla
inspiredBy: Argentine grilled chicken with chimichurri, cooked in a grill pan, with sweet potato (batata) and a tomato and onion salad on the side
about: Seared chicken breast, juicy inside, spooned with a sharp, garlicky parsley chimichurri, next to roasted sweet potato and a tomato and onion salad dressed with the same sauce. It tastes like a Sunday asado on a weekday. The chicken brings **protein and niacin**, and the big handful of parsley brings iron and vitamin K.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the sweet potato wedges with a quarter of the olive oil and a pinch of salt, spread them on a tray and roast until soft inside and browned at the edges, about 30 minutes, turning once.

Chop the parsley very finely, with the garlic, and stir them in a small bowl with the oregano, cayenne, vinegar, most of the remaining olive oil and half the salt. Loosen it with 1 tablespoon of warm water, as Argentines do. That is your chimichurri. Let it sit while the chicken cooks, so the flavours settle together.

Slice the breast in half horizontally into two thin cutlets, so it cooks quickly and stays juicy. Season with the rest of the salt and a little oil. Cook in a hot cast-iron or grill pan, about 4 minutes a side, until browned and the juices run clear.
Rest the chicken for 5 minutes, then slice it.
Toss the tomato and onion with a spoon of the chimichurri. Serve the chicken with a generous spoonful of chimichurri on top, with the sweet potato and the salad.
tip: Chimichurri keeps 5 days in the fridge and is great on any grilled meat or fish; make a double batch. Skinless chicken thigh works too and is more forgiving, so cook it a few minutes longer. Roast the sweet potato and make the chimichurri on Tuesday night while the salmon roasts. At lunch, sear the chicken in 10 minutes.

name: Feijoada made light, with collards, orange and vinagrete
inspiredBy: Brazilian feijoada completa, with lean pork and a little smoked sausage instead of the many cuts of salted and smoked meat, and brown rice
about: A deep, smoky black bean stew with tender pork and a little smoked sausage, served over rice with garlicky collards, juicy orange slices and a sharp tomato vinagrete. Lean pork and just a little sausage keep it lighter than the Saturday classic. The black beans and collards bring **fibre, iron, folate and calcium**, and the orange and tomato help your body absorb the iron.
steps: From dry beans: drain the soaked beans and put them in a big pot with the pork, the sausage, the bay leaf, a big piece of onion and water to cover by 4 cm. Bring to a boil, skim off the foam, then simmer partly covered until the beans are very tender and the pork is falling apart, about 1 hour 15 minutes. Add the salt for the last 15 minutes.
From the Sunday pot: simmer the pork, sausage, bay leaf and onion piece alone in water for 40 minutes, until the pork is tender. Add the cooked beans with their liquid, and simmer 20 minutes more.

Soften most of the remaining onion in half the oil for about 6 minutes, then add half the garlic and the smoked paprika and cook 1 minute. Stir it all into the pot with the pepper. Mash a few spoonfuls of beans against the side of the pot and simmer 15 more minutes, until the stew is thick and glossy.
Use a tub of Sunday rice, or start the rice first: cook 30 g of dry brown rice in twice its volume of salted water, covered, until tender, about 35 minutes.
Roll up the collard leaves and slice them into very thin ribbons. Stir-fry them in the rest of the oil with the remaining garlic for 2 to 3 minutes, until bright green and just wilted.
Dice the tomato with a little raw onion and stir with the vinegar, cilantro and a pinch of salt. Let it sit 10 minutes.
Serve the beans over the rice with the collards, the orange slices and the vinagrete. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: With the Sunday beans this is a 50-minute dinner, and a pressure cooker does the soaked beans and pork in about 35 minutes. Keep the vinagrete and orange fresh for the leftover lunch, and warm the stew with a splash of water.
ingredients: soaked overnight, or cooked beans from the Sunday pot
lean shoulder, trimmed and cut in 3 cm chunks
smoked pork sausage (linguiça calabresa or kielbasa), in thin rounds
half in the pot, the rest for the sofrito and the vinagrete

name: Baked salmon with pebre, potatoes and garlicky acelga
inspiredBy: Chilean salmon a lo pobre, with roasted potatoes in place of the fries, the egg left off, and a fresh pebre
about: Salmon baked on a tray with golden potatoes, with sweet caramelized onions, garlicky acelga (Swiss chard) and a spoonful of pebre, the Chilean table salsa of tomato, cilantro and chile. Chile farms much of the world's salmon, and pebre goes on everything. Salmon brings **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, and the chard brings vitamin A and K.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the potatoes with a third of the olive oil and a pinch of the salt. Spread them on a tray and roast for 15 minutes.
Slice half the onion and cook it slowly in a pan with a little oil and a pinch of salt, stirring now and then, until deeply golden and sweet, about 15 minutes.

Make the pebre: finely dice the tomato and the rest of the onion, chop the cilantro and stir them with the cayenne, a little of the garlic, the lime juice, most of the remaining oil and a pinch of salt. Let it sit.

Move the potatoes to one side of the tray. Rub the salmon with the last of the oil, the oregano, pepper and a pinch of salt and set it skin side down on the tray. Roast 10 to 12 minutes, until the fish flakes easily and the potatoes are golden.
Meanwhile, wilt the chard ribbons in a hot pan with a splash of water, the rest of the garlic and a pinch of salt until bright green and tender, about 4 minutes.
Plate the salmon and potatoes with the greens, top the fish with the caramelized onions and spoon over the pebre.
tip: Pebre keeps 3 days in the fridge and is good on everything. A fried egg on top makes it a proper a lo pobre.
ingredients: half sliced for the pan, half for the pebre

name: Argentine lentil guiso with chorizo and greens
inspiredBy: Argentine guiso de lentejas, a thick stew of lentils, chorizo, potato and vegetables, with less sausage and a handful of greens
about: A hearty, paprika-scented lentil stew with a little chorizo, potato and sweet pepper, finished with tender greens and a splash of vinegar. It is a classic cold-weather dish from Argentina and Uruguay, and it tastes even better the next day. The lentils and greens bring **iron, folate and fibre**, and the vinegar and tomato help your body absorb the iron.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a heavy pot and brown the chorizo for 3 minutes, until it has rendered some of its red fat.
Add the onion and pepper and cook, stirring, until soft, about 8 minutes. Stir in the garlic, paprika, cumin and oregano and cook for 1 minute, until fragrant.
Add the lentils, the chopped tomatoes, the bay leaf and enough water to cover everything by about 2 cm, roughly 800 ml for two portions. Bring to a boil, then simmer partly covered for 15 minutes.
Add the potatoes and keep simmering until the lentils and potatoes are both tender and the stew is thick, about 15 minutes. Add a splash of water if it gets too thick.
Stir in the greens, the salt and the pepper and cook 4 minutes, until the greens are tender. Take off the heat and stir in the vinegar.
Ladle into bowls. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Add the salt and vinegar near the end, since they can keep lentils firm. The guiso thickens in the fridge, so loosen it with a splash of water when you reheat.

name: Sardines with boiled yuca, salsa criolla and avocado
inspiredBy: the Peruvian pairing of boiled yuca with salsa criolla, with canned sardines as the main
about: Soft boiled yuca and creamy avocado with whole sardines, all topped with a sharp salsa criolla of red onion, tomato, lime, ají amarillo and cilantro. It takes about 40 minutes, or 20 with frozen yuca, and tastes like the coast. Sardines with their soft bones bring **omega-3, calcium and vitamin D**, and the lime and onion bring the brightness.
steps: Cut the yuca into chunky pieces and boil in well-salted water until a fork goes in easily, about 20 to 25 minutes. Drain, and cut out any tough core thread you find.

Make the salsa criolla: toss the sliced onion with the lime juice, the ají amarillo paste, the oil, the tomato, most of the cilantro and a pinch of salt. Let it sit for 10 minutes, so the onion softens and turns pink.
Pile the warm yuca on a plate, set the sardines beside it and add the avocado.
Spoon the salsa criolla over the sardines and yuca and finish with the rest of the cilantro.
tip: Frozen peeled yuca is already prepped and cooks in about 15 minutes. A boiled potato or a sweet potato works too.
ingredients: two small tins (about 3.75 oz each), drained, with the soft bones

name: Lomo saltado with roasted potatoes and brown rice
inspiredBy: Peruvian lomo saltado, the chifa stir-fry of beef, onion and tomato, with roasted potatoes in place of fries and brown rice
about: Strips of sirloin seared hot with red onion, tomato and ají amarillo, splashed with soy and vinegar and tossed with golden potato wedges, over a little brown rice. It is a Lima favourite, born of Chinese-Peruvian cooking, and it cooks in minutes once the prep is done. The beef brings **iron, zinc and B12**, and the tomato and ají bring vitamin C.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the potato wedges with a third of the oil and the salt and roast on a tray until golden and tender, about 30 minutes, turning once.
Use a tub of Sunday rice, or cook 30 g of dry brown rice in twice its volume of salted water, covered, until tender, about 35 minutes.
Toss the beef strips with the soy sauce, half the vinegar, the garlic, the cumin and the pepper and let them sit for 10 minutes.
Heat a large pan or wok until it is properly hot. Sear the beef in two batches in half the remaining oil, 1 to 2 minutes each, so it browns instead of stewing. Lift it out onto a plate.
Add the rest of the oil to the pan and stir-fry the onion wedges with the ají amarillo paste for 2 minutes, until they just soften but stay crisp at the edges. Add the tomato wedges for 1 minute.
Return the beef and its juices with the rest of the vinegar and toss over the highest heat for 30 seconds, so it just coats. Then fold in the roasted potatoes and the cilantro.
Serve over the rice. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Cut the beef and veg while the oven heats, and cook the stir-fry in two batches for two portions. The potatoes soften as the leftovers sit, so reheat everything in a hot pan, not the microwave.
ingredients: trimmed, sliced across the grain in thin strips

name: Moqueca de cavala with garlicky collards and brown rice
inspiredBy: moqueca capixaba from Espírito Santo, made with urucum, tomato and cilantro, without coconut or dendê
about: Mackerel simmered capixaba style, layered with tomato, onion, pepper, cilantro and scallion in urucum-red olive oil, served over brown rice with a side of garlicky couve. It is a weekend dish, but it is mostly waiting while the pot does the work. The mackerel brings **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, and the collards bring calcium.
steps: Put the fish in a bowl with the lime juice, a third of the garlic, a third of the salt and the pepper. Let it marinate for 15 minutes.
Use a tub of Sunday rice, or start the rice first: cook 30 g of dry brown rice in twice its volume of salted water, covered, until tender, about 35 minutes.

Warm two-thirds of the oil in a wide, shallow pot over medium-low heat. Stir in the colorau for 20 seconds, until it turns the oil orange-red. Make layers of onion rings, pepper rings, the tomato slices, the scallion and half the cilantro, sprinkling in a third of the garlic and a pinch of the salt as you go.
Pour 4 tablespoons of water over the vegetables, cover and simmer on low for 10 minutes, until the vegetables begin to soften.

Nestle the fish into the sauce, spoon some of the sauce over it, cover again and simmer gently for 8 to 10 minutes, until the fish flakes easily. Shake the pot now and then rather than stirring, so the pieces stay whole.
Meanwhile, roll the collard leaves and slice them into thin ribbons. Stir-fry in the rest of the oil with the remaining garlic and salt for 3 minutes, until bright green.
Scatter the rest of the cilantro over the stew. Serve with the rice and the collards, and pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Brazilians would use cavala (king mackerel) or any firm fish; Atlantic mackerel is richer in omega-3 and easier to find. Colorau (urucum powder) is sold at Brazilian and Latin shops. In Espírito Santo it is cooked in a clay pot. For a Bahian touch, swap a teaspoon of the oil for dendê (red palm oil) and add a spoonful of coconut milk.
ingredients: skin on, cut in 4 cm pieces

name: Ajiaco-inspired chicken and potato soup with corn and avocado
inspiredBy: Colombian ajiaco santafereño, with a simpler mix of potatoes, with avocado as in Bogotá, and lime in place of the cream and capers
about: A thick, golden chicken and potato soup from Bogotá, with sweet corn, plenty of cilantro and a creamy slice of avocado, brightened with a squeeze of lime at the table. It is the dish Colombians crave on cold days. The chicken brings **protein and niacin**, and the potatoes and corn bring potassium and fibre.
steps: Put the chicken, the scallion whites, the garlic, the guascas and the thin potato slices in a pot with water to cover by about 3 cm. Bring to a boil, skim, then simmer gently for 20 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through and the sliced potato has begun to dissolve into the broth.
Lift out the chicken and shred it with two forks.
Add the potato chunks and the corn to the pot and simmer until the potatoes are tender, about 15 minutes. The soup should be thick and golden.
Return the chicken to the pot with the salt, the pepper and most of the cilantro, and warm through for 3 minutes.
Ladle into a deep bowl. Top with the avocado, the green scallion, the rest of the cilantro and a squeeze of lime.
tip: Make double and freeze a portion, without the avocado. Guascas are sold dried at Colombian shops; a pinch of oregano is a distant stand-in.
ingredients: half peeled and sliced thin, half in chunks
a small cob, in 3 pieces, or the same weight of frozen kernels

name: Mamão with lime
about: Cool, sweet papaya with a good squeeze of lime, the way it is served at a Brazilian breakfast table. Papaya brings **vitamin C and folate**.
steps: Scoop out the seeds and cut the papaya into cubes or wedges.
Squeeze the lime juice over the top.

name: Açaí na tigela with banana and papaya
about: A frozen açaí bowl blended with banana and topped with sliced banana, papaya and crushed peanuts, as served at Brazilian juice bars. It is thick and cold, and since unsweetened açaí is earthy, ripe banana is the sweetener. Açaí brings **fibre and antioxidants**, and the peanuts add vitamin E.
steps: Run the frozen pulp under warm water for a few seconds to loosen it, then blend with half the banana until thick and smooth, adding a splash of water only if the blender stalls.
Spoon into a bowl and top with the sliced banana, the papaya and the crushed peanuts. Eat right away, before it melts.
ingredients: frozen unsweetened pulp, a standard pack
half in the blender, half sliced

name: Choclo con queso
about: Warm sweet corn kernels with a slab of queijo coalho and a squeeze of lime, the street snack of the Peruvian Andes. It is salty, sweet and chewy. Corn brings **fibre**, and the cheese brings calcium.
steps: Boil the corn kernels in plenty of unsalted water until tender and bright yellow, about 5 minutes. Drain.
Toss with the salt and the lime and eat warm with the queijo coalho.
ingredients: frozen kernels, or fresh off the cob

name: Maní with lime and ají
about: A small handful of roasted peanuts tossed warm with lime juice, salt and a pinch of cayenne. Peanuts bring **vitamin E, magnesium and protein**.
steps: Warm the peanuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until fragrant.
Toss with the lime juice and cayenne in a bowl.

name: Banana with peanuts and cinnamon
about: A ripe banana sliced over a spoonful of chopped roasted peanuts, with a dusting of cinnamon. It is sweet, salty and filling. The banana brings **potassium**, and the peanuts bring vitamin E.
steps: Slice the banana into a bowl.
Chop the peanuts, scatter them over and dust with the cinnamon.

name: Camote asado with toasted pepitas and lime
about: Sweet potato roasted until its edges caramelize, with a handful of toasted pumpkin seeds (pepas de zapallo) and a squeeze of lime, a roasted snack that pairs well with a salty crunch. Sweet potato brings **vitamin A and fibre**, and the pepitas bring iron, zinc and magnesium.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the sweet potato rounds with the oil and half the salt.
Roast on a tray until soft and caramelized at the edges, about 25 minutes, turning once.
Toast the pepitas in a dry pan over medium heat until they puff and pop, about 3 minutes.
Scatter the pepitas over the sweet potato, sprinkle with the rest of the salt and squeeze over the lime.

name: Naranja with cinnamon
about: Juicy orange segments with a dusting of cinnamon, a simple, refreshing way to finish a meal or fill a gap. Orange brings **vitamin C and folate**.
steps: Peel the oranges and cut them into rounds or segments.
Dust with the cinnamon.

name: Pepas de zapallo tostadas, with salt and ají
about: A small handful of pumpkin seeds toasted in a dry pan until they puff and pop, then tossed with salt and a pinch of cayenne. They are a common snack from Peru to Chile. Pumpkin seeds bring **iron, zinc and magnesium**.
steps: Toast the pumpkin seeds in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring, until they puff up and start to pop, about 3 minutes.
Toss with the cayenne and the salt while they are still warm.

name: Camote asado with cinnamon and lime
about: Sweet potato roasted until its edges caramelize, with a pinch of cinnamon and a squeeze of lime. Sweet potato brings **vitamin A and fibre**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the sweet potato rounds with the oil.
Roast on a tray until soft and caramelized at the edges, about 25 minutes, turning once.
Dust with the cinnamon and squeeze over the lime.

name: Arepita de choclo con queso
about: A small, sweet corn arepa with a little queijo coalho inside, cooked on a griddle until golden. It is the kind of arepa you buy hot from a Colombian street cart. Corn and cheese together bring **fibre, protein and calcium**.
steps: Blend the corn with a splash of water until mostly smooth. Stir in the cornmeal and the salt and let it sit for 10 minutes to thicken.
Fold in the cubes of queijo coalho.
Brush a non-stick pan with the oil over medium heat. Spoon in the batter and flatten to about 1 cm thick. Cook until golden, about 4 minutes a side, until the cheese is soft inside.

name: Toasted corn with lime and salt
about: Corn kernels toasted in a pan until golden and blistered, then tossed with lime and salt, in the spirit of Peruvian cancha. It is toasty, sweet and a little chewy. Corn brings **fibre and B vitamins**.
steps: Pat the corn kernels very dry with a clean towel.
Toast them in a wide pan with the oil over medium-high heat, stirring often, until golden and blistered, about 10 minutes. It spits, so keep a lid ajar.
Toss with the lime juice and the salt while still warm.
ingredients: frozen kernels, thawed and patted very dry

name: Chickpea sundal
inspiredBy: Tamil kadalai sundal
about: Warm chickpeas tossed with mustard seed, curry leaves, green chili and fresh coconut, the way they are served as a temple snack in Tamil Nadu. It is simple and savoury, with **protein and fibre** from the chickpeas.
steps: Warm the oil in a pan, add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then add the hing, curry leaves and finely chopped green chili for a few seconds.
Add the chickpeas and the salt and stir for 3 minutes, until hot.
Take off the heat and stir in the coconut and lemon juice. Eat warm.

name: Spiced neer mor
inspiredBy: Tamil neer mor, Kerala sambaram
about: Thin, cooling spiced buttermilk made from curd, ginger, green chili and curry leaf, the drink every South Indian household has in the afternoon. It is salty, sour and refreshing, with **calcium and protein**.
steps: Whisk the curd with about half a cup of cold water until it is smooth and pourable.
Crush the ginger, green chili and curry leaf together in a mortar or mini blender. Stir them into the buttermilk with the hing, cumin and salt.
Chill for 10 minutes if you have time, and serve over ice.

name: Guava with chili, lemon and almonds
inspiredBy: South Indian and Sri Lankan street-cart guava
about: Crisp, fragrant guava wedges with a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of chili powder and salt, the way they are sold on the street from Chennai to Colombo, with a few soaked almonds for crunch. It is sweet, sour and spicy, and it gives you **more vitamin C than an orange** plus **vitamin E** from the almonds.
steps: Cut the guava into wedges and put them on a plate with the drained almonds.
Squeeze the lemon over, then sprinkle with the chili powder and salt.
ingredients: soaked in water for a few hours or overnight

name: Steamed sweet potato with chili and lime
inspiredBy: Kerala and Tamil steamed kizhangu (tubers)
about: Sweet potato steamed until tender and tossed with a squeeze of lemon, a pinch of chili powder and fresh coconut, the way tubers are eaten as a snack in Kerala and Tamil Nadu. It is soft, sweet and a little spicy, and it is loaded with **vitamin A**.
steps: Steam the sweet potato chunks for 12 to 15 minutes, until a knife slides in easily.
Toss with the lemon juice, chili powder, salt and coconut and eat warm.

name: Kerala pepper egg fry
inspiredBy: Kerala mutta pepper fry
about: Boiled eggs tossed in a hot pan with onion, curry leaves and plenty of cracked black pepper, a tea-shop favourite in Kerala that works just as well at home. It is peppery and savoury, with **protein and choline**.
steps: Hard-boil the eggs for 9 minutes, cool them in cold water and peel. Halve them.
Warm the oil in a small pan, add the onion, the turmeric and the curry leaves (stand back, they spit) and cook until the onion is golden, about 4 minutes.
Add the pepper and salt, then the eggs, cut side down, and toss for 1 to 2 minutes, until coated and a little crisp at the edges.

name: Pesarattu with ginger chutney and curd
inspiredBy: Andhra pesarattu, the green moong dosa, with allam pachadi
about: A crisp, golden dosa made from soaked whole green moong blitzed with ginger, green chili and cumin, served the Andhra way with a sharp allam pachadi (ginger chutney) and a big bowl of curd. There is no fermenting, only an overnight soak. The moong and curd give you **plenty of protein, folate and iron** before nine in the morning.
steps: The night before, rinse the moong and soak it in plenty of cold water for at least 6 hours. Drain well in the morning.

Blend the moong with a third of the ginger, the green chili, the cumin, half the salt and about half a cup of water, until the batter is smooth and pourable, like thin pancake batter. It does not need to ferment.

Make the chutney: pound the rest of the ginger in a mortar with the tamarind, the rest of the salt and a splash of water until it is thick and spoonable. It should taste sharp and hot. Scrape it into a bowl.

Now the tempering, called thalippu or tadka. Warm a teaspoon of the oil in a small pan, add the mustard seeds and the dried chili and let them pop for a few seconds, then add the hing and the curry leaves (stand back, they spit). Pour the sizzling oil over the chutney. Hot oil wakes up the spices and gives the chutney its smell.

Warm a non-stick pan over medium heat and wipe it with a little oil. Pour in half the batter and spread it into a thin round with the back of the ladle. Scatter on half the onion, drizzle a few drops of oil around the edge and cook until the underside is crisp and golden and the top looks dry, about 3 minutes. You do not need to flip it. Repeat with the rest.
Serve the pesarattu hot, with the chutney and the curd.
tip: A pinch of jaggery in the chutney is traditional, because allam pachadi is sweet, sour and hot. Pesarattu is often filled with a spoonful of upma, which is called an MLA pesarattu.
ingredients: a third for the batter, the rest for the chutney
finely chopped, for sprinkling on the dosa

name: Kerala prawn roast with green bean thoran and red rice
inspiredBy: Kerala chemmeen roast and beans thoran, served as a home lunch plate
about: Prawns tossed in a dark, glossy masala of slow-browned onion, tomato, ginger and black pepper, with a dry stir-fry of green beans and fresh coconut and a portion of red rice. It is the kind of plate you find at a Kerala home lunch. The prawns bring **lean protein, iodine and selenium**, and the beans and coconut bring fibre.
steps: Rinse the red rice and cook it in plenty of boiling water until tender, about 35 minutes, then drain. Red rice takes longer than white, so start it first.
Pat the prawns dry and toss them with the turmeric, a pinch of the salt and half the pepper.

Warm half the coconut oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Add the onion with a pinch of salt and a splash of water and cook, stirring, until deep golden brown, about 10 minutes. Add a spoonful of water whenever it starts to catch. Browning the onion well is what makes a roast taste like a roast.

Add the ginger, half the curry leaves, the chili powder and the rest of the pepper and stir for a minute. Add the tomato and a splash of water and cook until it breaks down into a thick, jammy masala, about 8 minutes.
Add the prawns and toss for 3 to 4 minutes, until they curl and turn pink and the masala clings to them. Set aside.

For the thoran, warm the rest of the coconut oil in a second pan. Add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then the rest of the curry leaves (stand back, they spit). Add the green beans, a pinch of salt and a splash of water, cover and cook for 5 minutes. Uncover, stir in the coconut, crushed with a spoonful of the onion and a pinch of turmeric, and cook for 1 minute more.
Serve the prawn roast and the thoran with the red rice.
tip: Cook the rice and brown the onion masala on Sunday night. At lunch, the prawns and thoran take 10 minutes. Keep the pan uncovered at the end of the thoran, since it is meant to be dry.
ingredients: Kerala matta rice, or any red rice
red chili powder, Kashmiri if you like it milder

name: Vegetable sambar with brown rice
inspiredBy: Tamil sambar, the everyday lentil and vegetable stew
about: Toor dal simmered with drumstick, pumpkin and spinach in a tangy tamarind broth, finished with a sizzling tempering of mustard seed, dried red chilies, hing and curry leaves. It is the soul of the Tamil table. The dal and vegetables bring **protein, fibre and folate** in one pot, and the second portion is tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Rinse the dal and simmer it in a covered pot with plenty of water until completely soft, about 35 minutes (or 12 minutes in a pressure cooker). Mash it with the back of a spoon.
Meanwhile, rinse the brown rice and cook it in plenty of boiling water until tender, about 30 minutes, then drain.

In a second pot, simmer the onion, drumstick and pumpkin with the tamarind, sambar powder, salt and about 2 cups of water until the vegetables are tender but still holding their shape, about 12 minutes.
Stir the mashed dal and the spinach into the vegetables and simmer for 5 minutes, adding water as needed until the spinach has wilted and it is a pourable, soupy stew.

Now the tempering (thalippu), which gives sambar its fragrance. Warm the oil in a small pan, add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then the dried chilies, hing and curry leaves (stand back, they spit). The moment the leaves crackle, pour the sizzling oil into the sambar.
Serve the sambar over the rice. Pack the second portion, with its rice, for tomorrow's lunch. Sambar thickens overnight, so add a splash of water when you reheat.
tip: Scrape the soft flesh of the drumstick off the tough pod with your teeth, and leave the pod on your plate. A small pinch of jaggery rounds off the tamarind nicely if you keep some in the pantry.
ingredients: cut into 5 cm lengths, frozen is fine
small shallots if you can find them, halved
roughly chopped, as in a keerai sambar
